0.title: Introduction
0.body: What's up with the name? The title of this book is taken from Italo Calvino’s The Castle of Crossed Destinies (Italian: Il castello dei destini incrociati). The experimental novel’s narrative details a group of pilgrims who find themselves unable to speak. Thus impaired, they use a set of tarot cards to illustrate their backgrounds and tell each other stories. Because this game also uses tarot cards to tell stories, the allusion seemed apt. The forest’s thickness is lessening, with room for paths of turned earth, rectangular pits, a whiteness as of mushrooms peeping from the ground. With horror we see from the thirteenth tarot that the underbrush is fertilized with half-withered corpses and fleshless bones. “Why, where have you brought me, Fool? This is a cemetery!” And the Fool says, pointing to the invertebrate fauna feeding in the graves: “Here a monarchy reigns, mightier than you." The Underworld blasphemes the earth under the City at the center of the world . Most games begin with adventurers taking their first steps through the gate to the Underworld from the City. His Majesty the Worm is a tabletop role-playing game designed for dungeon-crawling. The Game Master uses the tools in this book to create a megadungeon called the Underworld. The players create adventurers to explore the Underworld in pursuit of their personal quests. Tarot cards are used as a randomizing element. This is a new-school game with old-school sensibilities. It’s designed to make the “boring parts” interesting. Slice-of-life subsystems like food, hunger, light, and inventory management are central to play. The game has robust procedures: characters adventure in the Underworld, rest in camping scenes, then plan longterm actions in the City at the center of the Wide World. The relationships between companions, called Bonds, power the rest and recovery mechanic of the game. Role-playing drives the game forward. Combat encounters are handled with an action-packed subsystem that ensures that all players have interesting choices every minute of combat: no downtime! We hope you will have fun with it!

2.title: Tarot
2.body: Why tarot? Tarot cards are informationally rich. They have number, suit, direction (upright vs. reversed), and symbolic meaning. This information is persistent. You can have cards in your hand, drawn from the top of the deck, drawn from the discard pile, facedown in front of you, etc. This is a rich space for game play. Plus, they’re just cooler and more interesting to look at than playing cards. Tarot cards are available online and in spooky new age stores that sell crystals and stuff. You’ll want a deck similar to a “classic” Rider-Waite deck: 78 cards total, with a minor arcana consisting of four suits of ten numbered cards + four face cards and a major arcana numbered 0 to 21. This game uses tarot cards (instead of dice) in its procedures and mechanics. Chapter 1 provides an overview of the basic mechanics used during the flow of the game.

3.title: Players
3.body: Players take on the role of adventurers . Adventurers descend into the Underworld in search of impossible things that can never exist on the surface world. They explore collectively as a guild —a chartered union of adventurers. - The procedure for creating adventurers and filling out the adventurer sheet is found in Chapter 2: The Adventurer. - The procedure for filling out the guild roster is found in Chapter 3: The Guild.

4.title: The Game Master
4.body: Before play, the Game Master (GM) takes on the responsibility of using the tools in this book to create a series of interconnected dungeons and populating them with interesting challenges. This process takes one or two lazy Sunday afternoons. - A procedure for creating interesting monsters is found in Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens. - A procedure for creating an evocative City for the players’ home is found in Appendix D: City Creation. - A procedure for creating a series of dungeons that connect to form the Underworld is found in Appendix E: Underworld Creation. During play, the GM takes on the role of a referee who arbitrates the actions of the players’ adventurers within the context of the City and the Underworld. - General advice for running the game is found in Chapter 10: The Worm Turns see Chapter 10: The Worm Turns — Gamemastering. The game—and indeed, this very book—contains mature, fantastic themes that can range from sophomoric to graphic. As adults, work together to find what works for your group and leave the rest behind. Be kind. It is the shared responsibility of everybody at the table to ensure that the trials, battles, romances, successes, and failures had by the guild are fun for everybody involved.

5.title: Game Principles
5.body: His Majesty the Worm aims to make dungeon exploration fun. It forefronts what might otherwise be fringe rules for food, light, and time, and shines the spotlight on the visceral experience of the dungeon crawl.

6.title: The (Demi-) Human Experience
6.breadcrumb: Introduction › Game Principles › The (Demi-) Human Experience
6.body: This game focuses on the personal experiences of the adventurers exploring the mythic Underworld. Players portray fantastic characters. However, the game is designed to make these adventurers feel real through a persistent focus on basic “human” needs. Adventurers will become cold, drunk, hungry, horny, stressed, happy, hurt, etc. This allows players to immerse themselves in the experience of their adventurer. The essential meta-currency of the game are the Bonds the adventurers share with each other. When players role-play with their guild-mates, they charge these Bonds. Players then spend these charges to recover from the mental and physical ailments accumulated from dungeon delving.

7.title: Rulings, Not Rules
7.breadcrumb: Introduction › Game Principles › Rulings, Not Rules
7.body: Ultimately, no rule system completely encapsulates every possibility of player action—and that’s the fun of tabletop RPGs! There are fringe cases, strange situations, and unconsidered possibilities that inevitably arise during play. Having a GM to arbitrate these situations is one of the advantages of tabletop games compared to other game forms. As such, these rules are presented as a resource with the expectation that there will be ample homebrewing and hacking. When unexpected questions arise, GMs can adapt the rules to fit the situation at hand. When that situation comes up frequently, the GM and the table can collaborate on turning that ruling into a more hard-and-fast rule. And, when hard-and-fast rules seem to fail the tests of common sense, verisimilitude, and fun, it’s the GM’s responsibility to make calls that change the rules for the better.

8.title: The Scaling Underworld
8.breadcrumb: Introduction › Game Principles › The Scaling Underworld
8.body: The Underworld is not a place of balanced encounters. There’s no expectation that the players are ever in a “level-appropriate” place. A sleeping dragon might be an unbeatable guardian for a beginning party and must be snuck past. A somewhat more experienced guild might try and defeat the dragon to win her treasure. Either way, the dragon provides some type of challenge for the adventurers, whether they are novices or veterans. Players should feel empowered to experiment and take risks, with all the rewards and consequences that risk entails.

9.title: The Deadly Underworld
9.breadcrumb: Introduction › Game Principles › The Deadly Underworld
9.body: The game—and the adventurer sheet—are actually pretty simple. There are few numbers and not a lot of special powers or abilities. There are no “spot checks”—only players describing where and how they’re searching. There are no “disarm trap” skills—only players describing how they move the knife across the tripwire or tap their ten-foot pole ahead of them. Ultimately, this game is about exploring the Underworld. As such, there are no abilities that mitigate the essential dangers of the dungeon. - Darkness is always dangerous. No adventurer can see perfectly in the dark. - Rations and torches are always precious. There are no “conjure food” spells, and the arts that sorcerers have to conjure light are dangerous. Being bereft of light or food means death. - Traps must always be navigated. There are no “perception” or “disarm” skills. Each trap is a unique puzzle to be solved. - Combat is always deadly. Healing is laborious, requiring that the adventurers undertake a Camp Phase. Adventurers draw their swords at their own peril.

10.title: Whimsy
10.body: A fair bit of His Majesty the Worm is whimsy. This is an RPG that knows it’s an RPG. You play adventurers who know they are adventurers. It is playful with its tropes. It’s unpretentious. During a game, both players and GMs will deconstruct and reconstruct common dungeon delving tropes. This should be fun. This should be delightful.

11.title: Chapter 1: The Basics
11.body: All roads lead to the City. It is a land rich with trade and culture, a land of ancient dignity. The fay and underfolk both claim that the City predated the coming of humans, but the City is now undeniably the seat of humankind. For generations, men and women of famous heritage and noble blood have ruled the City through ages of feast and ages of famine. And then, the Underworld opened beneath it. Beneath the world’s largest metropolis, passages in plaster mines were discovered that led to a gargantuan castle, surrounded by a ruined city, deep inside the stygian depths.

12.title: The Four Phases
12.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Four Phases
12.body: Against canon Throughout this book, there are references to an implied setting that are never elaborated on. We name and discuss people, places, and historical events without describing them in great detail. This is intentional. Instead of providing a gazetteer with everything carefully plotted out and a hundred-and-one nonsense fantasy words for you to memorize, we’ve painted with a fairly broad brush. It’s our intention to give you a sense of scope and flavor without bogging the game down with lore to memorize or binding your story to a metaplot. The game world and the storyline are intended to vary from table to table. It’s our hope that the implied setting of His Majesty the Worm stimulates your imagination and allows you to tell the stories that you want to tell. As the setting details provided invoke a certain aesthetic for you, we hope that you will use them. As the setting details provided feel frustrating in their obscurity or contradictions, we hope you will change them, ignore them, or tear them physically from the book. At times, the provided material will be inherently contradictory, obliging you to make a decision about which version you want to be “true.” Each adventurer has a personal quest that compels them into the lightless depths. Once their quest is fulfilled, they can finally retire and rest. Until then, it is a cycle of descending into the Underworld and returning to the City to restock and rest. The flow of the game consists of four distinct phases, each with its own style of play and rules. The Four Phases City — Turn in and take new contracts; spend wealth to restock and heal; pursue long-term schemes. 1. Death and Taxes 2. Noteworthy Deeds 3. City Events 4. Turn in Contracts 5. Upkeep 6. City Actions 7. Plan the Next Crawl 8. Restock the Underworld Crawl — Pursue your quest; accumulate wealth and avoid hazards; charge Bonds through roleplaying and fulfilling conditions. 1. Declare you enter the quest 2. A watch passes when you travel to the next room 3. The GM draws on the Meatgrinder table each watch Challenge — Fight the denizens of the Underworld; notch armor; gain Wounds. 1. Set the Scene 2. Draw Challenge Cards 3. Play Initiative 4. Take Turns 5. Minor Actions6 6. End the Round Camp — Burn charged Bonds; heal Wounds; gain Resolve. 1. Camp Actions 2. Break Bread 3. No Rest for the Wicked 4. Recovery 5. End Camp Phase

13.title: The Crawl Phase
13.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Four Phases › The Crawl Phase
13.body: During the Crawl Phase, the guild explores an interconnected network of dungeons called the Underworld. During this phase, adventurers test their wits and skills against inhospitable forces in order to fulfill their quests. During the Crawl, players charge their Bonds with their guild-mates. The Crawl is where you’ll spend most of your time.

14.title: The Challenge Phase
14.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Four Phases › The Challenge Phase
14.body: A Challenge Phase occurs when you need to focus on the beat-by-beat action. This phase is when choices and consequences bear the hideous, overripe fruit of rotting bodies and terminated possibilities! During a Challenge, play moves from a freeform style to a tactical system. Play is split up into rounds and turns, during which people perform various specific actions. “Many sink down and few return to the sunlit lands.” – The Silver Chair, C.S. Lewis

15.title: The Camp Phase
15.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Four Phases › The Camp Phase
15.body: As the adventurers get worn down by journeys and battles, they’ll pause and use the Camp Phase. The focus of the Camp Phase is interpersonal roleplaying, drama, and connections between members of the guild. During this phase, players burn charged Bonds to rest and recover.

16.title: The City Phase
16.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Four Phases › The City Phase
16.body: Each delve is punctuated by the City Phase. The City Phase resolves the entire sequence and gives the guild a chance to spend their hard-earned loot, advance their long-term agendas, and reflect on their progress.

17.title: The Flow of the Play
17.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play
17.body: Games usually take place at a regularly scheduled time and place. Finding time to play games with other busy people can be challenging. Consistent play is crucial to keeping a game alive. Most sessions have a basic flow:

18.title: Before play
18.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › Before play
18.body: At the start of a game session, a few important pieces of bookkeeping are taken care of:

19.title: Recap
19.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › Before play › Recap
19.body: One player—with help from others at the table, and with corrections from the GM as needed—recaps what happened during the last session. This gets everybody back into the game and refreshes their memory about where they were and what they’re doing. If this player does an exceptionally good job, the GM may give them a point of Resolve. They may keep this Resolve or give it to another player who needs it.

20.title: Returning players
20.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › Before play › Returning players
20.body: If anyone misses a session during the Crawl Phase, their adventurer is assumed to be about one room away, trailing behind the main guild. They have been slowed down performing a Camp Action. When the player returns, they tell the table what activity they performed, receive the benefit from it, and rejoin the main group. Some actions (e.g., Fellowship, Train) logically require another adventurer to be “absent” with the returning player; only choose activities that make sense for the circumstances. “Pataphysics means ‘beyond metaphysics’; It is the science of imaginary solutions that studies the exceptions rather than laws and aspires to provide imaginary solutions to practical problems.” – Italo Calvino

21.title: During play
21.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › During play
21.body: A typical game session flows between the different phases. Over the course of many game sessions, play will follow this sequence: - Decide to pursue one adventurer’s quest. - Adventure through the Underworld (Crawl Phase). - Struggle against the strange denizens of the Underworld (Challenge Phase). - Rest as well as possible in the lightless depths (Camp Phase). - Return to the City, broken and bleeding (City Phase). - Spend accumulated wealth to heal, stock up on equipment, and pursue long-term projects in the City. - Pick up a contract to finance the next crawl. - Descend back into the Underworld in continued pursuit of the current quest while working on their contract (Crawl Phase). - Repeat.

22.title: End of play
22.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › End of play
22.body: Play can end after any phase or simply at a specified time. It’s best for the GM to close play when there’s a good stopping point—when one scene has just ended, or just after introducing a new scene (so the players have something to look forward to next week). The GM can take time at the end of play to get feedback about what the players want to do or where they want to go next. Reminders about when they’ll play next, who might be absent, etc., can be dealt with at this time.

23.title: Adjudicating the game: GM responses
23.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › Adjudicating the game: GM responses
23.body: The Challenge Phase It's worth noting that the rules of the Challenge Phase are more bounded than the freeform nature of standard play. The Challenge Actions and the player's hand of cards usually determine what an adventurer can and can't do. The GM still adjudicates what the players try to do when there's ambiguity: "Oh, you're trying to squeeze past the slime as they squelch down the hall? Well, there's not really space to Avoid it — it takes up the entire corridor. Do you want to do something else instead?" An RPG is a conversation between the GM and the players. The GM describes a scene and the players describe their actions inside the scene. The GM and the players ask questions of each other to further define their shared textual reality. The GM adjudicates how the adventurers’ actions impact the world. To this end, GMs are armed with the following four stock phrases: - “Yes, you can do that.” - “Say more about what you’re doing.” - “Draw to see if you can do that.” - “No, you can’t do that.” These phrases (and their variants) are the four basic responses that a GM has for answering a player when they ask, “Can my character do…?”

24.title: “Yes, you can do that”
24.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › Adjudicating the game: GM responses › “Yes, you can do that”
24.body: The player describes their adventurer’s actions and the GM simply describes what happens. If there’s nothing preventing the adventurer from succeeding, they simply succeed. - “ It doesn’t seem that the door is locked. You open the door slowly and carefully.” - “Sure, you can climb the tree. There're plenty of handholds.” - “You know that it will take a few minutes of hard work and it'll make a shit ton of noise, but of course you can use your felling axe to hack down the wooden door.” Players portray members of the unfortunate caste called “adventurers.” As such, they have the skills and abilities that you’d assume adventurers would have by default. In practice, this means you ignore all the uninteresting parts of adventuring. You never test fate to see if an adventurer knows how to kindle a bonfire—they’re competent travelers. Don’t worry about what weapons an adventurer is proficient in—they’re competent fighters. Even difficult tasks can be resolved without a test of fate as long as: 1. there’s no interesting risk; 2. the adventurer has plenty of time; 3. they have the appropriate tools. If one of these factors is missing, it’s time to move to one of the other responses. If an adventurer's actions would incur some sort of penalty, the GM should make that clear and give them a choice. - If an adventurer’s actions would take a long time to complete, the GM should make this clear. If the player elects to spend the time, the GM draws on the Meatgrinder table to represent time passing; similar to the Moving carefully rules. Draw from the major arcana— torches gutter on a result of I-V. - If an adventurer's actions would create a lot of noise, the GM should give that info. If the player elects to risk the noise, the GM draws on the Meatgrinder table to represent an interested predator investigating the disturbance; similar to the Loud noises rules. The GM draws from the major arcana—a random encounter occurs on a result of XV-XX.

25.title: “Say more about what you’re doing”
25.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › Adjudicating the game: GM responses › “Say more about what you’re doing”
25.body: Sometimes it’s not exactly clear what actions the players are describing or what their intentions are. In these cases, the GM should ask for clarification. - “How exactly are you searching for traps?” “OK, because of the Linguist talent, you definitely speak the myconid language, but you know that their language is expressed entirely in the medium of spore bursts. How do you intend to communicate with the fungoid?” - “How can you read the text if you don't have any light?” Sometimes there is a miscommunication in what the GM has described—the GM might be picturing one thing but the players have understood something very differently. Sometimes there's ambiguity in what the player is trying to do. Asking for clarification keeps the shared hallucination of the game consistent by syncing information between the GM and the player. The GM can also ask clarifying questions about the tactics that the character would be employing. A player’s statement that they want to “Perform a coup de grace on the vampire” might be more successful depending on the precise methods employed—the GM may want to know what weapons are used, what exactly is done, etc. Once the GM has achieved clarity with “Say more,” they can then shift to one of the other three basic responses.

26.title: “Draw to see if you can do that”
26.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › Adjudicating the game: GM responses › “Draw to see if you can do that”
26.body: When an action is fraught with danger or its outcome is uncertain, it’s time to test fate . For an overview of tests of fate. Tests of fate should be relatively rare and relatively tense. Don’t call for tests of fate for inconsequential actions—only when something of importance hangs in the balance. - “The door is locked. If you have lockpicks, you can test Pentacles to try and pick the lock.” - “OK, you grab the portcullis before it slams down. You’re straining against it as the mechanism’s gears

27.title: “No, you can’t do that”
27.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Flow of the Play › Adjudicating the game: GM responses › “No, you can’t do that”
27.body: Sometimes, actions are not possible or will automatically fail based on the logic of the narrative world. - “No, you can't really try and tame a dangerous wild beast with a single test of fate. Something like that would need to be done by breaking it over the course of several weeks. You can try and capture it, though, if you want...” - “No, if you don't have any tools, you don't have any way to pick the lock. There's not any, like, bits of wire just lying around your jail cell.”

28.title: The Major and Minor Arcana
28.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › The Major and Minor Arcana
28.body: No tarot? One of the reasons His Majesty the Worm separates the major and minor arcana decks is to compensate for the fact that not everybody who wants to play this game necessarily has a tarot deck lying around. The mechanics can be replicated, in a pinch, by using a twenty-sided die (a d20) as a stand-in for the GM’s deck and a standard deck of playing cards (with one joker to represent the Fool) for the players. The numbers will be a little different, but the logic and game balance will be the same. Random number generation You can replicate the randomization of polyhedral dice with tarot cards if you so wish. - The major arcana can act as a d20 (if you redraw when you get the World [XXI]). - The minor arcana suits can replicate a d4. - The minor arcana is essentially a d14. - Dividing the minor arcana in half gives you a weird d7. This can act as a d6 if you redraw on the queen and king. And, lastly, one of the most random and evocative types of generation you can get from the tarot is inspiration . If you’re familiar with the “meanings” of the tarot, you can use those meanings to inform the environments, characters, and events of your game. If you’re not familiar with the traditional tarot interpretation, you can just look at the cool art and feel inspired. A single tarot deck is used in His Majesty the Worm to create random results. A tarot deck in its entirety consists of seventy-eight cards of two types: major arcana and minor arcana . The GM uses the major arcana cards except the Fool. The major arcana are numbered and have evocative names like Magician \[I] and Wheel of Fortune \[X]. Therefore, the GM’s deck has 21 cards, numbered I–XXI. Players use the minor arcana cards plus the Fool, which is borrowed from the major arcana deck. There are fifty-six minor arcana cards—reminiscent of a more traditional deck of poker cards—with four suits of fourteen cards. The four suits are Swords, Pentacles, Cups, and Wands. The minor arcana are numbered I–X, and each suit has four face cards. Each card in the minor arcana has a value. A card’s value equals the number shown on the card. The Fool has the value of 0. Aces have a value of 1. The face cards have the following numeric values: - Page - 11 - Knight - 12 - Queen - 13 - King - 14 At the beginning of each session, separate the minor and major arcana into the two separate decks and shuffle each. Place the major arcana deck near the GM. Place the minor arcana deck (with the Fool shuffled into it) in a central location where all the players can reach it. There are two discard piles—one for minor arcana and one for major arcana. As cards are played, place them into the appropriate discard pile. (Occasionally, certain rules will call for you to look at the top card of a discard pile, so it can be important to note this.) Whenever the Fool is drawn, both decks are reshuffled at the end of the round .

29.title: Tests of Fate
29.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Tests of Fate
29.body: Challenge Actions The Challenge Phase is a subsystem for handling dangerous situations blow-by-blow. Challenge Actions have occasional similarities to the test of fate rules—for example, favor and disfavor can adjust a Challenge Action’s total value. However, there are many important differences: for example, Challenge Actions are not bound by fate and you cannot push fate on Challenge cards. For the specific rules on how the Challenge Phase handles actions, see Challenge Actions. When an adventurer’s action within the game's narrative is uncertain, the GM calls for a test of fate . Adventurers have four attributes , rated 1-4. Each represents an “approach” towards problem solving, and says a lot about how an adventurer achieves their goal. The GM determines which attribute is most relevant to the test’s outcome. To do this, they ask questions of the player to find out how, exactly, they are attempting the action. The player's description will inform which attribute is being tested.

30.title: Attributes
30.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Tests of Fate › Attributes
30.body: Swords: Swords represents strength and skill with weapons. Test Swords to bend the bars of your cell or tip over a heavy bookshelf onto an unsuspecting goblin. Pentacles: Pentacles represents swiftness and slyness. Test Pentacles to sneak past a deathknight or slip the sea witch’s conch into your bag without her noticing. Cups: Cups represents wisdom and training. Test Cups to activate an ancient clockwork mechanism or coax a wild winter wolf to accept a gift of meat from your hand. Wands: Wands represents willpower and charisma. Test Wands to convince an art critic that your petrified companion is actually avant-garde art or overcome the dominating gaze of a vampire. If the player describes being sneaky or quick, the GM will call for a test of Pentacles; if the player describes being mystical or eloquent, the GM will call for a test of Wands—and so forth. To test fate, the player draws a minor arcana card and adds the associated attribute to the value of the card.

31.title: Example
31.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Tests of Fate › Example
31.body: - You test Pentacles and draw a IV of Pentacles. Your adventurer’s Pentacles score is a 2. Your total value is 6. - You test Pentacles and draw a Knight of Wands. Your adventurer’s Pentacles score is 2 and a Knight has a value of 12. Your total value is 14. There are four possible outcomes to a test of fate.

32.title: Success
32.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Tests of Fate › Success
32.body: If the total value is 14 +, the result is a success. The GM describes how the adventurer succeeds in their stated goal.

33.title: Failure
33.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Tests of Fate › Failure
33.body: If the total value is 13 or less, the result is a failure . The GM describes how the adventurer fails and asks what they want to do next.

34.title: Great success
34.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Tests of Fate › Great success
34.body: If the total value is 14 + and the player drew the suit being tested on the initial draw (not from pushing fate or another source), the result is a great success . Not only does the adventurer succeed, but they succeed extremely well, going above and beyond what was expected. The GM should invite the player to embellish how impressive , how effortless , how quick , or how thorough their success was.

35.title: Great failure
35.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Tests of Fate › Great failure
35.body: If the player pushes fate and the total value is still 13 or less, the test is a great failure . The GM describes a new significant setback, bad situation, or harmful repercussion as a result. See “Pushing Fate.” Additional advice for the GM on adjudicating tests of fate can be found under The blessing of chaos.

36.title: Pushing fate
36.body: If the result of the test is a failure, the player may opt to push fate . Pull an additional card and add its value to the original total. If the total result of the two cards plus the attribute is 14 +, the test succeeds as normal. You can never achieve a great success if you push fate. If the total result is 13 or less, the test becomes a great failure . When you push fate and achieve a great failure, you not only fail to achieve what you set out to do, you make things even worse. Narratively, a great failure creates new obstacles to overcome or severely hampers the adventurers’ path forward. For example, if a thief achieves a great failure while picking a lock, the sound of the broken lockpick jammed in the door alerts a passing guard, who catches the thief red-handed. Or, if a templar suffers a great failure when attempting to intimidate the ogre, the ogre flies into a rage and sucker-punches the templar in a surprise attack. Additionally, a great failure inflicts a mechanical penalty on the adventurer who failed. If the situation is a dangerous situation, the GM can inflict a Wound on the adventurer. If the situation isn’t life threatening to begin with, an effect—representing frustration, sorrow, madness, exertion, or some other emotional state—might be more appropriate. For example, the GM might say that until the adventurer’s next encampment they become Exhausted (suffering the Exhaust effect) because they have overexerted themselves.

37.title: Pushing fate with the Fool
37.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Pushing fate with the Fool
37.body: The Fool has a value of 0. - If you pull the Fool initially during a test of fate, you can push fate as normal. This could turn the test from a failure to a success or to a great failure. - If you pull the Fool when pushing fate, your result automatically becomes a great failure. When the Fool is drawn, remember to shuffle both the minor and major arcana decks.

38.title: Example test of fate
38.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Example test of fate
38.body: GM: The black dragon seems to be asleep. A rattling snore issues from its nose, as if it’s congested. Its eyes are closed, and occasionally it licks its lips with a long, forked tongue. Phynn: And you said that my cup is under it? GM: Yeah, like, not right under it—but on its bed of gold, which is all spread out around the dragon. So it’s near it. You can reach the cup if you’re careful. Phynn: OK, I want to sneak up to the bed of gold and steal my ancestral cup. GM: OK, that will be a test of fate. Test Pentacles. Phynn draws from the minor arcana deck and gets an 8 of Swords. He realizes that the odds are good since he needs a total of 14. Phynn: That’s an 8 of Swords plus my Pentacles score of 2. That’s a 10 total. I’m gonna push fate. Phynn draws again and gets a 10 of Wands. Phynn: Awesome. That’s 20 total. That’s a success. GM: Awesome. You sneak closer and closer to the dragon. At one point, the snoring stops and becomes a choking cough. A little cloud of acid fog smokes out of the dragon’s nostrils, but then the snoring begins again. You reach out and grab your cup. Now you have your ancestral cup in your hands, and you’re still sitting in a room with a sleeping dragon. What do you do now?

39.title: Favor and disfavor
39.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Favor and disfavor
39.body: Sometimes circumstances can influence a test of fate positively or negatively. When beneficial factors would aid an adventurer, they are said to have favor . Favor grants +3 to the total value in a test of fate. When negative factors would hinder an adventurer, they have disfavor . Disfavor subtracts –3 from the total value in a test of fate. Favor and disfavor are not cumulative. You do not apply additional adjustments for having multiple helpful or hindering factors. For example, if you have several favorable factors, just note that you have favor and add +3. Favor and disfavor cancel each other out. If there are both helpful and hindering factors, you simply make the test of fate as normal. Because favor and disfavor are not cumulative, you do not consider how many factors weigh on either side; multiple favorable factors may be canceled out by one disfavor factor.

40.title: Relevant motifs
40.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Favor and disfavor › Relevant motifs
40.body: If one of your motifs is meaningfully related to the test of fate, you gain favor on the test of fate. See Motifs for more information.

41.title: Resolve
41.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Favor and disfavor › Resolve
41.body: Resolve represents an adventurer’s fortitude as they pursue their quests—fortitude that dwindles as you go deeper and deeper into the Underworld. You may elect to spend a point of Resolve prior to a test of fate in order to gain favor on that test. See Resolve for more information.

42.title: Aiding others
42.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Favor and disfavor › Aiding others
42.body: It is usually assumed that adventurers fill various niches and take on different roles during the Crawl. One is the scout and always does the reconnaissance, another is typically the watchman for the group, and another always forages for herbs. In these cases, the adventurer most suited for the task simply makes the test of fate. Sometimes, however, players will have the opportunity to work together on a test of fate. If two players can collaborate meaningfully, the acting player gets favor (+3) on the test of fate. Adding more people to the mix isn’t necessarily helpful. It’s usually best to let the best-suited adventurer take point and have aid provided by the person most interested in helping. The caveat about aiding another is that both participating adventurers are affected by the consequences of the test. If the test of fate is successful, both succeed. If the test fails, both adventurers fail. However, it’s important to note that the player who takes the lead and actually draws gets to determine whether or not they push fate. In the case of great failures, both adventurers are affected equally.

43.title: Example test of fate with favor
43.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Favor and disfavor › Example test of fate with favor
43.body: Dorian: Alright, I’m going to try and pick the lock on the door with the crank on it. GM: Sure. You have lockpicks right? Go ahead and test fate with Pentacles. Chirm: Can I try and help? GM: How would you help? Chirm: Uh, like, standing beside Dorian and watching what he does and giving him advice. GM: Usually lockpicking is sort of a solo activity just because of, like, space considerations. Do you have a motif that would justify giving advice? Chirm: I mean, she is a “Wealthy Artificer.” GM: Sure, as an artificer, I can see her knowing a lot about locks and mechanisms. Dorian, take favor. Dorian’s player draws and gets an Ace of Wands. Dorian: Oh no. I got a 1. OK, even with favor and my Pentacles score, that’s only a 7 total. Do we want to push? Chirm: I don’t know. I don’t really want to risk it. Dorian: Me neither. GM: OK. So even with Chirm’s advice, Dorian, the door’s lock seems really inscrutable. The two of you can’t figure it out. If you can’t pick the lock, what are you all going to do?

44.title: Bound by fate
44.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Bound by fate
44.body: Whether you succeed or fail, your results are bound by fate. You cannot retry the same test unless the circumstances significantly change. If you fail to pick a lock, that lock is beyond your adventurer’s abilities. If you fail to climb a wall, that wall is unclimbable. But maybe the warrior in the company can bash down the door. And maybe the sorcerer has a magical cloak that allows you to fly over the wall. You’ll have to find another way past an obstacle if you fail in the test. You can also attempt a test again if the circumstances significantly change. Significant change usually means new ideas, new tools, or a new twist on an old situation. Because His Majesty the Worm is a fundamentally collaborative game, fellow guild members are also bound by fate. If one person attempts something and fails, it’s established that it cannot feasibly be done at present. No fair having each guild member try successively until somebody succeeds. However, additional guild members can attempt alternate methods to bypass the obstacle. It’s important to note the GM is also bound by fate. The GM may not call for multiple frivolous tests to see if an adventurer can accomplish a single task. The more times a successful test is reattempted, the more chances the player has to fail. The GM may only call for repeated tests when the situation meaningfully changes.

45.title: Group tests
45.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Group tests
45.body: In the face of discrete challenges, it’s best to have one adventurer be bold and test fate. There are times, however, when the entire guild must test their fates together. For example, the entire guild must sneak into the Tower Gnostic to steal an artifact or must perform the Operetta d’Serpentis perfectly for the master of the Broken Smiles Opera House. In such cases, the GM calls for a group test. Group tests are accomplished by having two adventurers test fate: the one most qualified and the one least qualified. If there are apparent ties, talk it out to determine who should make the tests. - If one of the adventurers succeeds in a test of fate, they give 1 hit to the group test. If they get a great success, they give 2 hits . - If one of the adventurers fails in a test of fate, they give no hits to the group test. If they suffer a great failure, they subtract -1 hit . The GM totals the amount of hits to determine the success of the group test. - 2 hits: Success for the entire group. - 1 hit: The group comes short of succeeding and are put in a tight spot. - 0 hits: Failure for the entire group. - <0 hits: Disaster for the entire group. Like other tests of fate, group tests are bound by fate.

46.title: Example group test
46.breadcrumb: Chapter 1: The Basics › Pushing fate › Group tests › Example group test
46.body: GM: OK, so what I’m hearing is that you’re all going to try and hold the door closed as the peryton slams into it. I think that’s a group test. Can I get the highest and lowest Swords people to draw? Dorian: I’m a 3 Swords. Chirm: I’m 2. GM: OK, that’s you, Phynn and Chirm. Chirm’s player draws from the minor arcana deck and gets a IX of Pentacles. Adding her Swords 2, that’s a total of 11. Chirm pushes fate and gets a IV of Wands. That’s a total of 15. A success. Chirm: OK, I got a 15 total. That succeeds. Phynn’s player draws a V of Swords from the minor arcana deck. With his Swords 4, that’s a total of 9. He also pushes fate and draws again, drawing a III of Swords. Despite having the higher Swords score, he only gets a 12 total. That’s a critical failure. Phynn: Jesus Christ. I thought I had it. But no, critical fail. GM: OK, that critical failure will reduce the success that Chirm generated, so you get 0 hits. The door buckles under the conflict between you and the peryton. Shards of wood and bits of the iron hinges shriek as they break. Phynn, take a Wound as the peryton gores you with its horns. You’re staring it in its weird, blank eyes. What do you guys do?

47.title: Effects
47.body: Not just for Challenges Many effects have important ramifications during Challenges. However, effects are not “combat only” rules. For example, outside of a Challenge, a trap with the Displace effect can knock an adventurer into a spiked pit. If that adventurer survives, a sorcerer can cast Gust of Wind to give the Displace effect and pull them back out. The GM adjudicates how effects resolve during the normal flow of the game. The GM and the players interpret the flavor of how effects interact with the world. For example, a dart envenomed with sleeping poison and a blow to the back of the head might both Knockout the target—however, shaking the sleeping person might be enough to wake them up, whereas the person hit in the head would need medical care. Effect names Note that capitalized effect names change conjugation depending on how they're used in game text, but all mean the same thing. For example, a Blinding attack Blinds a creature, after which they are Blinded. Terms that describe consequences that happen to characters or objects things like Blind, Destroy, and Heal are called Effects. Each effect has its own rules and implications, explained in the list below.

48.title: Blind
48.body: Blinded creatures cannot see or gain any visual information. - Blinded creatures make all tests and Challenge Actions with disfavor. - Blinded creatures can’t make missile attacks at all. - All harmful actions against Blind creatures have favor.

49.title: Control
49.body: Controlled creatures obey the order given to them. As soon as the order is completed, or if it cannot be completed, the effect ends. - During Challenges, Controlled creatures immediately perform the commanded action. The total value for the Controlled action is equal to the value of the action used to Control it.

50.title: Curse
50.body: Curse is a generic term for “bad thing” as determined by the GM. Turned to stone by a medusa? Fused with a party member? Changed into a baby? These are all Curses. The GM will tell you what it means.

51.title: Deafen
51.body: Deafened creatures cannot hear or gain any auditory information. Speak Incantation is made with disfavor.

52.title: Destroy
52.body: Destroyed objects are broken and unusable.

53.title: Disarm
53.body: Disarmed creatures drop one held item of their choice. - A dropped item requires a Recover action to retrieve during Challenges. - If an adventurer is carrying neither a melee weapon or shield, all attacks against them gain favor.

54.title: Displace
54.body: Displaced creatures are moved to another zone, as determined by the initiating creature or effect.

55.title: Exhaust
55.body: Exhausted creatures make all tests and Challenge Actions with disfavor.

56.title: Heal
56.body: Healed creatures instantly remove one Wound from a condition.

57.title: Inspire
57.body: Inspired creatures must immediately role-play one of the seven Dispositions to the best of their ability, following the basic guidelines. The Dispositions are: anger, distaste, sadness, joy, surprise, trust, fear.

58.title: Grow/Shrink
58.body: Grown creatures and objects double their original height. Shrunk creatures and objects half their original height. Gain favor when this would be advantageous (squeezing into holes, sneaking around) and disfavor when it would be disadvantageous (contests of strength).

59.title: Knockout
59.body: Knocked-out creatures are unconscious and incapacitated. They cannot take any actions.

60.title: Notch
60.body: When an item suffers an attack that compromises its durability, it is Notched. After suffering a certain number of Notches, the item is Destroyed. - Fragile items are Destroyed after one Notch. - Items intended for durability are Destroyed after two Notches. - Items made of tempered steel are Destroyed after three Notches. - Notched items can be repaired with a tinker's kit or in the City.

61.title: Root
61.body: Rooted creatures cannot move from the spot on which they are standing. - They cannot Avoid, Dash, Dodge, or Move. - Anybody engaged with a Rooted creature immediately disengages.

62.title: Shroud
62.body: Shrouded creatures are invisible. Shrouded creatures are impossible to see without the aid of magic or special senses. - Typically, if a Shrouded creature stands still and stays quiet, they cannot be deliberately targeted by creatures who can’t see them. - However, if the Shrouded creature is moving and interacting with their environment, they can be targeted, though all such attempts are made with disfavor. - Shrouded creatures make harmful actions with favor against creatures who can’t see them.

63.title: Silence
63.body: Silenced creatures cannot make any vocal sounds. As such, they cannot cast spells because they cannot Speak Incantations.

64.title: Stun
64.body: When Stunned, immediately choose and discard a Challenge card from your hand. You do not need to Recover from being Stunned. It is an instantaneous effect.

65.title: Trip
65.body: Tripped creatures fall prone. - Prone creatures cannot Avoid, Move, or Dash. - Melee attacks against prone targets have favor. - Missile attacks against prone targets have disfavor. - Anybody engaged with a Tripped creature immediately disengages.

66.title: Chapter 2: The Adventurer
66.body: “He is a prince of the other world on his travels through this one... The sun, which shines behind him, knows whence he came, whither he is going, and how he will return by another path after many days. He is the spirit in search of experience.” – The Pictorial Key to the Tarot, A. E. Waite There are four social classes in the City. The nobles field knights and have the wealth to supply them with the finest arms and armor. The nobles are the landowners; they make war when it is necessary to defend or expand the City. The clergy provide for the spiritual needs of the populace and tally the offerings to the many faces of the Monad. The clergy are the learned class; they perform the tasks of chronicling and remembering the histories of the City. The tradesmen power the economy of the City. This class of skilled workers is not given the privileges or powers of the nobility but they make enough money to avoid the life of the peasants. The peasants are indentured servants who work for the right to live on the lands of the nobility. They believe strange things. Adventurers, who delve into the Underworld for treasures and glory, break this system. Despite the half-century since the Underworld's appearance, the City still isn't used to this uncomfortably new fifth class. In many ways, adventurers are lower than peasants, for they do not have legal rights in the City. However, many become richer than even the nobility, for the Underworld boasts fabulous wealth. At once, adventurers are both respected and despised.

67.title: The Player’s Manifesto
67.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Player’s Manifesto
67.body: An RPG is simply an exchange of questions and answers between the players and the GM. These questions and answers can have nuance and texture. When playing His Majesty the Worm , this manifesto will help you frame your conversations with your GM.

68.title: Be careful, be fierce
68.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Player’s Manifesto › Be careful, be fierce
68.body: You don’t start out a hero. The only thing between you and a salivating dragon’s jaws are a few conditions unchecked on your adventurer sheet. You should never expect the world around you to be fair. You’re not in a tutorial level; your adventurer is journeying through a mythic Underworld that wants them to stay forever and ever. Keeping them alive requires caution and thoughtfulness. Encountering a dragon is different when your adventurer is inexperienced versus when they’re experienced. At first, the focus might be stealth—how much gold can you get away with before the dragon notices you? After you’ve built up your strength, you might feel confident enough to engage in combat with the dragon. But don’t fight fair. Make sure you choose the battleground. Ambush the dragon. Drop a rock on its head. And when the going gets tough, don’t be afraid to cut your losses and run away.

69.title: Solve problems orthogonally
69.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Player’s Manifesto › Solve problems orthogonally
69.body: You should be trying to make your GM say: “I didn’t even think of that.” In an RPG, you can do anything. That’s the appeal! When you’re playing a computer game, you can only do the things the game designer programmed in. They anticipated you moving left, right, and down. Going up is out of the question. Not so in a tabletop game. Most problems aren’t solved by fighting them. People can be reasoned with. Monsters can be placated. Traps can be avoided. Monsters can be led into traps. People can be sold the monster’s guts. Don’t expect to “use” your talents and motifs to solve a problem. The abilities and items you have listed are just tools—and they’re only one of the many tools in your arsenal. Think outside of your adventurer sheet.

70.title: Engage the world
70.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Player’s Manifesto › Engage the world
70.body: You don’t have to talk in a silly voice or wear a costume . You do, however, have to interact with the fiction of the world in a logical way. The essential way you have to interact with the fictional world is to ask questions. By engaging your GM in a give-and-take, you make the game real. The game world is layered. By asking questions, you begin to understand its bounds. There are no abilities on your adventurer sheet that give you the sort of insight that asking questions will provide. If you’re looking for a trap, pour water on the ground and see if you can find any trap doors. If you’re looking for a secret door, tap on the walls and listen for something hollow. The game is about you using your real-life thinking brain to solve problems, overcome obstacles, and figure things out. There are no stats or powers that are going to help you solve the essential issues. You can though. We won’t stop you.

71.title: Engage each other
71.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Player’s Manifesto › Engage each other
71.body: The most essential stats on your adventurer sheet aren't your talents or motifs. The most essential stats are your Bonds with your guild-mates. The economy of charging Bonds during the Crawl and spending them during the Camp Phase is essential to the flow of His Majesty the Worm . As such, make sure you're thinking of ways to engage other players. - Play to lift other adventurers up. When you see an opportunity for another adventurer to shine, take a step back. Share each other's burdens. Revel in each other's successes. - Be respectful and considerate. If you want to explore a particular story, engage with your fellow players to make sure they're comfortable with the themes that you're exploring. Don't be “that guy.” Read the goddamn room. - Let your relationships grow and change. Every session or two, touch base with another player. Discuss how your adventurers feel about each other in light of your most recent experiences. Have rivals become allies? Have allies become best friends? Have best friends become lovers? - Be funny in character. Be serious in character. Think in character. Stay in character.

72.title: Embrace the chaos
72.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Player’s Manifesto › Embrace the chaos
72.body: Part of the game is skill. Part of the game is chance. Sometimes, you can’t be careful or fierce enough to avoid a test of fate. And when fate isn’t on your side, you have to embrace it. Having something bad happen doesn’t mean that you’ve made a mistake. It’s just part of the game. It is easy to create a new adventurer. This is on purpose. If your adventurer dies, throw yourself into the next one. If your adventurer completes their quest, be excited to retire them. Games without consequences have no teeth. How boring would it be if you knew you would never fail and never die? The essential gimmick of question/answer with the GM would be boring: “How will your adventurer succeed today?” Thus, love the chaos. “An incalculable amount of human effort is directed to combating and restricting the nuisance or danger represented by chance.” – Introduction to the I Ching, Carl Jung

73.title: Session 0
73.body: Restrictions foster creativity It’s said that necessity is the mother of invention. If that’s true, we would add our own truism: restrictions are the mother of creativity. It can be hard for (even experienced) players to choose a compelling character or guild concept ex nihilo. A GM who provides some structure to session 0 can plant seeds of creativity for the players. For example, perhaps the GM runs an underfolk-only game. Or, perhaps they run a game where the guild is the Secret Pope’s Secret Strike Force. At first blush, these restrictions might be surprising for players. They might wonder how they can distinguish themselves from each other if everybody is of the same kith or path (or both). However, we’ve found that true distinction comes when the players don’t simply play their “race and class.” The more similar characters are on the surface, the less similar they are in truth. Sometimes, RPG players are expected to create their characters by themselves and show up on game night expecting to meet everyone else at an inn. This can sometimes lead to problems at the game table. We recommend that the players and the GM get together for a session before play starts to create adventurers and talk about everybody's expectations. This is called “session 0,” and it can go a long way towards making sure everybody is having fun.

74.title: Collaborative game creation
74.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › Session 0 › Collaborative game creation
74.body: During session 0, the GM should set expectations about what sort of game they will be running. The general assumption with His Majesty the Worm is that it will be a megadungeon-based exploration game where the adventurers pursue their own quests. Deviations from this formula should be discussed by the table. Have a discussion about what everybody enjoys in games: - Do you have fun with combat? Do you like learning and using the mechanics of the game? - Do you enjoy intra-party conflict? Does it stress you out? - Do you enjoy intra-party romance? Does it stress you out? - Do you enjoy getting deep into your own character's role-playing? - Do you enjoy spending an evening with your friends? - Do you enjoy the emerging story told by an RPG? Lots of players will have opinions about these sources of fun. Some sources will be more interesting to you than others. Session 0 is also an important opportunity to make sure that sensitive subjects are treated with the respect that they deserve. If the GM plans on including difficult themes in their game, they should make this apparent up front. For example, if you’re intending to deal with themes of slavery in the City, just say so. Role-playing games can be opportunities to confront important real-world issues. They can also be an opportunity to escape these and not think about them at all. GMs, be respectful when listening to player’s reactions to sensitive subjects. Don’t put players on the spot (e.g., “Are there any triggering subjects that we should avoid?”). Rather, ask open-ended questions that allow for honest feedback. Work together to find out what subjects are and are not appropriate for your friends.

75.title: Collaborative adventurer creation
75.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › Session 0 › Collaborative adventurer creation
75.body: During session 0, the players go through all steps of the Call to Adventure together. They discuss the sort of characters they want to play. If there are overlaps, players discuss how they feel about them. Maybe the overlaps are interesting (maybe the two dwarf adventurers are related), or maybe one player would prefer to play something that differentiates them. If a player has questions about a rule’s interpretation, the GM can answer it and the entire table benefits from learning the clarification. If a player wants to ask the GM for a rules change or special permission for something, the GM can run the potential change past the entire table to see if everybody is okay with it. Everybody is kept on the same page. As the GM hears interesting details about an adventurer’s background, early ages, apprenticeship years, etc., they can jot down plot ideas. Maybe that long lost brother can come back. Maybe they can make that failed marriage important. The GM can also use this time to smooth over potential difficulties. One of the players wants to play a cannibal. Is that appropriate for this game and this party? As part of the Call to Adventure, the players announce their adventurers’ initial quests. The GM can veto these quests or suggest changes to make them more interesting.

76.title: Collaborative guild creation
76.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › Session 0 › Collaborative guild creation
76.body: The adventurers begin the game as members of the same guild. During session 0, over the course of the Call to Adventure, the players fill out the guild roster sheet collaboratively. As everyone talks about their adventurers, the GM can try and encourage a guild theme. Are the players all pirates? All dedicated templars? All noble ladies? All named Greg? Collectively decide: - What is the name of your guild? - Why are you adventuring together? - How did you meet? - Is there a guild leader? - What are the looting rights? Role-playing games have been compared to sex. You usually do it with friends. Sometimes you pay someone to be your dungeon master. Sometimes safe words help. Sometimes you don’t need them. Ultimately, it’s important that everybody involved enthusiastically consents to the stuff that’s going on and everybody is having fun. “Dark hallways. Windowless rooms. Stairs. Then a new voice: ‘I’m lost. Out of food. Low on water. No sense of direction. Oh God...’ ...‘There’s something here. It’s following me. No, it’s stalking me. I’ve been stalked by it for days but for some reason it’s not attacking. It’s waiting, waiting for something. I don’t know what. Holloway Roberts. Menomonie, Wisconsin. I’m not alone here. I’m not alone.’” – House of Leaves, Mark Z. Danielewski

77.title: The Call to Adventure
77.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure
77.body: Creating an adventurer means heeding the call to adventure. When you create an adventurer, you answer questions and make a series of decisions. This will result in a character with a background, a history, equipment, and connections to other adventurers. Track the choices of the Call to Adventure and subsequent play on your adventurer sheet. A full version of the adventurer sheet can be found at hismajestytheworm.games .

78.title: 1. Origin
78.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 1. Origin
78.body: Your home, your hearth, and your heart are your adventurer’s biggest influences. - Choose a kith and kin from chapter 4. Write down your kin talent . - Your kin talent begins as mastered . A mastered talent can be used without spending XP. See Talents for details about talents. - Choose a path from chapter 5. Put a 4 in the corresponding attribute. - Write down all of your path’s talents . - Choose one of your path talents to be mastered . - The rest of your path talents are in-training . - Choose a name from the list on your kith’s page or make one up. - All adventurers have a maximum of 4 Resolve. Note that you start with a full 4 Resolve.

79.title: 2. Fitting in
79.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 2. Fitting in
79.body: Puberty is a hard time. There are so many weird changes, and you have to make decisions about your future career way earlier than you want to. - Tell a story to the table about something your adventurer struggled with while young. Based on the story, put a 1 in one attribute . - Choose a motif based on your origin story. This might be related to your parents’ professions or an apprenticeship. See Motifs for details about motifs.

80.title: 3. Failed career
80.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 3. Failed career
80.body: You had a shot at a normal life and you blew it. What was your previous job? - Tell a story to the table about your failed career. Based on your story, put a 2 in one attribute . - Choose a motif related to your failed career.

81.title: 4. Querent
81.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 4. Querent
81.body: Adventure calls to you. - Tell a story to the table about why you’re willing to brave the Underworld. What is your quest ? Note it down. - If it’s important to your group, choose two languages .

82.title: 5. Full-blown weirdo
82.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Full-blown weirdo
82.body: You set out to become that dreadful, ugly, and unwelcome thing: an adventurer. Your first foray into the Underworld was…what? - Tell a story about your first adventure into the Underworld. Based on your story, put a 3 in the last attribute . - Choose a motif based on this adventure. This is your last motif, so think carefully. - What does your adventurer look like? Briefly describe them to the rest of the guild.

83.title: 6. Guild bonding
83.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 6. Guild bonding
83.body: Who is in your guild and why are you traveling together? - Each player declares a Bond with every other player at the table (Bonds). Bonds are very important for the meta-economy of the game. - Get out the guild roster . Note down the members of the guild. - Collectively give your guild a name and have someone draw the guild’s sigil . - Collectively determine your looting rights in the terms section of the roster. - Each player chooses their marching order (first, second, third, etc.) and guild role . More information about guilds, marching order, and so on, is covered in chapter 3.

84.title: 7. Treats from Ma
84.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 7. Treats from Ma
84.body: Look at the Omphalic Market. - Choose 1 luxurious item, 5 common items , and as many impoverished items as you want. Keep choosing items until your belt and your backpack are full. - If any of your talents require specific items (an archwood wand, a bow, heavy armor, poultices, hermetic bottles, etc.), these items count as impoverished items for you during the Call to Adventure. You can have as many as you want.

85.title: Putting it all together
85.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › Putting it all together
85.body: In summation, your adventurer has: - Attributes set at 4, 3, 2, and 1 - A path - 1 mastered path talent, 1 mastered kin talent, and 6 path talents in training - A quest - 3 motifs - 4 Resolve - A full backpack and belt containing 1 luxurious item, 5 common items, and as many impoverished items and items used by your talents as you want - Bonds with the rest of the guild - An appearance - A name You’re now ready to heed the call to adventure and delve into the Underworld.

86.title: The adventurer sheet
86.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › Putting it all together › The adventurer sheet
86.body: Each section of the adventurer sheet is described in detail on the following pages! “Tell me a story. Make it a story of great distances, and starlight. The name of the story will be Time, But you must not pronounce its name. Tell me a story of deep delight.” – “Tell Me a Story,” Robert Penn Warren

87.title: 1. Name, kith, and kin
87.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 1. Name, kith, and kin
87.body: Knaves, rogues, and scoundrels Playing murder hobos gets so old so fast. Whee, you killed the barkeep because he looked at you wrong. Whee, you set the tavern on fire. His Majesty the Worm is a game for heroes. You can be dirty, rotten thieves—but at least you have a heart of gold. Adventurers have a kith and a kin . An adventurer’s kith is their “race”—whether they are human or fay or underfolk or otherwise. In game terms, kith is the broad cultural context that separates them from the rest of the world. Kin defines an adventurer’s clan, realm, or kingdom, and differentiates that adventurer from others of their kith. Two adventurers with the same kin are from the same sub-group—or maybe even related by blood. Chapter 4 details the various kith and kin that you can choose from during the Call to Adventure, and provides some sample names . - You automatically begin with a mastered talent determined by your kin. - Your kith determines your arête triggers. When all three triggers are checked, you automatically learn your kin’s arête talent. The kiths and kin are:

88.title: Humans
88.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 1. Name, kith, and kin › Humans

89.title: Fay
89.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 1. Name, kith, and kin › Fay
89.body: - High elves - Wood elves - Dark elves - Gnomes

90.title: Underfolk
90.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 1. Name, kith, and kin › Underfolk

91.title: Orcs
91.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 1. Name, kith, and kin › Orcs

92.title: 2. Attributes
92.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 2. Attributes
92.body: Attributes as class You might think of each attribute as a rating in one of four jobs: warrior, rogue, scholar, and sorcerer. When a particular task would fall within the purview of one of these jobs, you test fate with that particular attribute. An adventurer’s abilities are measured by four attributes . The attributes are:

93.title: Swords
93.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 2. Attributes › Swords
93.body: Swords is the attribute of warriors. Swords encompasses strength and endurance. It represents bravery, fortitude, directness, forcefulness, and all facets of combat.

94.title: Cups
94.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 2. Attributes › Cups
94.body: Cups is the attribute of scholars. Cups encompasses wisdom and learning. It represents cleverness, carefulness, patience, and everything related to the use of tools.

95.title: Pentacles
95.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 2. Attributes › Pentacles
95.body: Pentacles is the attribute of rogues. Pentacles encompasses swiftness and slyness. It represents quickness, quietness, manipulation, and everything related to stealth.

96.title: Wands
96.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 2. Attributes › Wands
96.body: Wands is the attribute of sorcerers. Wands encompasses your willpower and mysticism. It represents persuasiveness, showmanship, spirit, passion, and everything related to the occult. Adventurers have a spread of attributes ranked 4, 3, 2, and 1. Your highest attribute (4) will be the same as the path you belong to (Chapter 5: The Four Paths).

97.title: 3. Quests
97.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 3. Quests
97.body: Every adventurer has a reason to go down into the Underworld. This is called your quest . Your quest is your adventurer’s motivating objective. It is discrete and achievable . So, “Find the Grail of Mythrys” is a good quest, but “Get rich” is a bad quest. Yes, the Grail of Mythrys will make you rich, but riches is not what you're questing for.

98.title: Example quests
98.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 3. Quests › Example quests
98.body: - Capture a cockatrice and haul it back to the City alive so that the Order of Alchemists can save your petrified brother. - Kill the vampire who turned you into a thrall so that you can be restored to humanity. - Find the Well of Lethe so that you can forget the terrible things you’ve done and have a chance at a happy life. - Get a trophy from a dragon so that you can impress the pirate crew that mutinied against you. - Pluck a nega-rose from the Grave of the First Dead so that the Witchmother accepts your proposal of marriage to her daughter. Players and the GM should talk over their quests during session 0. The GM should set expectations for what’s reasonable to quest for. The players should talk about adventures that would be interesting to them. It’s the GM’s job to place each player’s quest objectives into the Underworld and hedge them with interesting, open-ended challenges. They should pepper hints, rumors, and associated characters into the game world so that players have things to explore and paths towards victory. See Create a path to success for more information about how the GM does this. Like rumors that you hear in the City, what you hear about your quest may or may not be correct. There might be twists. There might be competition. There might be trouble.

99.title: 4. Motifs
99.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 4. Motifs
99.body: You play an adventurer—a homeless mercenary who voluntarily delves into the depths of a mythical dungeon in hopes of treasure and glory and gods only know what else. But every adventurer in the Underworld has lived another life. Your motifs speak to the life that you lived before you became an adventurer. A motif is a short phrase that defines a moment in your adventurer’s history. Motifs have two primary uses: - When your adventurer has a motif that would prepare them or make them particularly qualified for a test of fate, you have favor on that test (+3 to the total). - You can bid lore to ask the GM questions about a subject if you have a motif that is appropriate to the question you’re asking; see Lore. A motif is made up of two parts: a descriptor and the name of a profession . To create a motif, combine two words from the lists on the following page, or create your own. An adventurer only ever has three motifs. You should never feel locked into the choices you make about your adventurer. You may change a motif during the City Phase if you and the GM feel it’s appropriate. “We’ve met before.” “Right! When I was a pirate’s ship-boy.” “And I was a wizard’s apprentice.” – Ill Met in Lankhmar, Fritz Leiber

100.title: Sample motif descriptors and professions
100.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 4. Motifs › Sample motif descriptors and professions
100.body: Example motifs • Gentleman thief • Heretical evangelist • Veteran witch-hunter • Constantly giggling rat-catcher • Drunken knight • Fallen templar • Penitent grave robber • Twisted inventor • Morbid jester Real-world inspiration In Britain’s first census in 1801, citizens were asked to state their “rank, profession, or occupation.” The following are true responses to this census. If this doesn’t inspire you for motifs, nothing will: • Turnip shepherd • Knight of the Thimble • Drowner • Fatuous pauper • Emasculator • Sampler of drugs • Examiner of underclothing • Gymnast to house painter • Colourist of artificial fish Descriptor Descriptor Profession Profession --- --- --- --- Apprentice Mute Acrobat Jailer Arrogant Nasty Artificer Jester Bastard Naughty Assassin Knight Boisterous Old (Very) Bard Necromancer Conscripted Overly Optimistic Baron Noble Cowardly Pacifist Berserker Oracle Deformed Penitent Bodyguard Pirate Dying Quarrelsome Bounty Hunter Raider Errant Quiet Burglar Ranger Eunuch Reformed Child-catcher Rat-catcher Fanatical Rude Chirugeon Senator Feral Sarcastic Cleric Scout Gluttonous Servant Courtier Scribe Giggling (Often) Thoughtful Diplomat Smith Heretical Twisted Drunkard Soldier Highborn Ugly Duelist Spy Idiotic Unwilling Engineer Templar Irresponsible Veteran Explorer Tomb Robber Jinxed Weird Friar Urchin Jovial Whispery Gladiator Vagabond Kindly Xenophobic Grave Robber Wanderer Kvetching Ye Olde Highwayman Witch Lazy Young (Very) Hunter Witch-hunter Lowborn Zen Illusionist Wizard Masochistic Zombielike Inquisitor Zealot

101.title: 5. Bonds
101.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds
101.body: Negative bonds and “That Guy” OK, let’s talk real quick about the connotation of some of these negative Bonds and problem players. Some of these Bonds ( Unrequited Love , Adversary , Rival ) seem like they’d incite a bad time with “that guy.” We hope this isn’t true for you. Whenever somebody is being “that guy,” there’s one real solution: talk to them. Maybe you got off track. Maybe there was a miscommunication. Maybe this player has had different experiences and expectations with gaming than the rest of the table. These things can often be worked through. Moreover, the session 0 rules we’ve included are designed to help mitigate having these experiences in the first place. But, if and when they arise, a frank, adult discussion can serve you well. The fact of the matter is that some Bonds are, in fact, representative of “negative” relationships and derived from adversarial relationships in the inspirational fiction. We think these can be fun—but only if done with the consent of all parties involved. Table consensus is a prime tool for everybody having a fun time. If the idea of Unrequited Love appeals to you, talk to the table. See who would be interested in that Bond, and make sure the GM is interested in that sort of story. GMs, talk to your players when they bring these things up. Facilitate communication. Are the players interested in ever moving the Unrequited Love towards Love? At the end of the day, it’s important that everybody is having fun with the Bonds. If they’re not, just swap them to “Ally.” It’s the default one. The relationships you have with all the other members of your guild are called Bonds . Bonds are reflected on your adventurer sheet in terms of simple sentences: “I am Petyr’s mentor,” or “Grendel is my ally.” Your Bonds become charged when you play them to the hilt or when they put you in danger . If you play a Bond to the hilt, you exemplify the relationship represented by the Bond. Basic suggestions for this role-play are given in the descriptions of the example Bonds below; however, the GM can call for the Bond to be charged by other examples of excellent role-playing, too. - Players, just ask the GM when you think you’ve done a great job. GMs, be generous and honest. If your Bond puts you in danger, you make a choice that puts your adventurer at a disadvantage or takes a big risk for the sake of exemplifying their Bond. - Players, ask your GM if you think your choice really jeopardizes you. GMs, be generous and honest. Charges may be burned during the Camp Phase to heal Wounds and recover Resolve. For each charge you burn, you heal 1 Wound or regain 1 Resolve. See Recovery for full details. By way of example, the Bonds below are illustrated using characters from Firefly and The Lord of the Rings. We figured this was geek lingua franca.

102.title: Ally
102.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Ally
102.body: Your allies are guild-mates that you are professional and amiable with. This is the default Bond. Examples: Wash and Kaylee, Aragorn and Gandalf - Charge this Bond when you make your ally laugh both in and out of character.

103.title: Adversary
103.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Adversary
103.body: If you have a significant problem with a guild-mate, you’re probably their adversary. This isn’t an excuse to be an ass to another player, but it’s an opportunity for interesting and fair conflict. Examples: Mal and Jayne, Boromir and Aragorn - Charge this Bond when you witness your adversary fail a test of fate.

104.title: Big/Little
104.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Big/Little
104.body: There's a special relationship between a diminutive halfling and her huge troll “brother.” If one adventurer is bigger than the other and you use this to your advantage, this is the Bond for you. Example: Éowyn and Merry - You both charge this Bond when your big/little aids you in a test of fate with your weakest attribute.

105.title: Best Friend
105.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Best Friend
105.body: You wouldn't let your best friend go on an adventure without you. You're there for each other, thick or thin. Examples: Mal and Zoe, Merry and Pippin - You both charge this Bond when you reveal a secret to your best friend.

106.title: Love
106.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Love
106.body: If both players are cool with it, use this Bond to represent someone you are in a romantic relationship with. If the relationship is one-sided, use the Unrequited Love Bond. Examples: Zoe and Wash, Faramir and Éowyn - Charge this Bond when you do something gushy and romantic for your partner, whether it’s writing an in-character love sonnet or risking your neck to pick a bunch of flowers for them.

107.title: Master/Henchman
107.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Master/Henchman
107.body: Players can be hirelings. When you have a managerial vs. subservient relationship with another guild-mate, this is your Bond. Examples: Mal and Wash, Frodo and Sam - Masters charge this Bond when they give their henchman an agreed-upon payment or compensation. - Henchmen charge this Bond when they use one of their Camp Actions to benefit their master but not themselves.

108.title: Mentor/Mentee
108.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Mentor/Mentee
108.body: Whether a parent, parent-figure, or merely the guild leader, a mentor guides and shapes the life of a mentee. Examples: Shepherd Book and River, Gandalf and Frodo - Mentees charge this Bond when they ask the mentor for advice and it is given. - Mentors charge this Bond when a mentee follows their advice.

109.title: Rival
109.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Rival
