109.body: You are in competition with your rival. You might want the same woman, the most kills, or something weirder. Example: Legolas and Gimli - Charge this Bond when you witness your rival succeed on a test of fate.

110.title: Sibling
110.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Sibling
110.body: Your first adventures were raiding your mother's cookie jar together. Now, you're guild-mates. Examples: Simon and River, Boromir and Faramir - Charge this Bond when you provide aid to your sibling in a test of fate.

111.title: Unrequited Love
111.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Unrequited Love
111.body: He’s just not that into you. If both players are cool with it, use this Bond to represent how you feel about a would-be suitor or ex-lover. Examples: Simon and Kaylee, Aragorn and Éowyn - Charge this Bond when you do something kind for your love and they rebuff you or turn you down.

112.title: Ward
112.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 5. Bonds › Ward
112.body: You have a guild-mate that you look out for. It’s important they survive. Example: Frodo, River - When your Ward survives an entire Challenge without taking a Wound, charge this Bond.

113.title: 6. Arête
113.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 6. Arête
113.body: Each adventurer has the capacity to exemplify the platonic ideal of their kin, which is called their arête . Arête (AIR-uh-tay) is a word of Greek origin meaning virtue, gnosis, excellence, and evolution. Each kin has an arête talent . Unlike talents associated with an adventurer’s path, arête talents cannot be trained with experience points. You gain arête when you perform certain accomplishments dependent on your kith. The first time you accomplish each particular deed, put a check mark beside it. When you have checked off all three of your arête triggers , you gain your arête talent . See chapter 4 for a list of your kith’s arête triggers and arête talent.

114.title: 7. Languages
114.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 7. Languages
114.body: There are five languages spoken commonly in the City, and a hundred uncommon ones. At a minimum, each adventurer is at least bilingual—choose two languages from the lists below. If you want to learn more languages later, train the Loremaster talent until you’re a skilled linguist. Alternatively, if tracking languages in your game doesn’t feel fun, don’t do it.

115.title: Vulgaris
115.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 7. Languages › Vulgaris
115.body: Vulgaris, the common tongue, is a creole language, developed from a pidgin mash of Ancient Mannish, Vetus, and Tylwyth. Despite a few decades of official censure by the Cult of Mythrys and the City’s rulership as a “base” tongue, Vulgaris is by far the most common language spoken throughout the Wide World by humans, underfolk, and orcs. Most inhabitants of the City speak it decently well.

116.title: Cant
116.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 7. Languages › Cant
116.body: Cant is the language of the lowborn. It is especially famous as the language of thieves, scoundrels, rogues, and ne’er-do-wells. The language is lilting and filled with rhyming couplets, so that it is quite musical when spoken. It is also filled with seeming banalities, so those who speak the Cant seem to be speaking about nothing at all. For example, two thieves might be discussing a planned heist, but seemingly referring to famous actors, the weather, and breeds of puppies. Cant is derived from Vulgaris and shares much of its grammar and vocabulary. However, those without proficiency in this language can absolutely not understand a single sentence of it.

117.title: Chivalric
117.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 7. Languages › Chivalric
117.body: Chivalric is the language of the nobility. All legal and courtly proceedings are conducted in this tongue. If a poor commoner is caught in the justice system without knowledge of this language, the case continues with or without their comprehension. Chivalric shares much of its grammar and vocabulary with Vulgaris, but is couched in romantic, philosophical, and pseudo-religious argot so that it is absolutely impenetrable by those unlearned in its application.

118.title: Tylwyth
118.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 7. Languages › Tylwyth
118.body: Tylwyth is the ancestral language of the fay and other spirits. Since the fay have dwelt within the bounds of the Wide World for much longer than Mankind, many of the spirits and minor divinities that live there speak Tylwyth almost exclusively. The fay, as a whole, are known for their love of languages and Tylwyth enjoys a certain fame among scholars and linguists as being a logical, subtle, and beautiful tongue. Careful cultivation by immortal linguists has developed Tylwyth into a purposeful and useful language, like a carefully pruned tree.

119.title: Vetus
119.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 7. Languages › Vetus
119.body: Vetus has enjoyed over five-hundred years of consistent use and is the official language of the Cult of Mythrys. As the Cult is the center of academia, almost every written text or scholarly book is written in this language. Scholars would be wise to master it. Mythrys made the language sacred by declaring that, in order to more deeply understand the Mysteries that he revealed, all adherents of the faith must learn Vetus, and so avoid the pitfalls and stumbling blocks that come with clumsy translation. Those adherents who do not speak it merely go through the motions during religious festivals. Vetus is written in a flowing cursive script from right to left. It is usually written in an abjad form. The Vetus script is the only language written in the City . Sometimes its script system is (crudely) borrowed for other languages, but books, scrolls, documents, proclamations, and other important texts are only rendered in Vetus.

120.title: Ancient tongues
120.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 7. Languages › Ancient tongues
120.body: History has many ancient modes of speech. These are mostly historical footnotes; few texts remain written in these scripts and there are almost no native speakers. However, some scholars study ancient languages to have a deeper connection with their own race, because their obscure branch of study necessitates it, or because of their love of philology.

121.title: 8. Conditions
121.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 8. Conditions
121.body: The adventurer sheet helps you track your adventurer’s status . Journeying in the Underworld is fraught with peril. It is even rumored that it contains powerful magics that bind your soul to your body. As you journey, you mark conditions to represent the slow degradation of your physical and mental health. Wounds accumulated during Challenges cause you to mark conditions to represent damage. See Wounds for the grisly details of taking Wounds.

122.title: Stressed
122.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 8. Conditions › Stressed
122.body: Stressed represents being physically or mentally exhausted. - Becoming Stressed is usually the result of environmental effects, such as being covered in sewage, being buried alive in a grave, or wading through an icy river. - Wounds do not cause you to be Stressed. - You cannot heal any other condition until you are no longer Stressed. - Learn more about being Stressed.

123.title: Staggered
123.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 8. Conditions › Staggered
123.body: Staggered represents being off balance and out of breath. - This condition has no immediate negative effects. - Staggered is healed automatically during the Camp Phase as long as you’re not Stressed. - It is usually the first condition players choose when Wounded. It’s kind of a “free hit.”

124.title: Wounded
124.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 8. Conditions › Wounded
124.body: Your talents can be Wounded. You may have up to two talents Wounded at a time. - Wounded talents cannot be used until they are healed. - If you already have two talents Wounded, you must choose another condition to mark.

125.title: Injured
125.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 8. Conditions › Injured
125.body: Injured represents being severely hurt. - If you are Injured, the next Wound must give you the Death’s Door condition. - During the Camp Phase, you must heal the Injured condition before healing Wounded talents. - Because being Injured puts you in danger of death, most players only take this condition if they have no other choice.

126.title: Death’s Door
126.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 8. Conditions › Death’s Door
126.body: Death’s Door represents being (almost) dead. You are unconscious and helpless. - Because of the nature of the Underworld, if nobody moves to heal you within a watch, you will become undead. See Death’s Door for more details about the nature of Death’s Door.

127.title: 9. Resolve
127.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 9. Resolve
127.body: You need grit to survive. This is represented with a resource called Resolve. Resolve represents an adventurer’s fortitude as they pursue their quests—fortitude that dwindles as you go deeper and deeper into the Underworld. You have 4 points of Resolve . You may use Resolve in the following ways: - When the GM calls for a test of fate, you may spend a Resolve to gain favor on the test. This can only be done before the test is actually made . Favor allows you to add +3 to the total result of the draw. - You may spend a Resolve to gain favor on a Challenge Action, adding +3 to the total value. - Certain talents require the expenditure of Resolve. You burn charged Bonds to restore your Resolve during the Camp Phase.

128.title: 10. Lore
128.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 10. Lore
128.body: Your adventurer’s motifs define what they are knowledgeable about. You may ask the GM a question related to these motifs and expect an honest answer. We call this bidding lore . When you bid lore, you’re essentially asking “Would my adventurer know this?” Lore represents things that your adventurer knows that you, as the player, might not. This might include the vulnerability of a particular monster, the taboos or habits of a foreign people, or the special properties of a particular plant variety. You may bid lore 4 times between Camp Phases. Your lore bid uses are reset when you Camp . When you bid lore, the GM has three potential responses: - “Yes, you know about this.” The GM then gives a detailed answer. Check off one of your lore bid uses. - “No, you wouldn’t know about this with that motif.” You don’t check off a lore bid use if you don’t receive an answer. - “That question doesn’t seem fair game.” The GM then explains why the lore bid question was too broad or vague. You may rephrase or reframe the question. “They are wrought of ithildin that mirrors only starlight and moonlight, and sleeps until it is touched by one who speaks words now long forgotten in Middleearth. It is long since I heard them, and I thought deeply before I could recall them to my mind.” – The Fellowship of the Ring, J. R. R. Tolkien

129.title: Lore bid questions are discrete
129.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 10. Lore › Lore bid questions are discrete
129.body: You cannot ask, “Have I ever seen anything like this?” The question is too broad. You may ask, “Do I know what the monsters depicted on the bas-relief are?”

130.title: Lore bid answers are thorough
130.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 10. Lore › Lore bid answers are thorough
130.body: The GM cannot say, “You’re not sure, but you think they might be related to dragons.” If an answer is this vague, the player does not need to bid lore. GMs should simply tell them this hint. The GM may say, “You know that these are dragons because you’ve seen their iconography before. As a dragon hunter, though, you recognize that these are fire drakes. These dragons are flightless and live in rivers of lava under the earth. They are famous for their uncontrolled rages and fiery breath.”

131.title: Lore bid questions aren’t a replacement for clever thinking
131.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 10. Lore › Lore bid questions aren’t a replacement for clever thinking
131.body: You cannot ask, “How do you defeat a dragon?” This question is too broad and too subjective. You may ask, “Do I know if a drake has any special vulnerabilities?”

132.title: 11. Talents
132.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 11. Talents
132.body: Talents are the special abilities that set you apart from the rest of the filthy peasants and help you survive delves into the Underworld. A talent can either be unknown , mastered, in training, or mentored .

133.title: Unknown talents
133.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 11. Talents › Unknown talents
133.body: All talents from paths other than your own are unknown . You can, however, train these talents using the mentoring rules below. Talents from other kith and kin are always unknown. They cannot be trained.

134.title: Mastered talents
134.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 11. Talents › Mastered talents
134.body: You begin play with two mastered talents. When you create your adventurer, select one of your path’s talents to master. Your kin talent is also automatically mastered. You may use mastered talents at any point as long as they’re not Wounded and you can pay costs associated with them (such as Resolve).

135.title: In-training path talents
135.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 11. Talents › In-training path talents
135.body: All talents from your path that you have not mastered are automatically in training . You may only use in-training path talents if you spend XP to power them. You must spend 1XP every time you wish to use one of these talents. Once you have spent 7XP powering an in-training path talent, it becomes mastered .

136.title: Mentored talents from other paths
136.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 11. Talents › Mentored talents from other paths
136.body: To train a talent from another path, you must find a willing trainer who has mastered that talent. Both the trainer and the adventurer must use the Train Camp Action or the Train City Action . During this action, the adventurer in training invests XP into the mentored talent. The adventurer in training may then use the new talent a number of times equal to the XP invested. Note that this differs from training talents from your own path. You choose to spend XP to power an unmastered path talent on a per-use basis, whereas you invest XP into a cross-path talent during training. You do not need an instructor to mentor talents from your path. Once you have spent 7XP on training a talent with a mentor, it becomes mastered .

137.title: 12. Experience
137.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 12. Experience
137.body: Wide, not deep, growth It’s worth noting that adventurers in His Majesty the Worm grow “wide” not “deep.” That is, XP allows you to use and master more talents, broadening the options available to you. You do not gain bigger numbers, +1s, more hit points, etc. In addition to XP, there are two other types of growth that adventurers benefit from. The first is arête, a feature of your kith. The second is “weirdness.” As you journey through the Underworld, you get weirder. You accumulate scars, mutations, magical items, pets, mutilations, phobias, etc. There are no rules governing the latter. Finding out how your adventurer gets weirder is essentially the whole game. Experience points (XP) represent an adventurer’s skills improving as they adventure. You spend XP to use talents that you have not yet mastered. During play, if nobody else is currently pursuing their quest, you may declare your quest to the rest of your guild. - If everybody agrees to help you, every player (including you) gains 3XP . - When the guild completes a quest, every player gains 3XP . A guild can only pursue one quest at a time. Once one quest has been completed, someone else should speak up and share the reason they’re descending into the Underworld. If the group agrees to help them, the guild starts the next quest. Pursuing and fulfilling quests is the main way to accumulate experience. There are two other ways to accumulate experience points: - When your guild fulfills a contract for an employer, everybody in the guild gains 1XP. See Current Contracts for information on contracts. - When you take the Carousing City Action, you spend your gold to gain experience points (but risk a splitting hangover). See City Actions for details on this City Action.

138.title: 13. Animal companions and familiars
138.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 13. Animal companions and familiars
138.body: Hirelings? There are no rules for hirelings, henchmen, mercenaries, etc. because that is what you are playing. If you’re going into the Underworld, you’re an adventurer . You’re going down there for some reason, not just gold. Nobody can go into the Underworld unless they’re a member of a guild and nobody is special enough to join a guild unless they’re going to be played by a player. Adventurers sometimes take pets into the Underworld—hunting falcons, small but vicious dogs, trained dire moths, riding boars, and so on. As a general rule, you may have as many animal companions travel with your guild as you can carry feed for. Animal companions need to eat each Camp Phase (just as you do). If they do not, they begin to starve. Starving animals might abandon you entirely in search of food. Animal companions do not have slots for carrying items. You must carry your animal’s feed. The Beast Master talent can train these animal companions so that they can serve at need during dungeon delves. Trained animals will perform one of their commands at your direction. Most normal animals can only learn three commands. If necessary, commands might prompt a test of fate. If the animal is uniquely suited to the test (e.g., monkeys are great at climbing and grabbing stuff, horses are great at pulling), the test is made with favor. Otherwise, no bonuses are added to the test of fate. If nobody in your guild has the Beast Master talent, you may pay animal trainers in the City to train your pets for you (see The Hippodrome of Amet).

139.title: War pigs
139.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 13. Animal companions and familiars › War pigs
139.body: During Challenges, an animal companion does not act unless its owner uses the Command action to have it perform one of its known commands. The GM interprets the pet’s actions, as even well-trained animals will use their own logic and understanding in stressful situations. An animal companion shares its master’s Initiative.

140.title: Wounds and healing
140.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 13. Animal companions and familiars › Wounds and healing
140.body: Unlike adventurers, animal companions usually only have two conditions: Staggered and Injured. Animals do not have talents to Wound. Once an animal companion is Injured, the very next Wound it takes will kill it. The exception to this rule is if the animal is a familiar: a familiar’s owner may spend a Resolve to reduce a killing blow (see Beast Master). These familiars are out of the action but not dead. Animal companions lose the Staggered condition if fed during the Camp Phase. A player may spend one of their charged Bonds to heal their animal’s Injured condition during step 4 of the Camp Phase. Animals can also benefit from the Heal effect.

141.title: 14. Pack space and gear
141.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › 14. Pack space and gear
141.body: Filthy lucre Gold can be easy to get and easy to lose in the adventuring life. Money is used to resupply with essential gear during the City Phase. There is only one denomination of money accepted in the City: gold coins marked with a pentacle. These coins are found in hidden troves in the Underworld. Gold coins (abbreviated “g”) take up slots in your belt or your pack. You can stack 100g to a slot. - A single coin is of small worth. You might toss it to a troubadour in a tavern or a beggar on the street. - 25 gold is a worthy sum. It would make an attractive bribe to a low-level official. - 100 gold is a significant amount of money. It is enough to purchase an item of exquisite craftsmanship or go on a truly epic bender. - 1000 gold is an absolute treasure trove. The contents of your pack are of central importance while adventuring. Do you have enough food to eat or are you starving and staring wild-eyed at your companions? Do you have enough rope to pull yourself out of the body-strewn pit trap? Do you have enough candles to hold back the encircling dark? Tracking the bulk and size of items—represented by slots—is more important than tracking an item’s weight. - Most items take up 1 slot. - Can you hold the item in one hand? If so, it takes up 1 slot. - Anything that you have to hold in two hands takes up 2 slots. - Some things are so bulky that they are oversized . Oversized items take up 2 slots and can only be carried on your belt. - Worn armor is like oversized items because it is carried in your belt slots. Heavier armor takes up more belt slots; see Armor for details. - Some items can be stacked—the whole group of items takes up one slot. - The amount of items in a stack varies; see the description of the item for full details. For example, arrows fit 12 to a slot. Use your adventurer sheet to track where you’re carrying your items. You have four slots to carry items on your belt, twenty-one slots in your pack , and (of course) your two hands . If you put your shield on your back (represented by putting it on your belt) and pull your lantern out of your pack, update your adventurer sheet to reflect this. During Challenges, it’s easier to get things off of your belt (see Pull Item from Belt) than out of your pack (see Pull Item from Pack). One of the things you track in your supply resources is your light source—see pages 94‑95 for rules on light and flickers . Note which hand you’re carrying it in. The adventurer sheet also contains circles so that you can track your gear’s durability. When an item’s durability is compromised, it suffers a Notch. - Fragile items break after 1 Notch. - Items intended for durability break after 2. - Items made of tempered steel can suffer 3. Notched items can be repaired with a tinker's kit or in the City. A list of adventuring items is provided in An incomplete list of pretty things.

142.title: Retirement
142.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › Retirement
142.body: Your quest is the reason you are adventuring. The Underworld sucks. Normal, healthy-brained people don’t want to go there. When you complete your quest, there are two options: retire your adventurer or declare a new quest. When you retire an adventurer, your next adventurer gains one of the following for each 10XP your retired adventurer had: - 1 mastered talent from any path - 1 arête check mark Retired adventurers live in the City and are under the command of the GM. Alternatively, it is possible to declare a new quest to avoid retiring your adventurer. Perhaps, while adventuring, you have found a new reason to journey to the Underworld. If you declare a new quest, you gain 3XP for completing your last quest like everybody else in the guild. Your new quest should make sense in context and be related to the adventures you’ve had. However, you always have to have some reason to go back down into the Underworld. That place seriously sucks. Note that adventurers who die and are lost in the Underworld do not transfer any XP to a new character without use of the Hold a Funeral City Action.

143.title: New adventurer checklist
143.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › New adventurer checklist
143.body: If you have retired your previous adventurer, or if you are a new player just joining the game, the checklist on the following page will help you integrate your new adventurer without the processes of a group-focused Call to Adventure or session 0.

144.title: NEW ADVENTURER CHECKLIST
144.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › NEW ADVENTURER CHECKLIST
144.body: If you’re a new player joining a group playing His Majesty the Worm and you missed session 0, here are the things you need to prepare.

145.title: Prior to your first session
145.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › NEW ADVENTURER CHECKLIST › Prior to your first session
145.body: - Have your adventurer sheet ready. - Have your kin talent and all seven path talents written down. - Determine which path talent you have mastered . The rest are in training. - Choose items from the Omphalic Market – 1 luxurious item, 5 common items, and as many impoverished items as you want. Items needed for one of your talents are impoverished items for you. - Know your own name .

146.title: At your first session
146.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › NEW ADVENTURER CHECKLIST › At your first session
146.body: - At the beginning of the session, select two players with whom you have Bonds . - Say what your adventurer looks like. - Ask questions . Ask about the game world. Ask about the rules. Ask for help about which actions to take. Ask for clarification about how things work. - Give feedback . Let the GM know how it went. Let them know if there’s something you thought could have gone better. Let them know if there was something you liked.

147.title: Prior to your second session
147.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › NEW ADVENTURER CHECKLIST › Prior to your second session
147.body: - Based on your experiences in your first session, fill out a Bond for every member of the Guild.

148.title: At the end of your second session
148.breadcrumb: Chapter 2: The Adventurer › The Call to Adventure › NEW ADVENTURER CHECKLIST › At the end of your second session
148.body: - Based on your experiences in your second session, either join the current guild or elect to create a new adventurer that’s more appealing to you or who meshes with the group dynamic better. - If you join the guild, sign the guild roster and state your role and marching order. - If you join the guild, you’ll join their current quest and gain 3 XP . Lasciate ogni speranza, voi ch'entrate

149.title: Chapter 3: The Guild
149.body: “Why do we travel to remote locations? To prove our adventurous spirit or to tell stories about incredible things? We do it to be alone amongst friends and to find ourselves in a land without man.” – Quoted in The Wildest Dream: The Biography of George Mallory, George Mallory After the First Crusade, the City was presented with a new problem: How to deal with the influx of money. The tops of the forested Spires were literally gilded. Horrible monsters brooded over ancient hordes of coins from a forgotten dynasty. The immense wealth brought by returning crusaders was a great boon and a terrible problem. The Beggar Prince, who was far from a beggar, inadvertently devastated the price of copper and silver when he returned from the Crusade. Prices in the Omphalic Market greatly inflated. To rectify the market, he borrowed all the gold he could house from moneylenders at high interest, founding the Centrum Bank. It was the Tyrant Emperor who imposed the 50% taxes on all coins returning from the Underworld. For every two coins plundered, one would join the royal treasury. Non-liquid assets, like gems, fine clothes, or works of art could pass onto the surface without being taxed: a surfeit of beauty to enrich the City. To better regulate the flow of coin from the Underworld, the Tyrant Emperor further sought to establish control over who descended and ascended. It was decreed that all adventurers must register their names with the Cult, as well as some sign or symbol that they might be identified by. This led to the formation of guilds, with adventurers incorporating as collective units and borrowing from the human custom of heraldry. When the Griffin King rose to power, many (very wealthy) adventurers asked him to unmake the Tyrant’s edicts—or, at the least, lower the tax rate. He did not.

150.title: The Guild Roster
150.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster
150.body: Collectively, you and your other adventurers form a guild during the Call to Adventure. In the same way that you track your adventurer by way of your adventurer sheet, the entire table tracks the guild by way of the guild roster . The guild roster can be downloaded from hismajestytheworm.games .

151.title: 1. Guild name
151.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster › 1. Guild name
151.body: All players collectively decide a guild name . This incorporates your guild as a legal entity in the City, for whom it is lawful to descend to the Underworld. Choose a name that is evocative of your guild’s theme and representative of your guild’s shared goals. Most importantly, choose a guild name that is cool and sounds fun to everybody. Example guild names: the Four Aces, the Maidens of the Moon, the Steel-clad Snakes, the Handmaidens, Justice’s Sons, the Faith Militant, the Kegbreakers, the Chimera Company, the Brotherhood of the Burned Banner, His Majesty’s Delvers of Unplumbed Depths, the Sword Sisters, the Finders, the Busy Bees

152.title: 2. Terms
152.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster › 2. Terms
152.body: The guild roster defines your guild’s rules for looting rights. The default contract stipulates that all members of the guild split loot equally and funeral rights are paid for by the guild. As you fill out the guild roster, take a moment to talk about your guild’s looting rights, who gets the most shares, how expenses are arranged, what happens to fallen adventurers’ gear, etc.

153.title: 3. Sigil
153.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster › 3. Sigil
153.body: Informed by the guild name, the players collectively choose the guild’s seal, heraldry, or portraiture. Fay guilds prefer the use of abstract seals: kaleidoscopes of shapes that roughly correspond to some natural phenomenon like a mountain range, a meaningful flower, or an auspicious star sign. Underfolk guild sigils layer meaning in beautiful calligraphy. Both orcs and humans prefer heraldic symbols of animals and monsters that evoke a sense of danger, humor, or power. The player with the most artistic skill should draw a sigil or a sketch of the guild in the space allotted on the guild roster sheet.

154.title: 4. Marching order
154.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster › 4. Marching order
154.body: It is important to understand the order in which the guild marches. For instance, if there is a pressure-plate trap in a hallway in the Castle of Crossed Destinies, the GM should consult the guild roster sheet. This trap ignores lighter adventurers, such as halflings or gnomes, but activates when someone human-sized or larger steps on it. The first adventurer in the marching order with enough weight to trigger the plate will suffer the consequences. Each player decides where they want their adventurer to fall in the marching order. Write down your marching order—whether you’re in the first position, second position, last position, etc. If you’re the first person in the marching order, you have an opportunity to react to dangers the guild approaches. - The GM will tell you what you see and ask you what you do. - For example, if you spot a goblin, will you attack, shout a warning, or order a retreat? - This action is a split-second decision on your part. - The GM might call for a test of Cups if the danger you’re marching into is particularly well hidden and your guild is not moving carefully. - If you’re first in the marching order, you will also be the first attacked by charging foes. If you’re in the middle of the marching order, you have someone in front of and behind you. This can be the safest position (sometimes). If you’re the last person in the marching order, you have similar responsibilities to the person in front. - You act as a lookout and must deal with ambushes (Ambushes and surprise). - If danger comes up behind you, the GM will tell you what you see and ask you what you do.

155.title: 5. Role
155.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster › 5. Role
155.body: Decide what job you have in the guild. There is no exhaustive list and no mechanics tied to this decision. Instead, your choice of guild role gives you a niche inside which you operate during play. Your guild role might determine what Camp Action (Camp Actions) you take. For example, a cartographer might be obliged to use the Update Maps action for the good of the guild, a smith might use their tinker’s kit to repair armor, and a cook might prepare rations from hunted game. Your guild’s theme will inform the guild roles available. A pirating guild that spends time raiding will feel very different from a witch hunting guild sent by the Cult to root out corrupt magic users. Here’s a quick, non-exhaustive list of guild roles for inspiration: Role Role --- --- bodyguard houndmaster burglar hunter cartographer link-boy captain look-out chirugeon man-at-arms commander navigator cook porter face scout first mate tinker guide translator henchman trapsmith If all else fails, just write “Sell-sword.” It’ll do in a pinch.

156.title: The guild contract
156.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster › 5. Role › The guild contract
156.body: We, the Undersigned, agree to a journey and subsequent extraction from the Underworld of any and all goods, valuables, and chattels (which activities are described collectively herein as the Adventure), which shall proceed in a timely manner and with all due care and consideration as seen fit by majority rule, to wit, the Guild, named: Funeral expenses to be defrayed by Guild or representatives, if occasion arises and the matter is not otherwise arranged for. Agreed hereto, freely and under neither duress nor force nor coercion nor extortion nor threat to life and/or limb, and superseding any prior contract, agreement or undertaking, survivable clauses notwithstanding, signed and witnessed below, as set forth hereunder:

157.title: 6. Current Contracts
157.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster › 6. Current Contracts
157.body: The Underworld has monsters and it has treasure. Powerful, influential, and rich people want things in the Underworld. They offer contracts: risk for reward. Do what they want in the Underworld and they’ll make you rich too. When your guild takes a contract, note it on the “Current Contract” space of your guild roster sheet. When you fulfill a contract, everybody in the guild gains 1XP. It’s the GM’s job to create interesting characters who offer interesting contracts in the City; see Plan the next Crawl for more details. Whereas a guild may only pursue one quest at a time, a guild may have as many contracts at a time as seems prudent. Patrons who aren’t receiving results, however, may withdraw the contract, defame the guild, or take matters into their own hands. In general, fulfilling a contract is a smaller and more discrete task than finishing a quest. A quest might require several descents into the Underworld; generally, contracts only take one or two.

158.title: 7. Noteworthy Deeds and Fame
158.breadcrumb: Chapter 3: The Guild › The Guild Roster › 7. Noteworthy Deeds and Fame
158.body: When great deeds are done in the Underworld, the whole City buzzes. Adventurers are big business—guilds that pull off big stunts will start to attract the attention of important people. Each discrete achievement your guild accomplishes are cataloged as noteworthy deeds . You track your noteworthy deeds on the guild roster during step 2 of the City Phase (Noteworthy deeds). Your guild’s Fame is equal to the number of noteworthy deeds you have performed. Fame is an abstract measurement of how much gossip and name recognition your guild receives. Fame is rated 0–5. The GM frames role-playing exchanges within the context of your current Fame score. Fame Reaction :---: --- 0 “Who are you again? Am I supposed to have heard of you?” 1 Token name recognition 2 Known generally in the Underworld 3 Famous within the Underworld 4 Known generally in the City 5 Famous within the City Note that Fame isn’t necessarily good . It just means people have heard of your deeds. If all of your deeds are dastardly, you’ll be known as dastards. If your guild’s Fame is very high, a GM character’s starting Disposition might be more or less favorable (Starting Disposition).

159.title: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin
159.body: There is no lore. As you’re reading this chapter, you’ll notice there’s a lot of fantasy gibberish. If it’s inspiring, riff on the provided concepts for your character. If it’s confusing, limiting, or contradictory to your own ideas, ignore it. Mark through it with a Sharpie. Write in the margins of the book. Make your game world your own. “Tyger, Tyger, burning bright In the forests of the night, What immortal hand or eye Could frame thy fearful symmetry? – “The Tyger,” William Blake The Wide World is a sprawling place, with many strange creatures, exotic cultures, religious schisms, warring clans, and ancient lineages. No two fay folk are alike, even as humans have infinite variation. From the solitary trolls of the Rimemark, to the noble elves of Alfheim, to the tribes of barbarians scourging the Ghostgrass Plains, to the stoic templars of Mythrys, there are many peoples in the Wide World—and they all congregate in the City in search of glory and riches in the Underworld.

160.title: Humans
160.body: When does pride become hubris? When does glory tarnish to vainglory? This thin line is embodied in humans, the knaves and the kings of the Wide World. Humans are not as hardy as the immortal fay, being given to sickness and age. Nor are they as crafty as the underfolk, being slow to develop the crafts of alchemy and lore of natural philosophy. Yet humanity has one gift that surpasses every other: war. Humankind is built for war. The crafts they have learned from dwarves and elves have been turned ingeniously to this purpose. They breed and mature quickly to resupply their cities with men and women, replacing those lost to hardship. They are fierce, doughty, and brave. Using their arts of war, mankind has conquered much of the Wide World. They are the conquering kings, proud and terrible. Even so, they are fractious. Humanity has never united themselves under a single banner (though various warlords have attempted the feat). Matters of philosophy, religion, or blood will divide them—as will ambition. Therefore, the power of men is spread through a handful of notable empires and hundreds of petty kingdoms. Still, humans display many praiseworthy traits. They are loyal folk, lauding fidelity as the most noble of virtues. They long remember the deeds of their fathers in song and story, and strive to emulate them. This, in turn, creates a drive to win glory and renown for their families. Their communities are strengthened by this desire for fame, as they eschew the unworthy for fear of bringing shame to their lineage. Indeed, few folk are more fiercely protective of their kith and kin than mankind. They have a great capacity for kindness, for all their ferocity.

161.title: A myth of humankind
161.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › A myth of humankind
161.body: The Monad is one. The Monad is many. Like a sky scattered with many constellations; like a building with many sides; the Monad has many faces that all reflect the greater truth of His unity. It was the prophet Mythrys who taught us these mysteries (praise be unto him). It was Maiden Wisdom who gave him birth (blessed be her name). Mythrys taught us that the many gods honored by the different great houses were all emanations of the one true god. This one true god is called the Monad. Mythrys taught that the Monad has twenty-one separate emanations. And, though maidens might pray to the Lovers for aid in love, and warriors might pray to the Strong for aid in battle, all prayers and honor are ultimately going to Him. For men have limited perceptions, and see many faces where there is but one. The Monad is the Magician, who long ago revealed the workings of magic to men. He is also the High Priestess, who heals the sick and protects children and mothers. He is also the Charioteer, who rides the night sky and guides sailors. He is the god of the Moon. He is the goddess of the Sun. He is Death. He is the World. He is the Devil, who made everything wrongly.

162.title: Human names
162.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human names

163.title: Male names:
163.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human names › Male names:
163.body: Addam, Alesander, Bennard, Carl, Dafyd, Edric, Fenton, Gregor, Jack, Justinius, Kevyn, Lews, Marq, Omer, Polliver, Reynard, Robin, Samwell, Sylvestris, Tybalt, Usher, Zachery

164.title: Female names:
164.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human names › Female names:
164.body: Alanys, Brenda, Catlyn, Colette, Dion, Eleanor, Imogen, Janna, Jonquil, Kaya, Lanna, Marla, Olivia, Regan, Rhonda, Saera, Sybelle, Tanselle, Ursula, Violet, Walda Every human is a member of a kinship group called a house . Humans either introduce themselves by saying “of House X,” or by simplifying their house name into a surname. There are hundreds of houses active in the City; six examples on the following page.

165.title: Human kin
165.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human kin
165.body: Humans divide the world into two parts: us and them. They do this by forming great and noble houses. They bind themselves together through marriage, love, and oaths. They fly beautiful banners over their keeps and display proud coats of arms on their crafts. They are instilled with a respect of certain virtues from a young age. Even the basest born and most wretched slave children are born where some banner flies. Two humans with the same house are of the same kin. They might not be directly related, but they probably know each other. Human characters begin the game with the following talent:

166.title: Kin talent: Proud and Ancient
166.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human kin › Kin talent: Proud and Ancient
166.body: Describe or draw the sigil of your house. Write the motto of your house. When your house sigil or motto is dramatically appropriate for an action being attempted, you test fate with favor. Additionally, during Challenges, you may spend a Resolve and use the Speak Incantation action to cry your motto aloud. You—and all members of your house that hear your war cry—gain favor on their next action.

167.title: Human houses
167.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses
167.body: Optional rule: Turncloak If you ever betray or turn against your house, you lose the Proud and Ancient talent and gain the Turncloak talent : Whenever you play up your legacy of deceit and your infamy, role-play what you say. If it would repulse your fellow humans or turn your heart blacker still, you gain favor on tests of fate that work against your house or humankind in general. Don’t start out as a Turncloak. Play and find out why you become one. The following houses are active in the City. Use them for your adventurers or let them serve as examples for new houses.

168.title: House Crowell
168.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses › House Crowell
168.body: Crest: A crowned porcupine Motto: I shall do as I will House Crowell never submitted to the Empire, preferring to dwell in the destitution of the highlands rather than bend the knee. But when the Empire failed, there were few compelling reasons to avoid real civilization. So, occasionally, highlanders will fly the crowned porcupine and descend upon the City, determined to drain every drop of ale from the taverns. The folk of Crowell are bold, brash, and quick in both anger and friendship.

169.title: House Gryphes
169.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses › House Gryphes
169.body: Crest: A gold griffin rampant Motto: Thus always to tyrants! House Gryphes just bleeds chivalry, and if you’re extremely good at jousting, you might get some on you. This three-part house was formed by the assassins who overthrew the Tyrant Emperor and destroyed the Empire. Previously, the griffin was thought to be a purely heraldic beast—a combination of the sigils of the three founding houses. Somehow, though, House Gryphes began breeding these hitherto imaginary creatures as mounts. Now, you’ll see the Griffin King and his circle of Griffin Knights flying above the City, smiling toothily down at the gravity-constrained commoners.

170.title: House Heartsbane
170.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses › House Heartsbane
170.body: Crest: A black dragon below a sword impaling a heart Motto: Eat the weak An ancient house, Heartsbane was known in the earliest ages for the gruesome practice of eating their fallen enemies. Though somewhat ignoble, their deeds in battle in recent years have earned them much fame. Their family's famous sword, which bears the same name as their house, was said to have felled many orcs—as well as Swart Arthi, a terrible black dragon. Rumors persist that secret trap doors in their dungeon’s cells lead directly to the kitchen’s ovens, but House Heartsbane has proved to be a potent and powerful house despite such gossip.

171.title: House Ironpax
171.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses › House Ironpax
171.body: Crest: A crown weeping blood Motto: Peace through strength Members of House Ironpax stretch the definition of “man-sized.” They are the biggest fuckers around, only a little shorter than trolls. It is said that in the first ages they bred with giants (but if that's true, the giants don't seem to remember any fair feelings for those of Ironpax, and will eat them just as happily as they eat everybody else). If it matters, House Ironpax supported the Tyrant Emperor. This makes them somewhat unpopular these days, as the Last Emperor is not remembered kindly. They also have a tendency to mutter about fealty and traitors when they're in their cups. Most people don't bother to ask them to speak up, though. They really are quite large folk.

172.title: House Mourn
172.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses › House Mourn
172.body: Crest: A white and black bend, with crow in white field and moon in black field Motto: For our sins For the crime of witchcraft two centuries ago, House Mourn was exiled to the frozen north. It was that hard land (or the sorcery) that has given members of this house a sunken, pale, unwholesome look—as if something not quite dead. Today, magic is thought of somewhat less dimly than in the days of the Empire (but only somewhat). The Wild of Mourn (which is how they style the lady of their house) guards the peaceful lands of the south from the rampaging orcish reavers by use of her sorcery. Occasionally, she’ll send one of her nephews or cousins down south to the City on some odd errand for the Tower of Penitence, wherein she dwells.

173.title: Arête
173.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses › Arête
173.body: Humans gain arête by performing the following deeds: - Getting married - Fulfilling an oath - Defeating a member of a rival house in fair tournament or duel When a human accomplishes all three arête triggers, they gain the following talent:

174.title: Human arête talent: Byname
174.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses › Human arête talent: Byname
174.body: Bynames For human bynames, we usually ask the player what event or instance was their proudest. Then, we elicit the help of the table to think of the coolest byname based on that event. This is done in secret, away from the player. We then have an important character grant the byname to the adventurer in a dramatically appropriate fashion. You are given a byname, like “the Tall,” “the Corpsegrinder, “the Patron Saint of Pilgrims,” or “the Blackhearted.” When that byname would be relevant to a test of fate, similar to a motif, you test with favor.

175.title: Human role-playing concepts
175.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Humans › Human houses › Human role-playing concepts
175.body: - Humans exhibit almost infinite variation . - Humans worship a confusing pantheon of gods (i.e., the major arcana of the tarot). They have a complicated theology to explain why they all worship the same god. - Humans are familial. They laud fidelity and filial piety as great virtues. - Humans are communal. They assemble themselves into great houses or clans. They internalize their community’s values. - Humans are individuals. They laud personal accomplishments and they shame personal failures.

176.title: Fay
176.body: “Oh God. They’re beautiful.” “Oh God. They’re terrible.” Some spirits are content with dwelling in the far realms as entities of Platonic thought. Others yearn to be bound with weight and hunger, and so come into the plane of Flesh. We call these spirits the fay. In the earliest ages of the world, troops of the fay came into freshly formed creation, eager to try out the pleasures and perils of wearing skin. It was to their very great surprise that it was easier to enter the realm of Flesh than it was to leave it. Those who did not go insane from this realization became known as the elves. Elves consider themselves the eldest people for they existed outside the circles of the Wide World long before it was even formed. (The oldest living sentient race that actually physically dwelt in the Wide World is, of course, the orcs.) And “being old” is one thing the elves do very well. They are ageless, and never die from old age or infirmity. Some elves alive today are, indeed, very, very old. And when you are very, very old, you have a lot of experiences to draw upon—you can be very, very wise. Hence, elves are commonly thought to be both the eldest and the wisest folk. It is noteworthy that elves do not breed and create clans like men do. Though their bodies have all the functionality of mortal life, immortality cannot generate life. All elven births are stillborn—with two exceptions. The first exception is if one of the elven parents lays down their life for the sake of a child: either parent can pass on their own spirit to reincarnate into their own child at the moment of birth. The second exception is gnomes. When elves realized that they could not generate new life (only reincarnate), they decided to solve the problem like they solved many other problems: magic. They stole the children of mortal mothers, rationalizing that they would “save” the children from eventual old age and death. They used rites from the realm of dreams, transforming the children from mortal to immortal. The early elves first assumed this would change the infants into elven children. They were mistaken. It transformed them into gnomes, their skin wrinkled and their forms hunched and twisted. Instead of being eternally beautiful and youthful, they became eternally bent and aged. Elves and gnomes, on the whole, differ in opinion about whether or not the creation of gnomes (and the continued practice) was good and justifiable or not. But one thing almost all fay agree on is to not share this secret with the mortal races. Gnomes are immortal, just like their elven “parents.” Unlike the elves, however, gnomes are hunched and wizened, not eternally youthful. Elves, as spirits, embody concepts easily. Gnomes lack this purpose and so are prone to feelings of existentialism. The largest problem that gnomes face, however, is a sense of otherness and exclusion. Gnomes don't “fit in” with elves easily and struggle to be fully integrated into the rites and rituals of the fay. Elves understand that the gnomes feel excluded from their society, but rarely know what to do about it. Unlike humankind, which has sprawled into many clans and principalities, elves and gnomes live together in Alfheim, the singular kingdom of the fay. The goddess and queen of the fay is a strange three-part spirit named the Tripartite. It is said that she (they? it?) is a single entity that coexists in three places. One of the Tripartite's three faces rules each of the three elven courts. The Maid of Mists, who rules the Court of the Sun, is a young queen of sixteen apparent years with a gentle and courtly demeanor. For her sake, elven knights ride out on errantry to do good works throughout the Wide World. Every winter, she holds a feast for her court where their tales of bravery and chivalry are recounted. The Witchmother is a potent huntress and warrior woman that leads the Court of the Maimed Moon. Horns spring from her head and she can assume many bestial shapes. Once a year she leads her court on a crazed hunt across the Wide World pursuing some unlikely game. This event is called the Wild Hunt. The third face of the Tripartite is the Crone, who rules the Court of Fallen Stars. The Crone is the stuff of children's nightmares. The less said about her, her loyal hairy skulls, her detachable eye, and her chicken-legged hut, the better.

177.title: A myth of the fay
177.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › A myth of the fay
177.body: There was, o’ what there was in the oldest of days and ages and times. The Sun ruled as king in Heaven, and the Moon was his queen. Together, they kindled innumerable Stars to be their children, and arrayed them in gold and silver. The Citadel of Heaven was beautiful and its people were happy. Among the people of the Sun’s retinue was one named Abyss, who wore a cloak that looks like the space-between-stars. The Sun called on Abyss and asked her to tell him of the goings-on of Earth, where water and sand were being scattered. Abyss told the Sun that the dragons had invented a thing called Death. The Sun became quite fearful. The Sun called on his eldest child, who was named Second Sun, to serve as his personal guard. He sealed the Citadel of Heaven to ensure that Death could not enter. He quieted the celebrations of the Stars so he could ensure he could always hear Death coming. He had Abyss forge a sword named Eclipse for Second Sun to wield in his defense. And o’, what a sad thing happened with that sword…

178.title: Fay names
178.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay names
178.body: Fay names mean something. They are rendered in the fay tongue, Tylwyth, and followed by a translation in Vulgaris (in the style of a human surname). For the fay, it is the meaning of the name that is particularly important, not just the collection of syllables and sounds. Names are not gendered; any name can be carried by a person of any gender.

179.title: Fay names (with Vulgaris surname):
179.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay names › Fay names (with Vulgaris surname):
179.body: Adahay Lives-in-Woods, Bidziil He-is-Strong, Cha Tima the Caller, Dadgayadoh Gambling-Men, Elsu Flying-Falcon, Fala Crow, Honiahaka Little-Wolf, Ituha Sturdy-Oak, Kizikoni Burning-Fire, Makya Eagle-Hunter, Nahiossi Three-Fingers, Onacona White-Owl, Qaleteqa Warden, Sakuruta Coming-Sun, Takoda Friend-to-Everyone, Vaive Atoish Alights-on-the-Cloud, Waban East-Wind

180.title: Fay kin
180.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin
180.body: Elves factionalize into three different kin, depending on the far realm from which they originally came. They call each faction a “court.” The gnomes, stolen into immortality, call themselves a “court” as well.

181.title: High elves
181.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › High elves
181.body: The Court of the Sun, sometimes called the high elves, have spiritual origins tied to the Welkin. The high elves dwell on mountain tops in beautifully carved castles of stone. High elves put much stock in the human notions of chivalry, courtly manners, and grace. They emulate the human traditions of knighthood and the chivalric code. Almost everybody agrees they have perfected this institution.

182.title: High elf talent: Read the Past
182.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › High elves › High elf talent: Read the Past
182.body: All high elves have eidetic memories. Bid lore to accurately recall anything you have ever seen or heard. You can go back and count the beads of sweat on your mother's forehead on the day of your birth, if you wish.

183.title: Dark elves
183.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Dark elves
183.body: Beneath the forest, beneath great hollowed out mounds, dwell the dark elves who call themselves the Court of Fallen Stars. The dark elves are descended from spirits of the Wastes, and their appearance and demeanor echo those grim specters. If mortals consider elves with a sort of awe, this awe becomes a reverential fear when considering the dark elves. Though never dying, dark elves are obsessed with the trappings of death. They spend their lives looking into the void between stars in hopes of foreseeing their eventual demise.

184.title: Dark elf talent: Foretell
184.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Dark elves › Dark elf talent: Foretell
184.body: Bid lore to ask the GM: “ If I do X, will Y happen?” You receive a “yes” or “no” answer in the form of a prophetic hunch.

185.title: Wood elves
185.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Wood elves
185.body: Below the high elven mountains there lies the sprawling forests of the Court of the Maimed Moon, also called the wood elves. The wood elves, who are descended from spirits of the Weald, do not make permanent shelters in the forest, but practice a nomadic lifestyle where they follow herds of game seasonally. Wood elves are great weavers, and weave wood and grasses into many beautiful things—ships, bridges, shelters, and armor. Wood elves often tattoo living plants onto their skin that grow and shift into new patterns over time.

186.title: Wood elf talent: Keen Senses
186.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Wood elves › Wood elf talent: Keen Senses
186.body: Wood elves have the eyes of a hawk and the nose of a wolf. A wood elf’s senses can grow so acute that they can hear the chatter of living stone, the gossip of growing roots, or the rumors of passing insects. Bid lore to temporarily sharpen one of your senses beyond normal limits and ask the GM a question based on these heightened senses. Example questions might include: - “ If I focus my sight, can I read their lips from here?” - “ If I listen very closely, can I tell if anybody is invisible here? Like, do I hear anybody breathing or any heartbeats or anything?” - “I take a tiny taste and spit it back out. Can I tell if it’s poisoned?” - “Based on their scent, can I tell which path the thief went down?” This ability only lasts a moment. As normal, if the GM does not give you any new information, you do not expend a lore bid.

187.title: Gnomes
187.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Gnomes
187.body: And, of course, there are the gnomes, who are called the Court of Redcaps for the stout red hats that gnome men wear and the large mushrooms in which they dwell. It is true what they say about children that run away and live with the elves: they find immortality and never grow up. They do, however, grow old. The human body was never meant to live forever. These children—these gnomes—soon find themselves twisted by the elven food they eat and their own strange dreams. Still, they learn a lot over the course of their unnaturally lengthened lives.

188.title: Gnome talent: Weird, Wise, Ancient
188.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Gnomes › Gnome talent: Weird, Wise, Ancient
188.body: When you bid lore, you can ask a follow-up question to the answer for free.

189.title: Arête
189.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Arête
189.body: Fay gain arête by performing the following deeds: - Killing something without using a weapon - Providing aid to a spirit - Making someone they’ve kissed cry When a fay accomplishes all three arête triggers, they gain one of the following talents:

190.title: High elf arête talent: Akashic Consciousness
190.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Arête › High elf arête talent: Akashic Consciousness
190.body: Some high elves can cast their memories back through their bloodlines and ask questions of their ancestors or past incarnations. Spend a Resolve and ask the GM any question about an event that happened in the past. If it’s at all possible that one of your ancestors would know about it, the GM will answer the question.

191.title: Dark elf arête talent: Spout Doom
191.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Arête › Dark elf arête talent: Spout Doom
191.body: Spend a Resolve to ask the GM: “ If I do X, what will happen?” The GM provides a prophecy, which pours unbidden out of your mouth.

192.title: Wood elf arête talent: Area Sense
192.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Arête › Wood elf arête talent: Area Sense
192.body: Spend 2 Resolve to meditate for a watch (Watches). Draw a card. The GM describes a number of interesting “visions” equal to the value of the drawn card during your meditation. (Remember, pages have a value of 11, knights have a value of 12, etc.) These visions are sensual experiences. For example, you could hear the clatter of dice as bored crusaders gamble, smell a nearby goblin taking a shit, hear two guards talking about who’s going to be on duty tonight, sense the quivering tension of a spike trap embedded in the ceiling, and so on. The GM provides these details by looking at their map and Meatgrinder table. Starting near the player’s current area and moving outwards, the GM provides one salient detail from the nearby rooms. Each vision should yield a meaningful detail (e.g., the presence of a hidden door, detected by an imperceptible draft in a nearby room), but need not be elaborate or detailed (i.e., the GM need not mention that the door is trapped, or that it is activated by pulling on a statue’s arm). Any Meatgrinder events that occur when a watch passes are resolved after the GM has given your visions.

193.title: Gnome arête talent: Uncanny Knowledge
193.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Arête › Gnome arête talent: Uncanny Knowledge
193.body: If nobody at the table has an appropriate motif to bid lore about a subject, you may bid lore about the issue at hand. This is similar to having a motif of “Whatever You Don’t Know, I Know.”

194.title: Elven role-playing concepts
194.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Elven role-playing concepts
194.body: - Elves are a lot like humans but everything is turned up to eleven. Heroes are so heroic. Villains are absolutely villainous. Elves love to play out archetypes. - Fay society is a lot like human society, but just a little different. Instead of dogs, elves keep foxes. Instead of horses, elves ride stags. Elves still have cats, though. - Elves succeed with less “technology” than humans. They do not write books because they can rely on the memories of the high elves. They do not practice advanced metallurgy because they have the weavings of the wood elves. Alfheim relies on magic for many of its crafts. - Gods are real to the elves. Their goddess (goddesses?), the Tripartite, literally rules their society. Having invisible gods is weird.

195.title: Gnome role-playing concepts
195.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Fay › Fay kin › Gnome role-playing concepts
195.body: - What if you made children super smart and let them live with demigods? Gnomes, that’s what. Gnomes act a little bit like the children in Village of the Damned. Elves probably don’t realize that gnomes are weird, but humans do. - Gnomes have a bad sense of humor. When impending doom is coming on them, they laugh. When they’re dying, they tell a joke. They really go in for physical humor and slapstick, too. - Seriously though, aren’t mushrooms the best?

196.title: Underfolk
196.body: Beneath your feet there are worlds. There are lives lived, tragedies experienced, arguments made, trysts discovered. There are wars fought, there are treasures wrought. Beneath your feet, there are the underfolk. The term “underfolk” refers to three distinct kins—the dwarves, the halflings, and the trolls. The underfolk, however, consider themselves to be one people. Dwarves and halflings consider themselves to be the same race, and happily consider trolls to be adopted siblings. Humans have trouble getting along, finding ways to split hairs over religion and heredity. The underfolk have no such difficulties—they consider themselves one family. The underfolk are the progenitors of civilization. True, humans really ran with the concept, but dwarves first thought of it. Writing systems, advanced math, complex forms of government, written contracts, common law—all underfolk inventions. These were all taught to humanity when humans first came to the Wide World from parts unknown. The underfolk and humans have always been allies. Underfolk society is ruled by the Council of Liveries. This is not as much of a plutocracy as it seems at first. Everybody in underfolk society is liveried—that is, a member of a mercantile organization—so everybody ostensibly has a voice. That’s the theory anyway. The underfolk have a practical view of religion. They acknowledge that the various deities of the men and elves might be real and potent, but also rationalize that these deities probably don’t care about the poor little underfolk hiding from their gaze under the earth. They do not believe that their spirits, on death, depart to any afterlife. Their souls are too heavy. They believe they all linger in the plane of Flesh after death as ghosts. Ghosts, of course, have needs too. That’s why the underfolk construct large tombs full of nice things to occupy themselves when they finally die. Since cities tend to get filled with tombs, underfolk are always tunneling out new homes. Whole cities have been left behind that are just necropoli now.

197.title: A myth of the underfolk
197.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › A myth of the underfolk
197.body: The underfolk are, compared to some of the other kith, decidedly non-religious. They do have three religious texts, which they love to quote and reference. These are the Book of Traditions, the Book of Proverbs, and the Book of Broken Oaths. The Book of Traditions, informally called the Doings, teaches how the underfolk should structure their births, deaths, marriages, oaths, do business, do work, take rest, and so on. Here is one example: When a child is born, the midwife shall keep it for seven days. On the eighth, she shall bring it and lay it on the doorstep of the household that carried and bore it. If the father picks the child up from the doorstep and carries it within, it shall be part of the household, and his responsibility. However, the father may decline to do this. If the father declines, the mother may pick up the child from the doorstep and carry it within; it shall be part of the household and, the mother must now take over the role of provider. The father is absolved of this responsibility. However, the mother may decline to do this. If the mother declines, let none weep. The little ghost shall be a brownie, and will serve the household well. The Book of Proverbs, informally called the Sayings, provides an endless resource of folk wisdom, moral tales, truisms, poetic turns of phrase, euphemisms, and good old-fashioned common sense. Here is one example: The Dog returns to his Vomit and the Sow returns to her Mire, And the burnt Fools bandaged hand goes wobbling back to the Fire. They also have the Book of Broken Oaths, a history of the early underfolk and their relationship with the Creator. It tells the story of how the underfolk broke ties with the Creator and suffered terrible hardships for breaking troth, but willingly did so in order that future generations might escape the burden of the oaths. This text is written in Ancient Underfolk, and few understand it. No examples of the text are included here.

198.title: Underfolk names
198.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk names

199.title: Underfolk male names:
199.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk names › Underfolk male names:
199.body: Angus, Bill, Clive, Felix, Geoff, Giles, Graham, Jack, Nigel, Pat, Prentice, Rodney, Ruel, Robin, Ted, Tom, Warwick, Wesley, Will

200.title: Underfolk female names:
200.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk names › Underfolk female names:
200.body: Alice, Bonnie, Bryonie, Camise, Dee, Edith, Evie, Gillian, Helen, Liza, Lulu, Maggie, Molly, Nuala, Patty, Pansy, Pippa, Rose, Ruth, Sue Underfolk use their livery—their profession—as their last name.

201.title: Underfolk livery names:
201.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk names › Underfolk livery names:
201.body: Bellowsmender, Blacksmith, Brewer, Carpenter, Chandler, Cooper, Joiner, Miner, Runescrivner, Sculptor, Stonemason, Tailor, Tinker, Vintner, Wainwright, Weaver, Whitesmith

202.title: Underfolk kin
202.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin
202.body: Crafting Crafting is important for the underfolk culture in general and their arête triggers specifically. In general, crafting something (especially something that will last for centuries) is a City Action. Underfolk players might be interested in making specialized weapons or armor, or they may want to raise statues or monuments to themselves. Writing a treatise, a biography, or a popular song might also qualify as “crafting something that will last centuries.” These efforts will probably require gold, with larger works needing larger payments. This is intentional. Underfolk are known to be ambitious, and this requirement encourages this behavior in play. The Build and Commission Craft City Actions are two options. But GMs will need to work with their players to work out expectations for what underfolk players want to accomplish. Whether large or small, halfling or troll, all underfolk consider themselves to be members of the same family.

203.title: Dwarves
203.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Dwarves
203.body: Dwarves are the core of underfolk society. They’re hard workers. In many ways, they are industry personified. Dwarves are obsessive creatures. They love to create. When they discover what craft most interests them, they dedicate themselves completely to it. Their hours are spent perfecting their craft, innovating in their craft, critiquing examples of their craft, and tearing it all down so they can start again and do it right this time. Really, drinking is the only thing that keeps a dwarf steady. It evens them out, mellows them down, lets their mind work on problems that aren’t exclusively about their craftwork. All this obsessiveness pays off. Dwarf-craft is both practical and beautiful. It is highly sought after, which makes them rich. This is important for dwarves, who know the purpose of life: construct your tomb, because that’s where you’re going to spend the rest of eternity. Woe to the dwarf whose ghost goes to the afterlife bored.

204.title: Dwarf talent: Labor Unending
204.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Dwarves › Dwarf talent: Labor Unending
204.body: You may mark the Stressed condition to stay awake all night and perform two Camp Actions instead of one; see Camp Actions for details.

205.title: Halflings
205.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Halflings
205.body: Halflings are a peaceable people, good-natured, and inclined to be friendly. When dwarves make stuff, it’s the halflings who turn that stuff into gold. Of course, they take a little commission for their trouble. This is generally agreed upon to be a good relationship, because dwarves and humans don’t always see eye to eye. Besides, dwarves would rather be making. Halflings fill in the gaps in domestic work. Dwarves might not notice that their workshops fill up with old scraps, empty oil cans, and soot, but the halflings certainly do. Halflings like the finer things in life. They like things to be clean, put together, and respectable. Therefore, if something needs cleaning, fixing, and putting-right, halflings often do that job themselves. If halflings have one failing, it’s their love of creature comforts. Few people like eating as much as halflings enjoy their auntie’s mushroom pie. Few people like drinking as much as halflings enjoy the pint of bitter from the Bird and Baby Tavern. Few people like smoking as much as halflings enjoy a pipe full of Old Toby from the summer harvest of ‘45.

206.title: Halfling talent: Hale and Hearty
206.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Halflings › Halfling talent: Hale and Hearty
206.body: If you eat two rations instead of one during step 2 of the Camping Phase, you may charge an uncharged Bond.

207.title: Trolls
207.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Trolls
207.body: Trolls were discovered, not born. Sculptors sometimes say that a statue is inside a block of marble, and you just need to scrape away everything that isn’t the statue. Dwarves found this to be true of trolls. As dwarves tunneled, they were surprised to find living beings embedded in the stone or twisted up in old tree roots. They carefully excavated these full-grown trolls, who awoke with no memories and no knowledge of the world. Dwarves carefully taught them speech and cheerfully integrated them into their society. In fact, dwarves think of trolls as little brothers who grew a little too big. Trolls are gentle giants. Well, most of the time. They do have great stature and incredible physical power, but spend much of their lives dealing with their kith who are smaller and weaker than them. All trolls learned very quickly to check their great strength. When they unleash it, however, the results are devastating—both to their foes and to themselves. Underfolk view trolls who actually unleash their strength very, very dimly. They believe these trolls to be monsters, and there are many infamous examples of cruel trolls that have contributed to this image. A troll who actually embraces his strength is not welcome in proper underfolk society. Trolls learn gendered roles from the other underfolk, but don’t really have any generative biology. That means trolls cannot reproduce. Every troll that dies means there is one less troll left in the world.

208.title: Troll talent: Giant’s Strength
208.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Trolls › Troll talent: Giant’s Strength
208.body: You automatically win contests related to raw strength (arm wrestling, lifting contests, etc.) against other non-troll kin.

209.title: Arête
209.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Arête
209.body: Underfolk gain arête by performing the following deeds: - Crafting something that will last for centuries - Recovering a precious gem or work of fine art and hoarding it as a grave good - Discovering something secret and forgotten When an underfolk accomplishes all three arête triggers, they gain one of the following talents:

210.title: Dwarf arête talent: Iron Beards
210.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Arête › Dwarf arête talent: Iron Beards
210.body: Spend a Resolve to automatically succeed on a test of fate related to strength, endurance, or stubbornness.

211.title: Halfling arête talent: Underfoot
211.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Arête › Halfling arête talent: Underfoot
211.body: Spend a Resolve to automatically succeed on a test of fate related to being quiet or subtle.

212.title: Troll arête talent: Colossal
212.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Arête › Troll arête talent: Colossal
212.body: Some trolls can perform feats of incredible strength that go beyond what would normally be attempted. Spend a Resolve to pull a portcullis up, smash down a door, push down a supporting column, or perform some other feat of impressive destruction. This talent can’t be used to do additional damage or give an effect, but can be used to change the battlefield during a Challenge.

213.title: Dwarven role-playing concepts
213.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Arête › Dwarven role-playing concepts
213.body: - Beards. You have one—it’s magnificent. Is it braided? Is it forked? Is it tucked into your belt? Is it hung with bells? Is it looped up into your hair? Is it fiery red? Cold blue? Bright blond? Pure white? - You think magic is perilous stuff. Even when demonstrably helpful, growing to rely on it is dangerous. There's always a way to do something that doesn't require magic. - You believe that you literally can take it with you. Get all the gold you can while you still have hands to grasp it. - Everybody does something in underfolk society. Almost every job is production based. Dwarves have a hard time understanding how humans can have jobs that are “preacher” or “lawyer.” What do they do exactly? (Halflings and trolls wrap their heads around this a little easier.) - Humans think that dwarves represent the best things about Joe Average: honesty, hard work, and heavy drinking. Humans are mostly right about this.

214.title: Halfling role-playing concepts
214.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Arête › Halfling role-playing concepts
214.body: - Halflings are anachronistic little British gentlepersons. They enjoy a day at the (rat) races, tea, and little strolls around the countryside. - Halflings like comfort. They're not lazy, as they're sometimes accused of being. They actually go through a lot of trouble to make sure things are nice and respectable. - Halflings are better at talking to humans than dwarves are, and so usually serve as the underfolk's diplomats and brokers to human societies. - Halflings fill in the gaps in underfolk society. Dwarves make the crockery, the silverware, the beer; harvest the mushrooms; and never question who makes the dinner. The answer, of course, is that halflings do. - Finding new and better ways to relax and enjoy themselves is a pursuit of each and every halfling. The new recipe, the better beer, the more inventive pipe—these are things worth questing for.

215.title: Troll role-playing concepts
215.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Underfolk › Underfolk kin › Arête › Troll role-playing concepts
215.body: - You've spent your whole life as a giant among children.
