You learned quickly to marshal your incredible strength, lest it cause great harm to your little siblings. - If you are scared of your own might, have any events in your past shaped this fear? - If you regularly call on your strength, how do you deal with the underfolk who are afraid of you? - Underfolk society on a whole likes trolls. They lift heavy rocks, they tear out tough roots, and they get things off of high shelves. - Humans think trolls are monsters. A troll first traveling in human lands after spending their life among the underfolk will have some rude encounters. - You'll never take a mate and have children. You see your dwarf and halfling brothers doing this. How does it make you feel? - When a troll dies, the number of trolls is reduced by one forever. This is something profoundly sad.

216.title: Orcs
216.body: The Secrets of Dragons The last part of an orc's life cycle is to become a dragon. Just like few goblins survive into orc-hood, few orcs grow old enough to become dragons. The change only comes around once the orc is around a hundred, and takes a long time. The orc begins “nesting” by tunneling down into the earth and setting a few booby traps. She then begins the decades-long process of slowly metamorphosing into a dragon. When adventurers find “dragon eggs,” they're really just finding “orc cocoons.” Even orcs don't know they metamorphose into dragons. Their society reveres dragons, but the transformation is either so taboo or rare that it is not discussed in orc society. A prayer to Rng: “O’ Rng, gracious and kind. We have all that we need. Your people are content and happy. Our lives are full, and we need nothing else. Please, visit your gifts on our enemies. Give them what they lack. Let them know your love and generosity.” At home, orcs are much like everybody else. They have families. They have farms. They like to drink horns of mead with their friends. They make crafts to sell at their religious festivals. They worry about their sick goats. Few people see this side of the orcs, though. Most people only see the raiders. Orcs are famous raiders and traders. They travel all over the Wide World and are the most accomplished seafarers. In the summer months, when the icy straits melt between their lands and the kingdoms of men, parties of orc raiders come plundering. They take gold and royalty. It's said that orcs have a fire in their guts that is only quenched by the presence of gold. Without gold, orcs really are crazy. Why do they take royalty? Well, nobody knows. Sometimes they ransom them to their noble houses for larger sums of gold. Sometimes they don't, though. Slavery is against the Orc-Law (an oral collection of laws and traditions), so royals that become permanent residents of orcish lands are usually integrated. Sometimes they spend the rest of their lives in the frozen north. Sometimes they're rescued by crusaders. About a hundred years ago, three major campaigns (and several minor ones) were mounted by various noble houses to win back some of these captives from the orcs. These campaigns are very much in the mind of both humans and orcs in the modern era. Orcs are mostly matrilineal. This is because some orcs don't have fathers. Orcs can reproduce asexually through parthenogenesis. This type of reproduction (curiously enough) produces both male and female orcs; each orc is a half-clone of their mother. A baby orc is called a goblin. Unlike human children, who take years to learn to walk and talk, goblins learn these skills incredibly quickly. Within a few days, a baby goblin is up on its feet, walking and talking and fighting and picking locks. Really, the little guys are remarkable. Not that they're cruel, but orcs have a somewhat blasé concern for their offspring's health. Few goblins get to grow up to be orcs. It's a rough world. It's better for an orc parent to survive long enough to make another clutch of goblin babies than it is for a single goblin (or even an entire clutch) to survive. Prioritize the elders.

217.title: A myth of the orcs
217.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › A myth of the orcs
217.body: We do not worship Rng out of devotion. We worship Rng out of fear. Their voice is the sound of the falling rain that will water your crops and flood your fields. Their breath is the wind that carries the scent of roses and fuels the forest fire. They once heard the cries of a starving people and sent to them a beast who would give meat eternal. The tarasque soon destroyed the town. Another time, they heard the prayers of those who had lost their way in the woods, and guided them safely to the nearest camp. The lost were soon put to the axe by the enemy soldiers. They are Rng, Helper and Harmer. They are Rng, the Lord of Chaos.

218.title: Orcish names
218.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish names

219.title: Orc male names:
219.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish names › Orc male names:
219.body: Ælfric, Bassa, Boris, Caedwalla, Dernhelm, Gyrth, Kiril, Harthold, Ine, Igor, Ivan, Lofwine, Mordar, Offa, Peragur, Sabor, Svein, Thorgils, Tostig, Ulf, Vlad, Wulnoth, Yuri

220.title: Orc female names:
220.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish names › Orc female names:
220.body: Ælflaen, Burhred, Caewen, Darya, Eahild, Gunhild, Gwillowen, Hereswith, Inga, Izolda, Lubov, Marta, Olgar, Raenburh, Svetar, Tatyana, Ulyana, Vera, Walburga, Zlata Orcs use matronyms as their surnames by appending “daughter” or “son” to the name of their mother (e.g., Ingason or Martadaughter). “I am brother to dragons and a companion to owls. My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat.” – Job 30:29–30

221.title: Orcish kin
221.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin
221.body: It is said that, in the past, orcs served dragons as slaves. There are four orc kins, each of which once served one of the four great dragons of old. Then the god Rng came and doomed orcs to terrible freedom. Note: All orcish kin talents are based on being Wounded. See Wounded for details on Wounds.

222.title: Earthblooded
222.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Earthblooded
222.body: Earthblooded orcs are green-skinned. They feel most calm when underground and prefer to dwell in caves instead of building traditional turf-roofed houses. The underfolk encounter earthbloods most frequently. Whereas the other kins usually sail south to human lands, earthblooded orcs have found great success in tunneling down into the veins of underfolk habitation. They prefer tomb robbing (fewer pesky dwarves actively biting at you with axes), but are happy to relieve a halfling of his gold if the chance presents itself.

223.title: Earthblooded orc talent: Quicksilver Blood
223.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Earthblooded › Earthblooded orc talent: Quicksilver Blood
223.body: Your blood has the appearance and consistency of quicksilver, and is incredibly caustic to metal. When this talent is Wounded by a metal weapon, the weapon is Destroyed.

224.title: Seablooded
224.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Seablooded
224.body: Black-skinned like the ocean's depths or a rain-laden cloud, seablooded orcs keenly feel the push and pull of the tides in their heart. Seablooded orcs are most calm when dwelling near shores or on the open water. Though all orcs raid human lands during the spring and summer months, this kin is especially feared on the oceans. They are famous pirates, rarely actually coming to shore for raids or skirmishes. It’s said that more than a few merfolk have taken seablooded spouses.

225.title: Seablooded orc talent: Poison Blood
225.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Seablooded › Seablooded orc talent: Poison Blood
225.body: Your black blood is a deadly poison. When this talent is Wounded by a bite, the attacker suffers Critical damage (Piercing and Critical damage).

226.title: Stormblooded
226.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Stormblooded
226.body: White-skinned like a cloudy sky, these orcs are tumultuously passionate. When great storms blow up off of the ocean, they can hear their own hearts singing to them. They’re most calm when the winds and rains howl. This kin’s ancestral homeland is the most northerly of all orcish territories. The stormbloods endure the most brutal winters and severe blizzards. They claim these hardships have made them the toughest of the orc broods. Indeed, the stormbloods are nothing if not long-suffering, resourceful, and enduring.

227.title: Stormblooded orc talent: Blur
227.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Stormblooded › Stormblooded orc talent: Blur
227.body: Your blood smokes like a thick mist. When this talent is Wounded, you become Shrouded. This lasts long enough for you to perform a single action or indefinitely if you stay still and take no actions.

228.title: Fireblooded
228.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Fireblooded
228.body: Fireblooded orcs bear dark red and black skin that’s warm to the touch. They are never calm. Firebloods are famously effective as shock troopers. Orc clans of other kins will sometimes bring a contingent of firebloods to be used in this way. For this reason, you might find fireblooded mercenaries attached to orcs of all stripes. When the firebloods go berserk, they can punch a hole into the shield-wall of even well-trained and veteran soldiers.

229.title: Fireblooded orc talent: Berserkergang
229.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Fireblooded › Fireblooded orc talent: Berserkergang
229.body: Your blood is boiling hot. When this talent is Wounded, you may choose to enter a berserker rage. While berserk during a Challenge, you cannot Avoid, Dodge, Speak Incantations, Banter, or Aid Another; however, all of your Attacks are made with favor. Your rage ends when you defeat every enemy on the field. If an ally has attacked or hurt you during this Challenge, they count as an enemy. You must spend a Resolve to end your rage prematurely.

230.title: Arête
230.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Arête
230.body: Orcs gain arête by performing the following deeds: - Hoarding a skull from a class of monster your guild has never killed before - Hoarding a treasure of great worth - Slaying a monster at least twice your size When an orc accomplishes all three arête triggers, they gain the following talent (regardless of kin):

231.title: Orc arête talent: Jarl
231.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Arête › Orc arête talent: Jarl
231.body: You may hatch or gather a horde of goblins to your cause. Goblins are pretty independent little creatures. They see you as “da boss” and take commands from you, but follow those commands in their own, strange, simple little ways. Assembling a goblin horde is a City Action. Spend any amount of XP to attract 2 + X goblins, where X equals the amount of XP you spent on this action. You may only ever have up to 8 goblins in your horde. A goblin horde counts as an animal companion. No matter how many goblins are in the horde, they always count as “one creature” and move around together. Goblins understand whatever language you speak, but can only follow one-word commands during Challenges (given using the Command action). They have tiny minds. Every time a goblin horde takes a Wound, one of its members is killed. A goblin horde carries or hunts for their own food and supplies their own gear. Their gear is crap; they do not have any items or tools that you can use. They can act as porters: For each goblin in the horde, they can carry one slot worth of items.

232.title: Orcish role-playing concepts
232.breadcrumb: Chapter 4: Kith and Kin › Orcs › Orcish kin › Orcish role-playing concepts
232.body: - Orcs are basically metalheads. If it looks like it’s part of the metal subculture, orcs would be into it. Guttural screams, mosh pits, big spikey bracelets, long hair headbanging—orcs have it all. - Orcs are brutal pillagers and savage pirates, merciless in battle. - Orcs are also family-oriented, honor-driven, poetic, loyal, and generally well-educated. - Orcs think a lot about fate. Orcs think that you make your own luck by doing either good or evil actions. Once you've made your choice, nothing can stop destiny from catching up with you. - Orcs propitiate Rng, god of chaos, in order to avoid their unlucky aid. They perform a dozen or more minor taboos or rituals throughout the day to try and avoid their wrath, such as throwing beads in moving water, making a sign to avert his gaze when they voice a desire, and ceremonially offering them a portion of their meal. - Orcs think that raiding is good, but stealing is bad. Sneaking into somebody's house and taking their gold is cowardly. Kicking in their front door, putting them to the sword, taking the gold, and setting the house on fire is good. - Orcs maintain long oral histories. They respect poets and bards as keepers of laws and traditions. These people are unlucky to kill. - Orcs think that magic is a woman's purview. Witchwomen are unlucky to kill. It is unlucky for a man to do magic.

233.title: Chapter 5: The Four Paths
233.body: A reminder During adventurer creation, you will prioritize your attributes—Swords, Pentacles, Cups, or Wands—from 1-4. Whichever attribute is rated 4, the highest rating possible, becomes your path. Your path determines the initial talents that you have access to. You will begin the game with one of your path’s talents mastered and the rest of your path’s talents in training. More information on learning, training, and mastering talents can be found in chapter 2. “Battle not with monsters, lest ye become a monster, And if you gaze into the abyss, the abyss gazes also into you.” – Beyond Good and Evil, Friedrich Nietzsche Here is a riddle. A fool stands between four kings. The fool bears a long and jagged sword. The kings are unarmed. The King of Wands speaks first. He is a wicked and powerful sorcerer. “ If you slay these others, I will cast a spell that will bind the heart of the most beautiful woman in the world to you. She will be your bride, and by my arts, you will bear many children.” The King of Cups speaks next. He is a pious man. “I am advanced in the initiations of Mythrys and speak with the true voice of the Monad. Slay these others, and I will teach you deep wisdom.” The King of Pentacles then speaks. He is a subtle man and very rich. “Feh. Pah! Bleh. I have enough gold to buy a woman and the Cult’s favor. Enough of this prattle. Run these other beggars through and you shall have as much gold as you can spend in your lifetime.” Last speaks the King of Swords—dullest and strongest of the four. “How is this still being contested? Thou hast a sword. Use it! If thou use it in my name, I shall make thee a knight. All these aforementioned shall be thy reward.” What does the fool do?

234.title: Path of Swords
234.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords
234.body: The initial forays into the Underworld were grisly affairs. It was plaster miners who discovered the passage into the first level. They curiously chiseled their way into the antechambers. Like tomb robbers, they discovered gilded treasures and heaps of ancient coins piled therein. And then they discovered the grue. There were no survivors. Before the First Crusade was finally mobilized, the death toll rose terribly as the lure of the Underworld proved irresistible to the very brave and the very foolish. As more of the Underworld began to be revealed, more creatures slithered out of half-remembered legends into reality. Strange beasts and malevolent entities crawled up out of the opened chambers and into the terrorized City. The Cult, at first overwhelmed with the practical considerations and theological questions the Underworld posed, united the proud and ancient houses of mankind with fiery speeches. Under the Cult’s leadership, the First Crusade hunted the monsters that had escaped into the City and encamped themselves on the threshold of the Underworld, warding the lands of men from further attacks. It was only during the Second Crusade that it was discovered that those who die in the Underworld do not stay dead...

235.title: Common motifs:
235.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Common motifs:
235.body: would-be knight, deposed king, charming pirate, retired gladiator, fanatic vampire hunter, barbarian warrior poet

236.title: Swords talents
236.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents
236.body: GM’s note It’s possible that the Monster Hunter categories can overlap. For example, a giant beetle might be a specialty for both a beast hunter and a witch hunter. That’s fine. There’s no reason to get into taxonomical minutiae.

237.title: Aegis
237.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Aegis
237.body: If you are carrying an intact shield and would suffer an effect from a physical source (an attack, a trap, etc.), you may elect to Notch your shield instead of taking the effect .

238.title: Doom Eye
238.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Doom Eye
238.body: When wielding a missile weapon during a Challenge, you may spend a Sword card on your turn to perform a perfect shot . This Attack automatically hits, regardless of the target’s Initiative.

239.title: Heavy Metal Machine
239.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Heavy Metal Machine
239.body: During Challenges, if you are wearing iron or steel armor, you may use a miscellaneous action (discarding any card) to add your Swords to your Initiative as an interrupt against a single action. You may only use this talent once per round.

240.title: Monster Hunter
240.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Monster Hunter
240.body: When you master or train this talent, choose both a hated foe and a specialization of that enemy. - You gain a motif called “\[Foe] Hunter.” You can use this motif to bid lore about these creatures or to gain favor in tests of fate related to them, as normal. - You make Attacks with favor against foes of your specialization. Choose a foe and a specialization from the following list—you can change your foe as a City Action if some new type of creature really gives you reason to be pissed off.

241.title: Beast Hunter
241.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Beast Hunter
241.body: You specialize in hunting, tracking, and trapping beasts of all shapes and sizes. What qualifies as a “beast”? Well, if it’s in a medieval bestiary, it’s probably a beast. Beasts are native to the realm of Flesh—they feast, fight, flee, and fuck. Specializations: Any specific species (e.g., bats, centipedes, chimeras, cockatrices, dinosaurs, tigers)

242.title: Elemental Hunter
242.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Elemental Hunter
242.body: Your focus is dealing with supernatural embodiments of nature. Specializations: Any specific creature (e.g., undine, salamander, siren, dryad, tree giants)

243.title: Man Hunter
243.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Man Hunter
243.body: You specialize in the most dangerous game. The term “man” is a bit of a misnomer. This category covers all kith, kin, and genders. Specializations: Any specific kith: fay, humans, underfolk, orcs

244.title: Spirit Hunter
244.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Spirit Hunter
244.body: Your focus is on alien intelligences from the far realms. You can deal with incorporeal spirits, manifested spirits, and possessing spirits. Specializations: Spirits from one of the far realms (i.e., Wastes, Weald, Weird, Welkin)

245.title: Undead Hunter
245.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Undead Hunter
245.body: You have experience pacifying the unquiet dead. Specializations: A specific undead type (e.g., skeleton, zombie, wraith)

246.title: Witch Hunter
246.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Witch Hunter
246.body: If the answer to the question “what is that thing?” is “a wizard did it,” you can deal with it. Specializations: Any specific type of magical manifestation (e.g., beastmen, golems, oozes)

247.title: Reaver
247.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Reaver
247.body: When you Attack during Challenges, you may also move one zone (Set the scene) as you charge towards your foe .

248.title: Two-handed Focus
248.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › Two-handed Focus
248.body: If you are wielding a melee weapon with both hands during a Challenge, you may Attack as a minor action with either a Pentacles or a Swords card.

249.title: War Stories
249.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Swords › Swords talents › War Stories
249.body: As a Camp Action, tell your guild the story of some of your past adventures. Maybe this was an adventure you've played out in-character, or maybe one in your backstory. You—and everyone who listens and role-plays with you a little— gets to choose one of the following benefits: - They may charge an uncharged Bond . - They gain an extra point of Resolve; this can bring their Resolve up to 5.

250.title: Path of Pentacles
250.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles
250.body: Treasure was, and remains, a powerful motivator for Underworld expeditions. The spires of the Castle of Crossed Destinies were literally covered in gold plating until explorers stripped them and hauled the plates back to the surface. The Underworld denizens possess strange coinage as well: round pieces of gold stamped with the faces of three beautiful women and a pentacle star on the reverse. Who these ancient sovereigns were is a matter of great scholarly debate and fanciful public speculation. By the same token, treasure is the primary motivator for the City’s current system of adventuring guilds. The fifty percent guild tax on recovered loot is a heavy burden for adventurers and is much bemoaned. The tax collectors posted at each known exit from the Underworld are a particularly hated lot, but the City has grown rich from this system. Of course, these heavy taxes have created a sprawling industry of smuggling, bribery, and fencing. In pursuit of both relic hunting and black marketeering, “thief” has become a particularly common profession.

251.title: Common motifs:
251.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Common motifs:
251.body: arrogant duelist, feral scavenger, morbid jester, bounty hunter, traitorous spy, urchin pickpocket, penitent assassin

252.title: Pentacles talents
252.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Pentacles talents

253.title: Acrobat
253.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Pentacles talents › Acrobat
253.body: You no longer need to test fate to climb sheer surfaces or walk across narrow ledges or tightropes. You climb and scamper along difficult or vertical terrain as easily as walking. During Challenges, you may move this way as a miscellaneous action, as easily as walking to a new zone. Additionally, if you are prepared, you may treat a fall as if it were 20’ shorter (Falling). If you are not prepared for a fall, you may spend a Resolve to treat it as if it were 20’ shorter.

254.title: Ambusher
254.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Pentacles talents › Ambusher
254.body: In the first round of a Challenge, whenever you would deal damage, you deal 2 Wounds instead of 1. Spend a Resolve to resist being ambushed. You raise a hue and cry to warn your guild of the threat beforehand.

255.title: Con Artist
255.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Pentacles talents › Con Artist
255.body: If you spend a few minutes observing a person in conversation or talking to them, you may bid lore to ask the GM to reveal either one of their likes or their dislikes (your choice); see Social Encounters & Disposition for more on Disposition and see Creating interesting characters for more about likes and dislikes.

256.title: Fight Dirty
256.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Pentacles talents › Fight Dirty
256.body: During Challenges, you may Roughhouse as a minor action with either a Pentacles or Swords card . Additionally, you gain several new Roughhouse options: - Exhaust - Notch - Silence

257.title: Quick!
257.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Pentacles talents › Quick!
257.body: During Challenges, if you are wearing light or no armor, you may treat Pentacles actions as interrupts .

258.title: Sneak
258.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Pentacles talents › Sneak
258.body: Sneak responsibly Be aware of whether or not other adventurers actually want you present in a scene. A heroic rescue out of a prison cell can be much more welcome than you intruding on a personal scene. A player having a solo scene has the right to veto your use of this skill. At any point, you may declare that you go sneaking . This allows you to go dramatically off-stage. Later, if you are not present in a scene and it’s at least somewhat plausible that you could have snuck there, spend a Resolve to arrive on the scene dramatically. If a Challenge has yet to begin, this arrival counts as an ambush (Ambushes and surprise). If combat has already begun, nobody is surprised because everybody is on edge—simply join the flow of combat per usual. If you go sneaking and all tension evaporates, you may rejoin the scene by slinking out of the shadows. This does not cost a Resolve. This talent also gives you a new Camp Action: Infiltrate . When you Infiltrate, you investigate a specific location that you know of in your current dungeon level. Thereafter, you may bid lore to ask the GM a specific yes or no question about something you’d know having infiltrated that location, e.g., “Is this door trapped?”, “Is this room guarded?”, “Is the wizard’s bedroom on this level?”, “Do the bandits have bows?”, “Were the orcs green-skinned?”

259.title: Up My Sleeve
259.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Pentacles › Pentacles talents › Up My Sleeve
259.body: You may declare that you have had a common, one-slot item with you the whole time. Twice per Crawl (one for each sleeve), spend a Resolve and declare that you had a [blank] up your sleeve. This can include a lockpick, a dagger, a handkerchief, an empty vial, a length of wire, or anything else that the GM generally finds viable.

260.title: Path of Cups
260.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups
260.body: When the Underworld opened, so many went on the quest for the Grail of Mythrys that a massive support system, both secular and religious, was assembled. Inns and public houses for the housing of pilgrims, coin changers for foreigners, shops of supply and purveyance, smithies for armament, chapels and shrines for the devout, charlatans and peddlers selling false maps and rumors, scribes and lawyers for drafting of charters and wills, apothecaries for the healing of those returned unsuccessful —all these sprang up almost overnight. The sign of the Cup has become synonymous for these tradesmen, as well as having a holy connotation, and is still used today to advertise needful service.

261.title: Common motifs:
261.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Common motifs:
261.body: grisly apothecary, adventurous cartographer, jolly cleric, daring archaeologist, jaded barber surgeon, young insect tamer

262.title: Cups talents
262.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Cups talents

263.title: Alchemy
263.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Cups talents › Alchemy
263.body: This talent gives you a new Camp Action: Brew Alchemy . When you Brew Alchemy, you use an alchemy kit to turn any number of reagents you have into alchemical substances . Reagents are harvested from the bodies of Underworld monsters. Alchemical substances are kept in hermetic bottles and divided into three categories: potions , oils, and bombs . See Appendix B for more information on alchemy.

264.title: Beast Master
264.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Cups talents › Beast Master
264.body: This talent allows you to train and issue commands to your animal companions. As a Camp Action, you may teach one animal companion one command . Normal trained animals may learn up to three commands . It is possible to retrain an animal with a new command, replacing one of their previously mastered commands. Pick from this list of commands (or new ones that the GM approves): - Sic ‘Em - Hunt - Get Help - Do a Trick - Heel - Guard - Fetch - Stay - Track If you have mastered this talent, one animal you own is considered your familiar . Familiars can learn five different commands . Furthermore, if your familiar would take a Wound that would kill them, you may spend a Resolve to declare that they’re only at Death’s Door and not actually dead. More information about animal companions can be found in War pigs.

265.title: Bookworm
265.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Cups talents › Bookworm
265.body: You have an almost encyclopedic knowledge of everything you have read. Once you have used the Read a Book Camp Action (Camp Actions), you may thereafter bid lore to ask a question about the subject of that text . Keep a list of books that you’ve read. These are treated like motifs for the purpose of bidding lore, but don’t aid you in tests of fate.

266.title: Chirurgeon
266.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Cups talents › Chirurgeon
266.body: You may provide healing to your companions. You can expend a poultice to Heal someone (Effects). This effect cannot be used to clear the Stressed condition. Additionally, this talent gives you a new Camp Action: Chirurgery . When you use Chirurgery on a non-Stressed guild-mate using the Rest and Recover Camp Action, you may Heal all of their Wounds.

267.title: Counsel
267.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Cups talents › Counsel
267.body: Any time during a Challenge, you may yell advice to another adventurer and hand the player a card from your hand . The card’s suit must match the action you counsel them to take. The other player may play that card as long as they use it to take your advice. In all other ways, it is treated as a normal Challenge card (Draw Challenge cards). If you spend a Resolve when you use this talent, the other player may play this card as an interrupt. Otherwise, the standard one-card-per-turn rule remains in effect (Take turns). You may use this talent once per round.

268.title: High Chant
268.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Cups talents › High Chant
268.body: This talent gives you a new Camp Action: Perform the High Chant . When you Perform the High Chant, speak at least two stanzas of epic poetry for the table. If you do so, you may select a number of cards from the minor arcana discard pile equal to your Cups. These are called inspiration cards . Distribute the cards to other players—you may keep one for yourself. No player can ever have more than one inspiration card. Inspiration cards may be spent as actions during a Challenge. Alternatively, you may spend your inspiration card instead of drawing from the deck when you test fate or push fate. Inspiration cards last until used or until the end of the session, whichever comes first.

269.title: Loremaster
269.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Cups › Cups talents › Loremaster
269.body: You are a student of ancient languages and lore. This talent confers three advantages: - You have knowledge of many languages and tongues. You are assumed to be passingly fluent in any spoken language that you might encounter. - You can translate ancient scripts and runes. Translating a short ancient runic passage that you encounter while delving takes a watch or two. Translating a longer text (such as a book) requires a City Action. - When you bid lore, you may spend a Resolve instead of spending a lore bid.

270.title: Path of Wands
270.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands
270.body: Sorcery Those who walk the Path of Wands are sorcerers. Casting spells and the practice of sorcery is described in detail in Appendix A: Sorcery . The relationship between the City and magic has been long fraught with bloodshed and sorrow. During the Age of the First Empire, sorcery was used as an act of worship towards the Crow-Headed Queen — —one of the earliest deified empresses. During the Age of the Republic, sorcery was seen as being fundamentally tied to both monarchists and elves, and it was made illegal. Still, several cabals flourished in secret. The Age of the Republic was marked by the increasing fanaticism of witch hunters as they attempted to root out these hidden sorcerers. A blanket ban on sorcery proved impossible with the advent of the Age of Dungeon. Too many trials and foes in the Underworld were essentially mystical in nature. The practice of sorcery became a necessary evil, and the Cult began to draw up the appropriate pardons and indulgences. Today, those who practice sorcery in the City must be licensed and registered with the crown. Official sorcerers are granted rods of office by the Tower Gnostic and allowed to join guilds in the exploration of the Underworld. Unofficial sorcery is punishable by fines, but is largely unregulated as long as it is not performed in the City itself. Still, the Witch Finder General remains an influential figure within City politics, and his templars have a much grimmer view of unregulated sorcery.

271.title: Common motifs:
271.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Common motifs:
271.body: court mage, insane astrologer, artisanal wand maker, conniving charlatan, morbid wizard, doomsday cultist

272.title: Wands talents
272.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Wands talents

273.title: Counter-spell
273.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Wands talents › Counter-spell
273.body: You can counter the effects of sorcery with an effort of will. There are two applications for this talent: - You can stop enemy sorcerers from casting spells in battle. During Challenges, if you can perceive a sorcerer casting a spell, you may spend a Resolve to Speak Incantations as an interrupt . - If your Speak Incantations value is greater than the enemy sorcerer’s total value, their spell fizzles out. - If your Speak Incantations value is equal to or less than the enemy’s total value, the spell fizzles out but you must draw on the maleficence table as the magic goes awry. - You can negate a spell already in play. You may spend a Resolve to immediately end the ongoing effects of a spell.

274.title: Dwimmercraft
274.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Wands talents › Dwimmercraft
274.body: Suffused with the arcane arts, you can perform small (but meaningful) expressions of magic. You may perform the following minor effects: - You may levitate an object in your zone that weighs about 10 lbs. and that fits comfortably in one hand. You have no fine motor control over this effect, but can bring things to you, lift them up, or push them away. - You may conjure a showy, harmless, and obviously magical illusion—a shower of sparks, a colorful rainbow stretched between your hands, a flickering image of your first love. - You conjure a simple illusion of something that you can hold in one hand. Anybody that tries to interact with this object will realize it’s an illusion, but the sight of it is fairly convincing. Additionally, by spending a Resolve, you can focus your second sight for a watch. Second sight allows you to see invisible and Shrouded things. You can perceive the true form of any illusion. You can automatically tell when things are magical or under enchantment. You can also tell if somebody else is a sorcerer. Using this talent during a Challenge counts as a miscellaneous action.

275.title: Gramarye
275.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Wands talents › Gramarye
275.body: You have learned how to draw on the energies of the far realms. Using this talent, you can release a blast of magical energy up to one zone away through an archwood wand , doing damage as a weapon. During Challenges, Attacks with your wand count as Wands actions. Additionally, you gain a new Camp Action: Make a Pact . When you Make a Pact, choose to observe one or more pacts from the facing page.

276.title: Magic of the Wastes
276.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Wands talents › Magic of the Wastes
276.body: You may cast spells of the Wastes. The Wastes are a grim place of death and decay. Spells of this realm deal with matters of undeath, spread fear, or cause harm.

277.title: Magic of the Weald
277.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Wands talents › Magic of the Weald
277.body: You may cast spells of the Weald. The Weald is a verdant and wild place. Spells of this realm affect the elements, command beasts, and reshape the natural world.

278.title: Magic of the Weird
278.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Wands talents › Magic of the Weird
278.body: You may cast spells of the Weird. The Weird is a place of dream, untouched by sanity. Spells of this realm affect one’s mind and emotions, conjure illusions, and bend reality.

279.title: Magic of the Welkin
279.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Wands talents › Magic of the Welkin
279.body: You may cast spells of the Welkin. The Welkin is a bright and holy place. Spells of this realm deal with angels, provide healing and protection, and invoke an awful wonder.

280.title: Pacts
280.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts
280.body: Damned if you do, damned if you don’t… Sometimes, pacts might put you in situations where you have to break one pact to keep another. This has its roots in mythology. Consider how Cú Chulainn couldn’t refuse food from a stranger, nor could he eat dog meat. When a stranger offers him dog meat, he’s on the hook one way or another. We recommend not shying away from these conflicts. If the fiction in your game demands that two pacts contradict each other, fine. It’s ultimately not that painful. Let it play out and see what happens. When you use the Make a Pact Camp Action, charge one spell component of your choice for each pact made. This charge may be spent in lieu of spending a Resolve to cast the spell, though additional Resolve must still be spent to grant the spell increased power. Each component may be charged only once. Your pact lasts until broken or until the spell is cast. Components remain charged until the spell is cast or until you break the pact. If you break the pact, draw on the maleficence table.

281.title: Devour the living
281.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Devour the living
281.body: You may only eat creatures that are yet living when they pass your lips: maggots, shrimp, mice, infants. If you did not bring these creatures (which are hard to carry and keep), you can test fate with Cups as a Camp Action to see if you can find any in the Underworld . If you fail, you are treated as starving (Break bread). If you succeed, you find enough vermin to keep yourself fed comfortably.

282.title: Forego armor
282.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Forego armor
282.body: You may not wear armor or helm or wield a shield of any kind, regardless of its construction.

283.title: Forego skins
283.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Forego skins
283.body: You may not wear the skins or furs of a beast, or anything derived from them (such as leather). You may wear woven garments of linen or cotton.

284.title: Forego weapons
284.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Forego weapons
284.body: You may not touch, handle, manipulate, or wield weapons of any kind—not even a rolling pin used as a club. Any weapons you own must be bound in cloth and lashed to your pack. Wands, curiously, do not count as weapons.

285.title: Forego wood
285.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Forego wood
285.body: You may not wield, touch, or carry anything made of felled wood. You may not carry a torch, shield, or club. You cannot enjoy the benefits of a fire if that wood was bought with gold in the City (for that wood was certainly felled)—instead, you must sit outside of the fire’s light and heat. Wands, since they’re made of willing archwood, do not count towards this prohibition.

286.title: Gluttony
286.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Gluttony
286.body: You must eat more than your share. You must eat double your normal portion (two rations instead of one) whenever you consume rations or this pact is broken.

287.title: Hide your face
287.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Hide your face
287.body: You must hide your face behind a mask at all times. Sorcerers might choose masks of porcelain, cloth, wood, bone, or more exotic materials. Wearing a mask incurs disfavor on all social tests, and the GM will accommodate your social encounters accordingly.

288.title: Self-mortification
288.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Self-mortification
288.body: You must purchase and wear a hair shirt under your normal clothing. This causes you to be Stressed. If you take off the hair shirt and clear Stressed, you violate this pact.

289.title: Self-mutilation
289.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Self-mutilation
289.body: When you make this pact, you cut runes into yourself. This causes you to take a Wound. If you ever heal this Wound, you violate this pact.

290.title: Silence
290.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Silence
290.body: If you must speak, you must speak in a whisper. People must be very close to you and it must be very quiet to hear your words. If you speak in a loud voice, you violate this pact.

291.title: Verity
291.breadcrumb: Chapter 5: The Four Paths › Path of Wands › Pacts › Verity
291.body: You must not tell a knowing lie. If you do so, even in jest, this pact is broken.

292.title: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase
292.body: “There’s a great maze of tunnels, a Labyrinth. It’s like a great dark city, under the hill. Full of gold, and the swords of old heroes, and old crowns, and bones, and years, and silence.” – The Tombs of Atuan, Ursula K. Le Guin There are strange things the rumor of which the sun has never heard. Between sprawls of empty space in the Underworld, there is weirdness. There are orreries that presage the position of alien moons un-glimpsed by the eye of man. There are colonies of lost adventurers driven mad, endlessly critiquing the architecture of the Inverted Castle. There are hallways filled with gnashing teeth. There are fields of dragon bones that roar whenever an orc walks among them. There are three wells, reflecting scenes of the past, the present, and the future. There are exiled stars seeking to marry off their daughters with the dowry of a wish. There are fungi gardens watered by the tears of nymphs. And what is in the center of the maze?

293.title: The Flow of the Crawl Phase
293.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › The Flow of the Crawl Phase
293.body: The mythic underworld His Majesty the Worm’s setting is a place described in fiction, folklore, and games as a mythic underworld. A mythic underworld is not merely a cave system with kobolds and goblins hiding in every shadowy corner. It is another world, charged with unconventional physics, inhuman entities, and alien architectures. Characteristics of a mythic underworld 1. It’s big, and has many levels; in fact, it may be endless 2. It follows its own ecological and physical rules 3. It is not static; the inhabitants and even the layout may grow or change over time 4. It is not linear 5. There are many ways to move up and down through the levels 6. Its purpose is mysterious or shrouded in legend 7. It’s inimical to those exploring it 8. Deeper or farther levels are more dangerous 9. It’s a (the?) central feature of the campaign – “The Dungeon as a Mythic Underworld,” Philotomy’s Musings The rumor mill A large part of His Majesty the Worm is exploring and discovering. If one (or, gods forbid, all) of a guild’s adventurers die, it’s boring to rediscover and retread old ground. That’s why we have a rule called the rumor mill . Adventurers are always talking in taverns about what they’ve discovered, what they’ve fought, and what’s almost eaten them whole. Unless the adventurers make an effort to keep something about their delvings secret, assume that it’s generally common knowledge. Therefore, adventurers who are introduced later into the game’s story can know things that previous adventurers discovered. They know where the secret switches are, they know how to defeat Mother Maggot, they know how to safely cross the invisible bridge. A new game of His Majesty the Worm starts at the gates to the Underworld. The Crawl begins with the guild taking their first steps into those lightless depths. The Crawl is the phase of the game centered on exploring the Underworld. When the guild leaves the safety of civilization to pursue their quests, negotiating with strange creatures, avoiding traps, and excavating ancient treasures, they are Crawling. Most of the game is focused on this phase. The Underworld is what is called a megadungeon . A megadungeon is inherently strange. It does not need to conform to the players’ conceptions and expectations. It does benefit from having internal logic, however. Learning the “rules” of the Underworld is fun, and having internally consistent logic allows players to make meaningful choices (which is the point of the game). A megadungeon is composed of smaller, constituent dungeons . Each dungeon is a thematic level, section, or subsection. For example, your Underworld might be composed of five dungeon levels, which are called the Spires, the Castle of Crossed Destinies, the Inverted Castle, the City of Ruin, and the Necropolis of Ot. Dungeons are separated into different rooms . A room can be any discrete space: a chamber, a feasting hall, a natural cavern, an underground river, etc. Each room should have something interesting for the players to interact with. For example, one room in the Castle of Crossed Destinies could have a giant throne constructed of a titan’s bones, another room could be the lair of a reverse sphinx who needs to hear riddles to survive, and so on. As the guild explores each room, random events called the Meatgrinder create tension. The Meatgrinder represents the passage of time: torches burning low, patrolling monsters, and other hazards. Each dungeon level has both a map and a Meatgrinder table, both full of interesting things to discover. When players travel into a new room, the GM looks at the room description. Simultaneously, the GM draws a random card from the major arcana and consults the Meatgrinder table. They then describe the newly-entered room in the context of the random Meatgrinder encounter. This chapter details what players need to know about the Crawl Phase. Advice for the GM for running the Crawl Phase is found in chapter 10. Procedures for the GM to create the Underworld are found in Appendix E: Underworld Creation. Play happens through a combination of what the GM describes and the decisions the players make. It’s not a preplanned story. During the Crawl, the players tell the GM where they want to go. They use an in-character map to make sure everybody is on the same page about where the guild currently is. The GM describes what the guild encounters as they travel. The GM describes the contents of each room within the context of a random Meatgrinder event. When the guild encounters dangers—crushing walls, minotaurs, anti-life fields, swindling merchants—the players and the GM engage in a dialogue. - The GM describes the situation, the players ask questions about the scene, and the GM clarifies. - The players describe what their adventurers attempt, the GM asks questions about their actions and their intentions, and the players clarify. - The GM describes what happens as a result of the adventurer’s actions. If there’s risk or doubt about the adventurer’s ability to accomplish their goals, the GM calls for a test of fate (Tests of Fate). “Folk like to pretend they know everything about the world. \[...] You don’t have blanks on your map, so the folks who draw them shade in a piece and write, ‘The Eld.’ You might as well burn a hole right through the map for what good that does.” – The Wise Man’s Fear, Patrick Rothfuss Despite the presence of otherworldly and strange beings, very few creatures attack on sight and fight to the death. (Well, perhaps skeletons. They want to free their boney brethren from the flesh prisons that you’re cruelly keeping them in.) Almost everything can be talked to, negotiated with, or at least avoided. See “Disposition” see Social Encounters & Disposition for an overview of negotiating with the GM’s characters. When combat cannot be avoided, the Crawl Phase transitions into the Challenge Phase. Once the Challenge is resolved, the Challenge Phase transitions back to the Crawl. Mysteriously, the Underworld has a property that preserves life. When a mortal blow is dealt, the victim lingers at Death’s Door before dying. This property has prolonged the life of many adventurers who have run afoul of the Underworld’s treachery. Those who do die in the Underworld rise again as undead…

294.title: Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here
294.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here
294.body: As you explore, you will find hazards that need to be navigated around, avoided, or retreated from. This is a game about interacting with the world as if it actually exists. Because RPGs are conversation games, you explore the game world through asking questions. You can ask what your adventurer can see, feel, hear, etc. No need to draw cards—just ask what you can perceive and the GM will answer you honestly. As the GM describes things, follow up with specific questions to dig deeper into the game world. There’s no list of skills or abilities to limit what you can do within the fictional world. Don’t ask “Can I make some sort of test to look for…” or “Can I make a test to disarm…” Instead ask questions like “Is there any tension as I slowly open the door?” or “Do I hear anything if I tap on the wall here?” Interrogate your surroundings by asking questions and state your character’s actions: the GM will tell you if you need to make a test of fate. That said, your character sheet might contain something you can use to your advantage! You might have an item, spell, or talent that you can put to a clever use. Your success and your failure are defined by your ideas.

295.title: Locked doors
295.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Locked doors
295.body: Some doors are locked. If the door has a keyhole, you might find the key in the pockets of a dungeon denizen on this level. Keys tend to be coded: the copper key fits in the copper door, the mermaid-shaped key fits in the door painted with mermaids, etc. If the door has a keyhole, you can also try to pick the lock with lockpicks. Picking a lock with lockpicks requires a successful test of Pentacles. You can also try to force a door. You might bash it down with a test of Swords. A tool like a battering ram or crowbar provides favor to this test. Some doors can only be opened by a particular mechanism. You need to say a particular pass phrase, twist the taxidermied moose head, depress all four pressure plates in the room, etc. If a door seems stuck, come back to it later. You might have more perspective on how to open it after exploring further. Ask dungeon denizens if they have any advice.

296.title: Secret doors
296.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Secret doors
296.body: Some doors are secret. These doors might be obscured (behind a bookshelf ) or built to be all but invisible (stone doors that only open when you twist a candle sconce). You find secret doors by describing how you search for them. You can look at a wall to see if you can see any seams. You can tap on a wall to hear if it sounds hollow. You can look behind curtains, inside wardrobes, and under rugs to see if there’s anything there. Look at your map. Are there any gaps where a room would logically make sense? Look for secret doors there. Look for patterns. Secret doors are hidden in places that make sense for them to be. If you find a secret door behind one portrait, search behind other portraits to see if there’s a pattern to be found. If you don’t ask for specific information and simply say, “I spend as long as it takes to search the room for hidden doors,” the GM can use the “Moving carefully” rules. They tell you if there’s a secret door but draw on the Meatgrinder to see if your torches gutter due to the time you take searching.

297.title: Checking for traps
297.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Checking for traps
297.body: Some doors, rooms, or passageways are trapped. You find traps by describing how you search for them. Open the door very slowly to feel if there’s a trigger in the hinges that activates a trap. Bend down and check to see if there’s a tripwire in the door frame. Walk carefully to check if there are any pressure plates in the hallway. If you create a procedure like “We walk down the hallway tapping the floor in front of us with our ten-foot pole,” the GM can use the “Moving carefully” rules due to the time involved in the search. They tell you if you find any traps but draw on the Meatgrinder to see if your torches gutter due to the time you take searching.

298.title: Dealing with traps
298.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Dealing with traps
298.body: Some traps might be unavoidable no matter how carefully you search. You decide how to deal with the traps you trigger. Some traps will simply occur—the room begins to fill with water as soon as the door is opened. Other traps allow you to make a test of fate to avoid the worst outcome—you test Pentacles to grasp the edge of the collapsing bridge as it falls apart. The way you describe your actions when a trap is triggered will determine how the GM adjudicates what happens next. Here are some examples.

299.title: Example the first
299.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Dealing with traps › Example the first
299.body: As the guild steps into a room, the door slams shut and locks. With a grinding sound, the east and west walls slowly begin moving towards each other, threatening to crush all within like a giant trash compactor. What do you do? Some suggestions: - Was a guild member trapped outside when the door slammed shut? Are there controls anywhere they can use to deactivate the trap? - Do you have pitons in your pack? Can you drive them into the wall to slow or stop the walls’ advance? - Is the door flush with the wall? Is there any space in the door frame in which to hide yourself? - Can you search for a secret door? Is there a service panel on the walls? In the ceiling? On the floor? - Do you have a crowbar? Can you pry open the door? - Is there a troll in your party? Do they have the Colossal talent? Can they smash down the door or break the mechanism behind the walls through sheer strength? - Do you have a slime bomb? Can you throw it to Destroy part of the wall or the door? - Do you have the Portable Hole spell? Can you cast it on the wall to see the mechanism beyond? Can you jam or disrupt the mechanism if you reach your hand through the hole?

300.title: Example the second
300.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Dealing with traps › Example the second
300.body: You find a door set into a frame resembling the face of a green devil. Inside the green devil’s mouth is a black hole. It’s not just dark, a literal void exists within the green devil’s mouth. What do you do? Some suggestions: - Discretion is the better part of valor. If you don’t need to deal with the green devil face, can you simply leave? - If you need to deal with the face, are there any switches or buttons hidden? Can you press the eyes? Can you twist the horns? - Don’t interact with the void in the mouth with your bare hands. Throw a sling stone into it. Touch it with a staff at a distance. - Does someone in your guild have the Counter-spell talent? Does it have any effect on the face?

301.title: Example the third
301.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Dealing with traps › Example the third
301.body: As you walk down the hall, you step on a pressure plate. You hear a “CLICK!” as it sinks into the floor. You hear mechanisms whirring in the walls, like a machine spinning up. With a split-second decision to make, you don’t have a lot of information to act on—but doing something is better than nothing. What do you do? Some suggestions: - Can you keep pressure on the pressure plate in case releasing it is the trap’s trigger? - Can you drop prone to try and avoid whatever is coming? Can you do so while depressing the plate? - Do you have a shield? Can you bring it to bear to protect yourself from potential threats? - Does somebody in your guild have the Aegis talent? Can they use it for your benefit if the trap is sprung?

302.title: Maps
302.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Maps
302.body: Before the game, the GM will map out the Underworld and create detailed notes about each room’s contents. They will also create a basic map for each dungeon level for the players: this is your guild’s in-character map . Your map lets you tell the GM where your guild wants to go. For example, you might say, “We’re going to head towards Room 202.” Because the room numbers will be the same between the GM’s notes and the player’s map, the GM can turn to their description for Room 202 and continue play with minimal page flipping. The player-facing map does not contain any information about the contents of dungeon rooms. However, each map should: - Show the basic outline of the rooms; - Show the paths through the dungeon; and - Be keyed, with each room having a different number. Although you’re given some information on the map, it might not be complete! As you travel, you might find hidden rooms that you can draw directly onto your map. Exploring and discovering secrets is the fun part of play! As you fill your (mostly) blank map in with notes about the rooms, traps, and dungeon denizens you encounter, you’ll be able to make informed decisions as you explore.

303.title: Watches
303.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Abandon All Hope, Ye Who Enter Here › Watches
303.body: Travel time is measured in watches . A watch isn't a concrete period of time; it might be an hour or ten minutes or all night. It’s hard to tell how much time is actually passing in the Underworld. Time moves weirdly—happy moments burn away quickly, whereas tense moments stretch like lengthening shadows. Watches are just a way to talk about how quickly, quietly, and carefully you're moving. A watch passes: - Each time the guild passes into a new room on the map; - Whenever the guild spends a long time performing a task (such as taking a door off of its hinges, repairing a broken machine, counting the jelly beans in a jar); and - Each Camp and Challenge Phase. When a watch passes, the GM draws a card from the major arcana deck and compares the result to the Meatgrinder table for that dungeon. The GM then describes the Meatgrinder event in the context of the new or current scene.

304.title: Meatgrinder
304.body: The Meatgrinder is a collection of impermanent events—things like monster patrols, weather, or bumping into a rival guild. Importantly, the rate at which your light sources flicker and go out is controlled by the Meatgrinder; see Light for more information on light sources. As you travel, the GM will describe scenes that combine the contents of each room and the results of the Meatgrinder. For example, if the room you enter is a dragon’s lair and the GM randomly pulls a patrol of goblins from the Meatgrinder table, you might find goblins attempting to sneak into the dragon’s lair for treasure—and making entirely too much noise in the process. When a Meatgrinder event is triggered, the GM should mark it off. If the cards are shuffled and the GM draws the same event twice, nothing happens and the guild has a watch of respite. The GM repopulates their Meatgrinder tables after each City Phase. The full procedure to create a Meatgrinder for a dungeon level is detailed in Appendix E, see Create the Meatgrinder. Here are the basics. In general, Meatgrinder tables follow this formula: - Torches gutter (I–V): Torches guttering represents time passing as your light sources grow dim. When torches gutter, all light sources flicker . - Torches gutter events are not marked off from the Meatgrinder. They can occur multiple times. - Curiosities (VI–X): Curiosities are moments of serendipity. “Nothing happens” is a boring result for a random table. Curiosities are an opportunity for a GM to interject color into the black depths of the Underworld. They can serve as inspiration for role-playing exchanges or provide hints about the local environment. - Travel events (XI–XV): Travel events represent things that go wrong during the journey. They might require you to make a hard choice about resource management or ask you to test fate to avoid a hardship. Travel events might prompt Challenges. - Random encounters (XVI–XX): Random encounters are chance meetings with the denizens of the Underworld. These might be friendly encounters with would-be allies, hazardous encounters with hungry animals, or murderous encounters with monsters. Interesting random encounters don’t simply list “monster type.” The best random encounters paint a small scenario that the GM can use as inspiration for a Challenge. - Quest rumor (XXI): Quest rumors lead you one step closer to your current quest. Quest rumors provide hints or directions towards your quest goal. If you’ve already made significant progress on your current quest, this result might even feature the object of your quest.

305.title: Loud noises
305.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Meatgrinder › Loud noises
305.body: Every time the guild makes a loud noise or otherwise draws attention to themselves, the GM should pull on the Meatgrinder table. If the draw results in a random encounter (results XVI–XX), the GM describes an encounter with the wandering creature drawn to the noise. Otherwise, nothing happens.

306.title: Moving carefully
306.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Meatgrinder › Moving carefully
306.body: If the guild is proceeding very slowly or methodically, tapping in front of them with their ten-foot pole, the GM should pull again on the Meatgrinder table after resolving potential encounters. If the second draw results in torches guttering (results I–V), the GM keeps the result to represent additional time passing. Otherwise, nothing happens.

307.title: Example Meatgrinder table
307.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Meatgrinder › Example Meatgrinder table
307.body: What work is the Meatgrinder doing? The Meatgrinder introduces the tension of a ticking clock to your Crawl. If you linger too long or travel too deep, your torches will all burn out and you will be lost in a lightless void. Also, the alchemical reaction between the random event and the specific room ensures that the scene is interesting for everybody at the table—GM and player alike. A trapped hallway encounter can be fun on its own, but the (randomly generated) inclusion of a rival adventuring party approaching from the opposite direction adds a dynamic element. And, if you ever retrace your steps and enter this hallway again, some other random element will be encountered here. Since you’ve traveled here before, you can leverage what you learned from the first encounter to your advantage in the second. Card Meatgrinder Event :---: --- I Torches gutter II Torches gutter III Torches gutter IV Torches gutter V Torches gutter VI [Curiosity] Local Fauna: The guild startles up a flock of luminescent cave butterflies. They flutter away quickly. VII [Curiosity] Cockatrice Call: The guild hears a cockatrice’s peacock-like shriek, distantly. VIII [Curiosity] Orcish Graffiti: The guild notices some graffiti in Vetus chalked onto the cavern wall. It reads: “Ulf is no true orc. If he wishes to win my hand in marriage, he must defeat me in combat.” (The GM can accept lore bids on this curiosity as appropriate.) IX [Curiosity] Blind Fish Pool: The guild wanders by a shallow pool. The water looks clear, but the pool is full of toothy, blind fish. X [Curiosity] Nearby Flowers: The air is full of a heady floral scent. If the guild searches around a little, they’ll find a bunch of pale blue and purple lilies sprouting nearby. Appropriate lore bids will show that they are normal flowers with few (if any) meaningful alchemical properties, but they are quite lovely and might make a nice bouquet for someone. XI [Travel event] Droppings: The first person in the marching order accidentally steps in some droppings. If they can’t find a way to get clean soon, they’ll become Stressed. If the guild investigates, they realize that the droppings are from an ogre. It looks no more than a day old. XII [Travel event] Rushing River: The guild encounters a rushing river which has risen past its banks. It’s impossible to ford without getting soaked. The guild can either turn back and try and find an alternate route or attempt to cross. Swimming across the river requires a test of Swords. If successful, they make it across safely. If the test fails, they suffer a Wound from almost drowning. Whether successful or not, anybody who braved the cold waters becomes Stressed. If no precautions were taken, fragile items in backpacks (scrolls, provisions) are soaked and Destroyed. XIII [Travel event] Hole in Pack: While traveling, a random adventurer discovers that their pack has a hole in it. The last listed item in their pack has fallen out and disappeared. (Backtracking and performing a thorough search will prompt additional watches to pass.) XIV [Travel event] Bad Scene: The guild comes upon a field of faintly glowing green mushrooms sporadically sending up little clouds of dust. In the middle of the field is a corpse in rusted armor. A cracked chest lies near the corpse. (It’s all bad news. Mushrooms are poisonous. Corpse is a zombie. Chest? Probably bad too. But there’s also gold in the chest and that’s good.) XV [Travel event] Webs: The guild’s path forward is blocked by thick layers of web. However, they can see several hanging sacks dangling from the cavern ceiling. Are these other adventurers who met a grim fate? Could they be rescued? XVI [Random encounter] Red Herring Tavern: The guild happens upon a squat but cozy-looking tavern. A wooden sign depicts a red fish leaping from the water (a herring, if anybody bids lore). Inside is a tapped barrel of ale and a cauldron full of stew, but no innkeeper to be seen. In fact, the tavern is a giant mimic occupied by several smaller mimics. Sleeping in the mimic tavern is a notably bad idea. XVII [Random encounter] Cockatrice: A cockatrice has taken its chicks out to teach them how to hunt. XVIII [Random encounter] Ogre Courting Ritual: An amorous ogre is trying to impress a she-ogre with increasingly ridiculous feats of strength. They are both making a terrible racket. XIX [Random encounter] Orc Hooligans: A gang of three orc youths accompanied by a random number of goblins are on a quest to make a name for themselves before returning to their clan. They might see the guild as an appropriate challenge or be convinced to join with the guild against some greater foe. XX [Random encounter] Gentle Simon: An owlbear has treed Gentle Simon of Heartsbane, a notoriously shrimpy sorcerer. All of Gentle Simon’s Resolve has been expended trying to rescue himself, and he’s now beginning to weep. XXI [Quest rumor] Victims of Geralt Mourn: The adventurers find a rival guild crucified. They are still alive, though grievously injured and dehydrated. If the adventurers can provide aid, healing, and food, the rival party gasps about their recent encounter with the vampire Geralt Mourn, who the guild has sworn to slay. It was this dread vampire who crucified them as a warning to others. They have news of his current whereabouts, but would be loath to tangle with him again.

308.title: Light
308.body: What lurks just outside the halo of your torchlight? In the sunless depths, a candle is the difference between life and death. There are three levels of lighting while exploring dark places: bright, dim, and dark .

309.title: Bright light
309.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Light › Bright light
309.body: If you are holding a light source, you benefit from bright light. Bright light means that you can operate without penalty. If you’re holding a light source, you’re always clearly visible. Hiding is impossible.

310.title: Dim light
310.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Light › Dim light
310.body: Even a little light offers hope in the darkness. If you aren’t carrying a light source (while someone else in your guild is), you’re considered to be in dim lighting. Any complex or visually-dependent task—such as picking locks, surgery, investigation, crafting—suffers disfavor on tests of fate while you are in dim lighting unless an adventurer with a light source actively provides illumination. If you are in dim lighting, you may attempt to hide behind cover.

311.title: Darkness
311.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Light › Darkness
311.body: No matter how accomplished an adventurer is, darkness is crippling. You are Blind while in darkness. Most activities are simply impossible to accomplish in the dark—others may be attempted but suffer disfavor . Crawling in the dark is a futile pursuit. The guild is at risk of every pitfall and every trap, and creatures accustomed to darkness will find them easy prey. “It is pitch black. You are likely to be eaten by a grue.” – Zork, Infocom

312.title: Flickers
312.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Light › Flickers
312.body: The Omphalic Market lists candles, torches, and lanterns for purchase. Each type of light source can flicker a certain number of times before it is extinguished. Your light source flickers when the Meatgrinder says torches gutter . Candles can flicker 2 times. Torches can flicker 3 times. Lanterns can flicker 4 times. Candles, torches, and lanterns are not designed for violence. Your light source automatically breaks and is extinguished if: - It is hit in combat - You use it as a weapon in combat You can tie your lantern to your belt, but if you suffer a Wound, your lantern is also Destroyed, covering you in oil. Dropping your light source might cause it to go out. - Torches have a 50% chance of staying lit or being extinguished when dropped. Extinguished torches can’t be relit. - Candles are extinguished when dropped. Candles may be relit. - Lanterns are Destroyed when dropped.

313.title: We’re doomed!
313.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Light › We’re doomed!
313.body: If the guild is completely out of light sources, each player draws on the table below. Card Doom :---: --- I–VII You are eaten by a grue. VIII You are captured by monsters. The GM chooses an appropriate monster based on the Meatgrinder table. Escaping guild members know your general location and the type of monster. IX You are held for ransom by the bird-faced Olu Gang. It takes 1,000 gold per guild Fame (Deeds and Fame) to buy your freedom. X You are lost in the Underworld. The GM places your adventurer as an encounter on the Meatgrinder table. That character may reenter play if you are encountered. Make a new adventurer for the time being. Page You make it back to the surface, but only after making solemn oaths to forsake the adventuring life. You retire. The GM controls your character in the City. Knight You scramble back to the surface naked and shivering. You lose all of your equipment, both from your belt and backpack. Queen You limp back to the surface, shaken to your core. You have a 50% chance to have lost each item carried, tested individually. King You limp back to the surface, mostly unscathed but raving about the twelve different flavors of darkness.

314.title: Stress
314.body: The logic of Stress Have you ever had a player in a game who insisted their character would happily sit in a dungeon room for twelve hours and just count coins until they found the cursed one? Or that their character would jump into an open sewer to search for the dagger they just dropped? Has the same friend ever turned down a slice of pizza because it had pineapple on it? The Stressed condition does two things. First, it represents the trauma of the human experience in the mythic Underworld. Second, it disincentivizes choices that are on the extremes of human tolerability but have no other mechanical weight. If a player wants their adventurer to ford the freezing river, they’re welcome to do it. However, such an event would be physically taxing. As such, the GM should warn the player that such an action would cause them to become Stressed . Adventuring is nasty and uncomfortable. When you undergo a traumatic experience or suffer physical distress, check the Stressed condition. In short, when you’re shivering, hungry, or terrified, you are Stressed. Being Stressed has no immediate negative effects, but it makes recovery during the Camp Phase more taxing. You must clear Stressed before healing any other condition . The GM is the ultimate arbiter of what introduces Stress or not. In general, being Stressed is less serious than taking actual physical harm, but makes your adventurer angry, weak, sore, or miserable. Example stressors: exposure to extreme elements without the appropriate gear; magically terrifying monsters like liches or dragons; self-harm; extremely mundane, boring, and repetitive tasks; long-term social isolation; witnessing torture; and so on.

315.title: Item Durability
315.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Item Durability
315.body: Repairing items Tinker’s kits can be used during the Camp Phase to repair Notched items (but not Destroyed items). Spending your Camp Action to use a tinker’s kit removes 1 Notch. Notched and Destroyed items can be repaired if carried back to the City, see Replacing and repairing gear. Adventuring is hard on both your body and your gear. Items can be Notched or Destroyed while adventuring. Items might be damaged by environmental hazards. For example, a trap that shoots a jet of fire might Notch any flammable items on your belt. Items can also be damaged as a consequence of your actions. For example, if you throw your net over a charging manticore to help your companion escape, the manticore tears the net to shreds. The GM arbitrates when items are damaged. Fragile items are Destroyed after 1 Notch. Items intended for durability are Destroyed after 2 Notches. Items made of tempered steel are Destroyed after 3 Notches.

316.title: Falling
316.body: If you fall from a great height, you suffer 1 Piercing Wound (Piercing and Critical damage) for each 10’ you fall (rounded down). For example, if you fall from a 25’ height, you would suffer 2 Wounds that cannot be absorbed with armor. Whenever you fall, you may test Pentacles. - If you fail, take damage as normal. - If you succeed, treat the fall as 10’ shorter. For example, if you fall 25’ and succeed in the test of Pentacles, you only suffer 1 Piercing Wound. - On a great success, treat the fall as 20’ shorter (e.g., a 25’ fall would do no damage). - On a great failure, you take damage as normal and any fragile items (like hermetic bottles) on your belt or in your pack are Destroyed.

317.title: Afflictions
317.body: If you’ve drunk tainted water from a huldra’s body-choked well, inhaled a cloud of spores from a creeping mold, or developed an infected cut from a goblin’s shit-covered dagger, you become afflicted . Afflictions—be they poison, disease, infection, addiction, or otherwise—are essentially countdown clocks to doom. Each affliction has a number of stages, each with a specific effect. - Most afflictions have increasingly negative effects for each stage. - Some afflictions—notably drugs—have positive effects at their early stages. - Some afflictions have death at their final stage. When you gain an affliction, you immediately gain its stage 1 effect. To track your progress with the affliction, draw a circle . Draw as many sections as there are stages of the affliction. Color in the first section with hatch marks . For example

318.title: Curing an affliction
318.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Afflictions › Curing an affliction
318.body: To cure an affliction, take the Rest and Recover action during the Camp Phase (Camp Actions). During this action, you’ll burn charged Bonds. One stage of the affliction is cured after a certain number of charges are spent. Burned charges are cumulative. For example, if a stage of an affliction is cured for every 3 charges spent, you can burn 1 charge over the course of three Camp Phases to cure a single stage. The GM determines the number of charges needed to cure a stage of a particular affliction. Players are not told this information up front, but a well-worded lore bid might reveal these details. When Resting and Recovering, you tell the GM how many charges you are burning and hope for the best. Burned charges cure the most severe stages first, whether or not the affliction has progressed to that point. To represent a cured stage, color a section of the circle in black . You will never experience the effects associated with a cured stage. The affliction is completely healed when all stages are cured .

319.title: In summation
319.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Afflictions › Curing an affliction › In summation
319.body: - Your affliction begins at stage 1. - During the Crawl Phase, you have the opportunity to search for healing items or chirurgeons to help your recovery during the Camp Phase. - During the step 1 of your next Camp Phase, you can Rest and Recover to burn charges in an attempt to recover from the affliction. These charges can come from charged Bonds or healthful items. These charges go towards curing the final stage first (sections are blacked out on the affliction clock in a counterclockwise manner). - At the end of the Camp Phase, your affliction progresses one stage (clockwise on the affliction clock). If the stage beyond it has already been cured, you remain at your current affliction stage. - If you cure the stage that you are already on, your affliction regresses by one stage.

320.title: Example afflictions
