320.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Example afflictions
320.body: Here are some “common” afflictions to use as examples. GMs can tweak these to create any manner of gross old disorders for their players.

321.title: Giant rat venom
321.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Example afflictions › Giant rat venom
321.body: A green rat the size of a dog, covered in buboes, welts, and goiters, bites you. It only gets worse from there. Stage 1: The wound turns ugly: green and fetid. It begins to stink, but there are no other effects. Requires 1 charge to cure. Stage 2: You feel like hot garbage. You become permanently Exhausted. Requires 1 charge to cure. Stage 3: Your lungs are filled with green mucus. Every time you test fate, you take a Piercing Wound after the test is resolved. Requires 2 charges to cure.

322.title: Black honey
322.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Example afflictions › Black honey
322.body: A thick molasses that tastes so, so sweet. It’s like meth and speed had a terrifying demon baby. You act preternaturally fast while on the honey. Each time you take black honey, you are re-exposed to the affliction. If you’ve previously cured stage 2, erase the marking in the stage 2 section. Stage 1: If you’ve recently taken black honey, you may choose to draw 5 cards during an encounter instead of 4. If you do so, you spit out 1–4 teeth. Requires 5 charges to quit. Stage 2: You’re jittery and sweaty. Your Cups score equals 1 and you suffer disfavor on all tests of fate that require fine motor control. Requires 1 charge to calm down to stage 1.

323.title: Ghost lotus
323.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Example afflictions › Ghost lotus
323.body: The seeds of the ghost lotus rewrite pathways in the user’s brain. The feeling is incredibly addictive. Habitual users of the lotus (called lotusphages) become very strange and otherworldly: their personalities change, their memories become distorted, and they have trouble distinguishing between the waking world and dreams. Stage 1: You experience euphoria. This effect cancels out any effects that hamper your ability to sleep. Requires 1XP to recover from stage 1. No charges are otherwise needed. Stage 2: At this stage, you lose the ability to understand representative thought. Paintings and illustrations are just blobs of color. Words are meaningless lines on paper. You cannot read. You cannot write. You are also immune to illusions. Requires 2 charges to cure. Stage 3: You become lost in a waking dream. Rewrite one of your motif descriptors. For example, if you have the “Romancing Swordsman” motif, replace “Romancing” with another word (e.g., Ambitious, Addled, Drowsy, Sadistic, etc.). Requires 1 charge to cure.

324.title: The great contagion
324.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Example afflictions › The great contagion
324.body: “Oh Mythrys, do I have the red welts? I have the red welts don’t I? I’m going to die. Tell Mama I love her.” Stage 1: Your skin breaks out into red whorls that are very painful to the touch. You take a Piercing Wound. Requires 2 charges to cure. Stage 2: You take Critical damage. Requires 2 charges to cure. Stage 3: You die.

325.title: Social Encounters & Disposition
325.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition
325.body: In the Underworld, you’ll encounter the bizarre denizens of the dungeons and the adventurers trying their best to slay them (or you). Role-playing the characters you encounter is one of the GM’s many jobs. The GM is provided with guidelines for role-playing called Disposition. Advice for GMs creating characters with interesting personalities and running social encounters is provided in Creating interesting characters. Each Disposition has three steps of severity: mild, basic , and intense . Mild emotions are on the inside of the circle; intense emotions are on the outside of the circle. Related emotions are grouped near each other.

326.title: Starting Disposition
326.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Starting Disposition
326.body: A character’s starting Disposition informs the GM how that creature should initially act, how hostile or friendly it is to the guild, and what they’re likely to demand in a parlay. Sometimes a character’s starting Disposition will be obvious based on the scenario in which the guild encounters them. If there is any question, or if randomness is desired, the GM should look at the top card in the discard pile of the minor arcana. Card Disposition :---: --- I–II Anger III–IV Distaste V–VI Sadness VII–VIII Joy IX–X Surprise Page–Knight Trust Queen–King Fear Characters with positive Dispositions (e.g., joy, trust) negotiate in good faith. They will acquiesce to reasonable requests in exchange for a reasonable exchange from the guild. Characters with intense positive Dispositions might even provide extra aid and advice. Characters with negative Dispositions (e.g., angry, distaste) want to bring the conversation to an end. They don’t have any interest in exchanging goods or services with the guild. If the encounter continues at all, it will be in a combative capacity—transition to the Challenge Phase.

327.title: Influencing Disposition
327.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Influencing Disposition
327.body: As you role-play with a GM character, their Dispositions change based on how your actions interact with their personality. All intelligent creatures can be negotiated with (assuming a shared language). When role-playing with the GM’s characters, you don’t have to speak in a silly voice or use faux Shakespearean language. You don’t even have to say exactly what your character is saying, word for word. You do have to say what you want and how you are approaching the conversation. - You might flatter the vain countess. - You might make pious platitudes to the unctuous priest. - You might offer rare trash to the goblin trash merchant. These strategies only make sense when applied towards that particular character; offering trash to the vain countess would be unwise. The GM judges the results of a negotiation based on how what you said aligns or conflicts with their character’s personality. Depending on the outcome of the role-playing exchange, the GM character’s Disposition either increases/decreases in severity or shifts to a related emotion. - Good ideas and strong bargaining chips that appeal to a character’s likes and wants will automatically create positive Dispositions. - Approaches that conflict with the character’s dislikes will automatically create negative Dispositions. - When the situation is risky and there’s something at stake, the GM will call for a test of Wands . - Success on this test moves the character’s Disposition to an adjacent, beneficial emotion or increases their current emotion’s severity. - Failure moves the character’s Disposition towards a negative emotion.

328.title: Role-playing Disposition
328.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Role-playing Disposition
328.body: There are seven basic Dispositions: anger, distaste, sadness, joy, surprise, trust, and fear . Each of the seven Dispositions are listed below, with the core emotional state of each flanked by its mild and intense states. A list of emotional synonyms is also given, as one of those terms might be more appropriate and might aid in the GM in appropriately role-playing the Disposition. Some notes are also given as to how a creature with that Disposition might act in a Challenge.

329.title: Acceptance | Trust | Admiration
329.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Role-playing Disposition › Acceptance | Trust | Admiration
329.body: Trust is a measure of belief in the general honesty, fairness, or capability of the other party. A base level of trust is a common starting Disposition for many benevolent creatures. Creatures who trust the guild will generally negotiate in good faith, but will still cautiously ensure the exchanges are fair. Betraying the trust of a character is a good way to change their Disposition to sad or angry. Synonyms: confident, hopeful, optimistic, playful, interested, inquisitive, curious In a Challenge: Typically, creatures with this Disposition are not inclined to fight. If the situation obligates a fight without changing the trust Disposition, the creature might attempt to learn more about the guild’s prowess through non-lethal methods.

330.title: Annoyance | Anger | Rage
330.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Role-playing Disposition › Annoyance | Anger | Rage
330.body: Anger is an intense emotional response that arises from a perceived provocation, threat, or hurt. Displays of anger are very aggressive and intimidating, and might quickly devolve to violence. It is a common emotional response for creatures with bestial intelligence or maladjusted humans. Anger is one half of the fight or flight response. Anger can impair the creature’s ability to take in information or make wise decisions during the encounter. Synonyms: hurt, humiliated, threatened, hateful, violated, furious, provoked, hostile, ridiculed In a Challenge: Anger makes people stupid and clumsy. The angry creature will try and focus on the source of their anger. An angry creature will attack recklessly, with little regard for the environment.

331.title: Pensiveness | Sadness | Grief
331.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Role-playing Disposition › Pensiveness | Sadness | Grief
331.body: Sadness is emotional pain associated with loss, despair, helplessness, or disappointment. Sad creatures often have obvious needs to be alleviated, which might change their Disposition for the better. However, sadness often causes creatures to lose interest in activities they once enjoyed, and sadness can create a significant barrier to positive influences. Synonyms: anxious, empty, helpless, hopeless, depressed, irritable, guilty, lonely, abandoned In a Challenge: In battle, those afflicted with deep sadness fight with abandon. They take chances they might otherwise not take. Often, they attempt to move first in Initiative, recklessly charging into battle and exposing themselves to danger.

332.title: Boredom | Distaste | Loathing
332.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Role-playing Disposition › Boredom | Distaste | Loathing
332.body: Disgust is a reaction to something offensive, distasteful, or unpleasant. This revulsion is often a product of breaking hygiene norms or moral codes. It is a common starting Disposition for potentially antagonistic creatures you encounter. Remember, the adventuring life is a dirty, dirty business. Synonyms: disapproving, repelled, judgmental, appalled, nauseated, horrified, hesitant In a Challenge: Creatures full of loathing delight in violence against the targets of its distaste. The creature’s main desire is to cause harm or pain. This harm might be centered on a particular creature type (a witch-hunter pursuing a witch), or perhaps it’s more general (a vampire’s general disdain for all mortal life).

333.title: Anxiety | Fear | Terror
333.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Role-playing Disposition › Anxiety | Fear | Terror
333.body: Fear is an emotional response to a perceived danger or threat. Fear is one half of the flight-or-fight response. Creatures responding with fear often want to just end the social encounter and might make any concessions necessary to accomplish this. Or, if they think they can do so successfully, frightened creatures will try and abandon the encounter altogether. Synonyms: weak, rejected, threatened, exposed, nervous, persecuted, inferior, worried, helpless In a Challenge: Fearful creatures will attempt to flee the source of their fear, avoiding combat unless it is necessary to escape. They prioritize high-value cards for their Initiative.

334.title: Distraction | Surprise | Awe
334.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Role-playing Disposition › Distraction | Surprise | Awe
334.body: When there is a disconnect between expectations and reality, a creature reacts with surprise. Surprise might come when the guild interacts with the more “normal” society of the City—not everyone is accustomed to the adventurer’s life. Surprise might also occur during confusing or bewildering encounters in the Underworld. Synonyms: startled, confused, amazed, shocked, dismayed, perplexed, excited In a Challenge: A surprised creature wasn’t planning on fighting today. It will fight if it believes itself threatened, but won’t pursue combat for its own purposes. It will try to disengage as early as possible.

335.title: Contentment | Joy | Ecstasy
335.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Role-playing Disposition › Contentment | Joy | Ecstasy
335.body: When their needs are met, creatures feel a sense of joy or happiness. Like anger, feelings of joy can cloud judgment. This is the ideal state for influencing a creature, as they are well-disposed to entreaties and exchanges. Synonyms: happy, peaceful, intimate, aroused, proud, thankful, powerful, respected In a Challenge: Creatures who are joyful will not usually desire to engage in conflict. However, if the situation calls for it, joyful creatures might be cocky or overbold, perceiving the combat as a game. Cocky creatures might toy with, taunt, or tease adventurers during battle.

336.title: Example social encounter
336.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Social Encounters & Disposition › Example social encounter
336.body: GM: The face in the middle of the door suddenly animates. It’s still made of gold, but its mouth and eyes open and move and look basically human. It speaks in a deep voice and says, “Password?” Jaesh: Aw, come on baby. Don’t be like that. Everybody at the table laughs and Jaesh charges his Bonds with the adventurers who are his Allies. GM: Wait, are you trying to sweet-talk the magical face door into opening? Jaesh: Yeah. I lean in and say, “Honey, you know I know how to open you up. Make you feel good. Come on. Let daddy pass.” GM: Ha. OK wait. Let me think. The GM reasons that the magical door has basic social motivations because their notes stipulate that the door can hold a reasonable conversation, can report on things that it sees, and knows a lot of lore about this area of the Underworld. They figure that nobody has ever really been kind to the door, probably only seeing it as an obstacle to be overcome. They set the door’s initial Disposition to weak surprise. GM: The door seems surprised. It seems like nobody ever has really treated it nicely. Go ahead and draw Wands with favor. Jaesh’s player draws from the minor arcana deck and gets a Page of Pentacles. Jaesh adds his Wands attribute—a 4—and gets a total of 15. The GM rules that the success moves the Disposition from surprise to a related emotion and chooses weak joy (contentment). GM: OK, the door seems to be taken in by your sweet talking. It says, “ Oh , you sweet thing. How I long to open for you. Alas! It is against my enchantment unless you can speak the password. Long have I waited here, bored, waiting for some nice man to spend time with me.” Jaesh: Ah! If you’re bored, I can read to you from my book. I have a book of children’s fables that I grew up reading in my pack. The GM notes that Jaesh is offering something concrete and just automatically switches to the next emotion – “acceptance.” GM: It’s face brightens up. “Oh would you?” it says. Jaesh: Sure. I’m going to spend some time reading a story from that picture book I’m carrying. I make sure to show it the pictures as I turn the pages. GM: That’s going to take a little time. I’m going to draw on the Meatgrinder to see if your torches flicker, but sure, you can do that. The GM draws from the major arcana deck to see if the guild’s light source grows dim as they waste time. They don’t draw a I-V, so they continue the scene. GM: OK, after the story the door seems extremely grateful. It says, “That was excellent. What a strong reading voice you have. I’ll give you a hint. The password is a six-letter word for a striking tool or weapon.”

337.title: Example Crawl Phase
337.breadcrumb: Chapter 6: The Crawl Phase › Example Crawl Phase
337.body: A guild named the Steel-Clad Snakes has just descended into the Castle of Crossed Destinies, a dungeon level they’ve explored only briefly in the past. The guild consists of Daria the shaman (orc, Path of Wands), Fergus Crowell the alchemist (human, Path of Cups), and Chirm the acrobat (wood elf, Path of Pentacles). GM: OK, you follow the stairs down into room 201. The GM looks at their notes for a description of 201. They then flip over a major arcana card to get an event from the Castle of Crossed Destinies Meatgrinder table. They get a Hierophant [V ]. The Meatgrinder entry is “Torches gutter.” GM: This place is dark, and in your torchlight you can tell that it’s a large space—like a ballroom. Who has the light again? Fergus: I have a lantern. GM: And you’re in the middle of the marching order? OK, so, in the lantern light you all see a large space with high ceilings. It’s like an indoor garden or closed-in atrium. There are silvery bushes growing here in the middle of cobblestone paths. Interspersed among the bushes are black soapstone statues—nude, Greco-Roman style, in various positions. The room is so large that your lantern light doesn’t quite make it all the way to all four walls, but you can see exits in the north, east, and west walls. As you enter the room, your torches gutter. Fergus: OK, that was my lantern’s last flicker. Can I keep the flame alight if I add in another bottle of oil? GM: Of course. Fergus’s player erases a flask of oil from his backpack and erases the previous flickers from his light tracker on his adventurer sheet. Chirm: I want to take a closer look at one of the statues. I approach one and take a close look but don’t touch it. GM: Well, with Fergus refilling his lantern you don’t have a light source until he catches up. Fergus: I’m on my way! I’ll hold up the lantern for her. GM: OK, Fergus holds up his lantern high so you can both look at the statue. It looks like the statue of the Dying Gaul—do you know that one? It’s like, a human who is sitting on the ground, twisted in pain. Chirm: Do I see any veins or cracks in the statue that would indicate it could be opened? GM: Good question. No, the black soapstone is seamless. But! As you lean in to get close to it, it suddenly shifts position and reaches out and grabs you. Chirm: I jerk back! GM: OK, you had said before you weren’t touching it, so you’re able to step back. The statue stops moving—it looks like it has always been in that position, half turning, reaching out. Chirm: Nobody touch the statues, y’all! Daria: Do we see anything else in this room besides the statues and the bushes? GM: Nothing obvious, no. Daria: Let’s move on, guys. All pain no gain here. GM: Where do you want to go? The guild looks over their map, planning out their route towards the middle of the dungeon level. Daria: We’ll move to…203. Chirm: And as we walk through the room, we’ll make sure we’re staying well out of the reach of the statues. GM: Sure. You choose a safe path on the cobblestones and tiptoe past all the statues on your way to the door. The door is wooden with a brass Venetian door handle. Daria: I listen at the door. The GM checks their notes for room 203. The room is called “Pond of ferric fluid” in the GM’s notes, which is enough to remind them of the contents. The GM then flips over a major arcana card and reads the entry on the Castle of Crossed Destinies Meatgrinder table. The GM pulls Temperance [XIV ]. The Meatgrinder entry reads: “[Discard] deconstruction imps have rigged up a heavy stone above the door to this room so that it will fall as soon as the door is opened. They are giggling in the corner, waiting to see their trick pay off.” The GM looks at the top card of the minor arcana discard pile. It’s a V of Cups. The GM knows now that there is a trap and five imps hiding behind the door. GM: Uh, yeah, you hear a muffled giggling from behind the door. Daria: Like, a lot of giggling or a single giggler? GM: A lot of giggling, and a lot of shushing. Daria: Do they sound high pitched or low pitched? GM: Uh, pretty high pitched. Daria: Are they goblins? GM: You can’t really tell. Well, wait, do you want to bid lore? Do you have a motif that would let you identify the giggling of goblins? Daria: Nah, that’s okay. I say “Hey guys, I think there’s somebody in the next room. Get ready.” I’ll make sure that my stiletto and my shield are ready as I slowly push the door open. GM: Your caution is warranted! As you push open the door, CRASH! An enormous stone block slams down from above you. Test Pentacles to see if you stepped back quickly enough or if part of the falling stone clipped you. You can test with favor because you were acting cautiously. Play continues from there. After resolving the test of fate, the game possibly shifts to a Challenge Phase as the imps block the guild’s path into the room.

338.title: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase
338.body: “Our pockets were full of deng, so there was no real need from the point of view of crasting any more pretty polly to tolchock some old veck in an alley and viddy him swim in his blood while we counted the takings and divided by four, nor to do the ultra-violent on some shivering starry grey-haired ptitsa in a shop and go smecking off with the till's guts. But, as they say, money isn't everything.” – A Clockwork Orange, Anthony Burgess The Crypt Titan was the former dungeon lord of the Ossuary and the first dungeon lord to fall to the crusades. An army flooded the bone-lined halls, and the skeletal giant devoured wave after wave as it crawled down the passages. Here, war was waged in its most antique form. Underfoot, bodies and parts of bodies were trampled until the ground was slick and there was a terrible stink from the wet innards. The Ossuary became so littered with internalments that the huge form of the Crypt Titan was entangled and slowed. Passages behind the thing were choked with bodies and passages in front of it bristled with resistance. Shoulder to shoulder, the crusaders beat and bashed the Crypt Titan’s arms from its body, and with a cry, crushed its skull to nothingness. It stopped moving. By the end of the battle, ten-score crusaders had been felled. Of the two-hundred to die in the battle, fifty rose again from (seemingly) deadly wounds. All were amazed, and it was declared a miracle. And yet, the other fallen were no less restless. Those dead who were utterly desiccated by the Titan’s jaws became howling specters. Those who were merely crushed by the Titan’s bulk struggled up as zombies. And thus was the Crusade of the Ossuary declared victorious.

339.title: The Flow of the Challenge Phase
339.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase
339.body: Learning the Challenge Phase The Challenge Phase rules are designed to be fun—players make tons of small decisions: which cards to use, how to collaborate to get the maximum effect, how to take damage. The rules are also designed to be deadly—things can quickly go from bad to worse as characters Notch armor, Wound talents, and realize they’ve gotten in over their heads. Getting used to card-based combat sequences can be daunting or slow going at first, but once your table falls into the swing of it, the Challenge system ensures that nobody is sitting around waiting for their turn. To learn any game, take it slow and go through each step slowly. After two or three Challenges, you’ll get the sense of the flow and find there’s a lot of interesting tactics embedded in the rules. Do you use a low Initiative to go first so you can see what the GM’s monsters Initiative is for the rest of the round? Do you bluff with a low Riposte? Do you put down a Riposte first, then draw your sword to make your counterattack more deadly? Players who put in the due diligence to learn the tactics underlying the Challenge Phase will have a lot of fun. During the Crawl Phase, players and GMs exchange questions and answers. During Challenges, things become much more bounded. A Challenge narrows the lens of the adventure into every blow, every maneuver, every stunt that the players attempt. In this phase, everybody at the table draws cards that represent their opportunities during combat. The players play these cards to choose specific actions—attacks, movement, pulling something from their pack, etc. The GM controls the hostile characters, be they monsters or mortals. Both sides pursue their goals while exchanging blows. When one side retreats, surrenders, or lies defeated, the Challenge Phase transitions back to the Crawl. The Challenge Phase uses the following procedure. Play cycles through steps 1-5 until the Challenge is resolved. The rules for players and GMs differ slightly; GM-specific rules start see GMing the Challenge.

340.title: 0. Set the scene
340.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene
340.body: As the Challenge begins, the GM frames the scene. They describe the different zones, note the combatants and their positions , and articulate if any scenery and hazards have special rules .

341.title: 1. Draw Challenge cards
341.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 1. Draw Challenge cards
341.body: Challenges are split up into rounds. At the beginning of each round, each player draws four Challenge cards from the minor arcana deck. The GM draws a certain number of major arcana cards based on what enemies are being fought, see Draw Challenge Cards.

342.title: 2. Play Initiative
342.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 2. Play Initiative
342.body: Players choose one of their Challenge cards as their Initiative for the round. They place it facedown in front of them. The GM plays an Initiative card for every significant character or group of characters they control.

343.title: 3. Take turns
343.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 3. Take turns
343.body: The GM counts up from lowest card (I) through the highest card (king). When the GM announces the Initiative of a GM character or adventurer, that character takes their turn.

344.title: 4. Minor actions
344.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 4. Minor actions
344.body: After a turn is resolved, the GM asks: “Any minor actions?” Anybody who wants to take a minor action declares their action. Minor actions are resolved simultaneously. After all actions of a particular Initiative number are resolved, the GM continues the count upwards. Steps 3 and 4 repeat until everybody has had their turn.

345.title: 5. End the round
345.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 5. End the round
345.body: Once everybody has had their turn and the subsequent minor actions have been resolved, the round ends. Everybody discards any unused Challenge cards in their hand. Everybody discards their current Initiative card. Facedown cards remain in play. If the Fool was drawn during this past round, both minor and major arcana decks are shuffled. A new round begins.

346.title: 0. Set the scene
346.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene
346.body: Before the Challenge procedure begins, the GM sets the scene. They describe the zones the encounter occupies, note the combatants, and clarify everybody’s positions relative to each other. If one of the sides of the combat surprises the other, they begin the scene with some advantage (Ambushes and surprise). If a combatant’s position or a hazard in the scene warrant special consideration, the GM will create special rules for the Challenge. The assumption is that most Challenges are played out in the “theater of the mind.” That is, the GM describes the location and the players merely describe their adventurer’s journey through this imagined space. If things are a little confusing and players aren’t exactly sure what is being described, the GM should sketch a quick map. If things are complicated and position really matters, feel free to create a more elaborate map and use tokens or miniatures to demarcate the positioning of various adventurers.

347.title: Zones
347.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene › Zones
347.body: The GM describes the encounter and demarcates the scene’s zones. Zones are an abstract way to talk about the different parts of dungeon rooms. You can interact with things and characters in the same zone as you. Imagine an auditorium. In this room, the GM might demarcate the following zones: - Backstage - Stage - Orchestra pit - Seating - Balcony A scene can have any number of zones. Often, there are at least two zones: the room you’re leaving and the occupied room you’re entering. More complicated scenes will have more. As you throw open doors, run down hallways, destroy walls, etc., the GM will add new zones to the scene. Zones are important for the Challenge Phase, but the concept of zones is easy to use in other phases . Several spells use “zones” to explain their effects. Outside of a Challenge, the GM should make it clear how these spells work if zones have not previously been established in the scene.

348.title: Combatants and position
348.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene › Combatants and position
348.body: The GM describes all of the characters involved in the Challenge and their positions in the scene. It should be clear which zone you’re in and which zones the GM’s characters are in. Generally, positioning around a zone during a Challenge is abstract. Even if you use miniatures as visual aids to represent your position on the map, it’s assumed that your adventurer is moving around a lot within the zone. You Move or Dash to go to a new zone. If there is something preventing you from moving between zones, like a big ogre guarding the door or a hallway of swinging blades, you must Avoid the hazard to get past it. Characters (both adventurers and the GM’s characters) are either engaged or disengaged during Challenges. You begin most Challenges disengaged . - While disengaged, you can move freely. - While engaged , you are actively struggling against opponents in battle.

349.title: Disengaged
349.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene › Combatants and position › Disengaged
349.body: By default, all characters are disengaged. They can take actions freely. Disengaged characters can make missile attacks against other creatures, but can’t make melee attacks without becoming engaged.

350.title: Engaged
350.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene › Combatants and position › Engaged
350.body: When a character successfully makes a melee attack against another, they both become engaged. - Engaged characters can make melee attacks against each other. - Engaged characters can’t make missile attacks . It’s very difficult to bring a missile weapon to bear against someone actively threatening you. If you are engaged and try to Move to a new zone, each opponent engaged with you may deal 1 Wound to you or allow you to pass. You are then disengaged and move to an adjacent zone. If you are engaged, you can use the Avoid action to disengage safely; see Pentacles actions for the rules on Avoiding. Some effects like Trip and Root automatically disengage a character as well.

351.title: Ambushes and surprise
351.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene › Ambushes and surprise
351.body: Usually, adventurers and GM characters notice each other at the same time. In remote, dark places, the existence of light sources is immediately noticeable at a distance. Sometimes, however, combat begins with an ambush .

352.title: Adventurers
352.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene › Ambushes and surprise › Adventurers
352.body: When an adventurer sets up an ambush, use the rules of the Vigilance action (Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit)). You’re making a statement that says, “When X happens, I’m going to do Y.” For example, “When I see an intruder, I’ll ring the warning gong,” or “When the bandits walk into the room, I’ll shoot the first one.” This action is automatically successful . Afterwards, the Challenge begins as normal.

353.title: GM characters
353.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 0. Set the scene › Ambushes and surprise › GM characters
353.body: Sometimes the GM’s characters will have the opportunity to ambush you. When ambushed, the adventurer closest to the ambush in the marching order tests Cups. If successful, they raise the alarm before the ambush occurs. A Challenge begins as normal. If unsuccessful, the entire guild is surprised. If you are surprised, each GM character takes an action before the Challenge begins; the action is automatically successful and doesn’t require a card to be played. GM characters prefer tactic 1 to tactic 2, and tactic 2 to tactic 3. TACTIC 1: CREATE AN ADVANTAGE . The GM characters make sure the battlefield is to their advantage. Examples include: - Yell a warning - Collapse the bridge - Lock the door - Set the tapestry on fire TACTIC 2: DEPRIVE ADVENTURERS OF RESOURCES . The GM characters try to get the upper hand over the adventurers. Examples include: - Disarming an adventurer - Extinguishing their torches - Filling the area with web TACTIC 3: SHANK THE ADVENTURERS . The GM characters sucker punch the guild. Each attacker deals 1 Wound, but each individual adventurer can only be attacked once.

354.title: Special rules
354.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › Special rules
354.body: As the GM sets the scene, they tell the players if anything in the scene has special rules . The GM might set special rules for the scene based on the position of the combatants relative to the guild. Are they in zones near, far, or obscured from you? For example: - Is the elvish assassin darting between the ancient trees? - If so, missile attacks against the assassin suffer disfavor. - Are the imps hanging off of the giant idol like monkeys? - If so, the imps cannot be attacked with shorter weapons; only polearms and missile weapons can be used. - Is the fat monk hiding in his empty barrel? - If so, the players won’t be told about the monk until they are in the same zone and can see down into the barrel. The GM might also declare that certain elements of the scene—like traps or hazards—need special rules to navigate. For example: - A bladed pendulum might require a test of fate to move past. - A pit trap might be leapt by taking the Dash action. - A chasm may only be descended safely if a rope is used.

355.title: Example scene
355.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › Special rules › Example scene
355.body: Consider a fight aboard a ship. As the GM sketches out the scene, they demarcate the following zones and special rules: Zone 1 is the rigging. - To move into this zone, you must spend a Pentacles card and have both hands free. - Missile attacks from the crow’s nest have favor because of your superior perspective. - If you are hit while in this zone, discard a card to test Pentacles. If you fail, you fall onto the deck (zone 5) and take a Piercing Wound. Zone 2 is the poop deck. - There are no special rules for the poop deck except that making too many jokes about the poop deck will cause the GM to throw chips at you. Zone 3 is in the water. - If you fall into the water, you automatically drop whatever is in your hands. You will drown unless you choose to shrug off your pack. Everything in your pack is lost. - If you fall into the water wearing metal armor, you will drown unless rescued. - It is a miscellaneous action to throw one of the ropes from the deck to a drowning character. Zone 4 is atop the forecastle. - There are no special rules about the forecastle. Zone 5 is the main deck. - This zone contains a winch that controls the anchors of the ship. It is a miscellaneous action to use this winch. - This zone contains the steering wheel. It is a Cups action to steer the ship purposefully.

356.title: 1. Draw Challenge cards
356.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 1. Draw Challenge cards
356.body: Challenges are split up into rounds. ^draw-challenge-cards At the beginning of each round, each player draws four Challenge cards from the minor arcana deck. The GM draws cards from the major arcana deck based on what kind of enemies they’re using, their powers, and their numbers; see GMing the Challenge for a full explanation of how to GM the Challenge Phase. Challenge cards are spent on the following: - Initiative - Actions - Minor actions Initiative is a measure of how carefully or recklessly your adventurer is acting during that round. The lower your Initiative, the faster you take your turn. However, the lower your Initiative, the easier you are to hit during that round. Actions are decisive deeds that determine whether you will survive or perish. The “acting player” is the player whose turn it is. Characters take one action on their turn. Each player has one turn per round (unless they draw the Fool, see Interrupt actions). The GM will take a turn for each important character they control. Minor actions are quick actions that take place during other characters’ turns. They happen after another person’s turn and take place simultaneously to all other minor actions taken at the same time.

357.title: 2. Play Initiative
357.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 2. Play Initiative
357.body: After drawing your Challenge cards, select one card and play it facedown . This is your Initiative for the round. The GM will play one Initiative card for each significant character or group of characters they control. ^play-initiative Initiative determines how quickly you act during the round. Initiative also determines your defenses. When making a test of fate, if the total of the card’s value plus bonuses is 14+, the test is a success. The chaos of a Challenge changes this paradigm. To successfully attack, trip, cast a spell against, or otherwise affect a combatant in a Challenge, the total value of your card plus bonuses must equal or exceed that character’s Initiative. When other characters attempt to perform an action against you, flip your Initiative card face up (if it’s not already) . Compare the action’s value against your Initiative. - If the value is greater than your Initiative, the action succeeds. - If the value is less than your Initiative, the action fails. - If the value ties your Initiative, it succeeds unless you are wielding a shield.

358.title: Tied Initiative
358.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 2. Play Initiative › Tied Initiative
358.body: If two people have the same Initiative, they act at the same time. Players with the same Initiative decide among themselves who will declare their actions first. If there is a tie between a GM character and an adventurer, the GM determines who declares first.

359.title: 3. Take turns
359.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 3. Take turns
359.body: Each round, the GM counts up from lowest card (I) through the highest card (king). When the GM reaches your Initiative in their count, flip your Initiative card face up to declare that you are the acting player. ^take-turns To perform an action, play one of your Challenge cards. There are a range of actions you can perform during Challenges, each of which is tied to one of the four suits. The rules for Challenge Actions are detailed below.

360.title: Action value
360.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 3. Take turns › Action value
360.body: Card values Just a reminder: - Aces have a value of 1 (I). - Pages have a value of 11 ( XI ). - Knights have a value of 12 ( XII ). - Queens have a value of 13 ( XIII ). - Kings have a value of 14 ( XIV ). On your turn, your action’s total value equals the card’s face value plus the associated attribute . For example, if an acting player makes an Attack action with a IV of Cups card and has a Swords attribute of 3, their Attack has a total value of 7 (4+3). All Challenge Actions (both actions and minor actions) can have favor/disfavor applied, per the rules see Favor and disfavor. The GM is the arbiter of when to apply favor and disfavor during Challenges. - Favor adds +3 to the action’s total value. - Disfavor subtracts -3 from the action’s total value. For example, an adventurer dangling from a tower window by a rope might be given disfavor to an Attack action against a circling harpy due to the precariousness of their situation. Alternatively, an adventurer might be given favor to a Roughhouse action against a character who is standing near a puddle of oil because the ground is so slippery. You can spend a point of Resolve to gain favor on a Challenge Action (Favor and disfavor). Resolve cannot be spent to adjust your Initiative score.

361.title: Facedown cards
361.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 3. Take turns › Facedown cards
361.body: No peeking! When a player declares an action that places a card facedown, they state what action they are taking, but only they know the card’s value until it is flipped up. Nobody but the player can look at the facedown card until the action is triggered. No peeking! You usually play Challenge cards face up, but some actions (such as Dodge or Aid Another) are played facedown to represent your adventurer readying themselves to act. You may only have one facedown action at a time. (Your Initiative card does not count towards this limit!) If you take an action that would cause you to place another card facedown, replace the current facedown card and discard the last one. If you no longer want to take the facedown action, discard the card. Facedown actions played on your turn add the appropriate attribute to the card’s value when the card is revealed. To help you remember when you played a facedown card (and to visually distinguish it from your Initiative), set the card down in a different position relative to your Initiative card . - If you play a card facedown on your turn, set the facedown card sideways above your Initiative card. When the time comes to reveal the card, add the appropriate attribute to the card’s value. - If you play a card facedown as a minor action, set the facedown card sideways below your Initiative card. When the time comes to reveal the card, use the face value of the card for the total. Facedown cards remain in play until they’re activated, you replace them with another action, you discard it, or the Challenge Phase ends. Facedown cards do not impact how many cards you draw at the beginning of the round—players always draw four Challenge cards . You can use a defensive action (like Dodge or Riposte) for the benefit of anybody in your zone. It stays facedown until activated, as usual. If you move away from your ally before the defensive action triggers, discard your facedown card.

362.title: Interrupt actions
362.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 3. Take turns › Interrupt actions
362.body: Some talents or circumstances can turn an action into an interrupt . Interrupt actions take place before the acting player’s action. For example, a halfling adventurer wielding a polearm might Riposte against a goblin charging at them before the goblin's Attack is resolved. If the halfling slays the goblin, they’re safe; if the goblin survives the interrupt, they follow through on their Attack. Interrupt actions do not count against the limit of one action per turn.

363.title: The Fool
363.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 3. Take turns › The Fool
363.body: If you pull the Fool when drawing Challenge cards, put it in your hand as normal. The Fool is not played like other Challenge cards. The Fool has a value of 0 and is always played in conjunction with another card . When you play the Fool, you get an additional turn—you can play any card to perform any action and add the associated attribute to your total value. Additionally, this counts as an interrupt action . The Fool always goes first, no matter what. Essentially, drawing the Fool allows you to take two turns (but no minor actions) during a round. When the Fool is drawn, shuffle both the minor and major arcana decks at the end of the round .

364.title: Skipping your turn
364.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 3. Take turns › Skipping your turn
364.body: You do not have to take an action on your turn. If you do not take an action, the GM continues counting. Nobody takes minor actions. Similarly, if you have no cards in your hand when the GM calls your Initiative number, you do not take an action and nobody takes a minor action. The GM continues counting.

365.title: 4. Minor actions
365.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 4. Minor actions
365.body: After the acting player’s action is resolved, the GM asks the table if anybody wants to perform a minor action. To make a minor action, spend a Challenge card whose suit matches the action . A Cups card must be spent to make a Cups action, a Pentacles card must be spent to make a Pentacles action, and so on. ^minor-actions Minor actions all happen essentially at the same time . Everybody who wants to perform a minor action declares what they want to do and puts down a card to represent this action. Then, everybody reveals their cards simultaneously. The GM describes the results of these actions in whatever order makes the most sense and is the most cinematic. The players and the GM can both make minor actions. If the GM is performing a minor action, they declare their action at the same time as the players do. Because the GM uses the major arcana (which has no suits), they ignore the requirement that the card played must match the action’s suit—the GM can play any card to take a minor action. After all minor actions of a particular Initiative number are resolved, the GM continues the count upwards until all characters and enemies have had a turn.

366.title: Minor action value
366.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 4. Minor actions › Minor action value
366.body: A minor action’s total value equals the card’s face value . You do not add your attribute to minor actions. A minor action’s value can also be affected by favor/disfavor. For example, to use Roughhouse as a minor action, play a Pentacles card. The card only has its face value. For instance, the Knight of Pentacles has a total value of 12—your Pentacles attribute is not added.

367.title: 5. End the round
367.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › The Flow of the Challenge Phase › 5. End the round
367.body: When every player and each GM character has had their turn (and all minor actions on the last turn have been resolved), the round is over. Facedown actions are left facedown. Any remaining Challenge cards in your hand are discarded. The players and the GM draw more Challenge cards and begin a new round. If the Fool has been played, shuffle both the minor and the major arcana decks before dealing new cards.

368.title: Challenge Actions
368.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions
368.body: Four aces Sometimes luck isn’t with you. Sometimes you draw and get a bad hand. This happens in games; it’s okay. What are your options though? We’ve seen players default to attacking an enemy they know they won’t hit. It’s what they would do in other games since they don’t know what their dice roll will be. That’s not a good strategy in His Majesty the Worm. The Challenge rules are a minigame; a poker face is part of that mini-game. If you play a low Initiative, but then defend with a Dodge or Riposte, you give the GM pause. Why the low Initiative? What defensive cards do you have? This strategy only works if you don’t say, “Shit. I have nothing.” (Or maybe you’re bluffing.) If all else fails: be supportive. Maybe you won’t achieve much by yourself, but you can give an added boost to an ally. Below is a list of common Challenge Actions and their associated suits. This set of actions isn’t comprehensive. These are simply common actions that we have given rules to so that GMs know how to handle common types of interactions. GMs should use these as examples and interpret the rules for whatever actions the players attempt. Players can attempt to do just about anything—swing from chandeliers, ride blazing hay carts down hills, shove burning brands into cyclops’ eyes—whatever. The GM can use this list of actions as a starting point to help them frame these narrative actions. If players are consistently only using the basic actions, the GM can introduce scenes where other actions are important as a way to shake things up.

369.title: Free actions
369.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Free actions
369.body: You don’t need to play Challenge cards to talk in character or move around within a zone. You can freely do these things on anybody’s turn unless something is restraining you.

370.title: Swords actions
370.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Swords actions

371.title: Attack
371.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Swords actions › Attack
371.body: Unarmed combatants Combat is a dance of hit or be hit. If you are not wielding a weapon or are only carrying a missile weapon, you are particularly vulnerable. Attacks against you gain favor (+3 to their action’s value). Similarly, you can make an Attack with your bare fists, but if your opponent is armed with a real weapon, your Attack has disfavor. Furthermore, unarmed adventurers can deal no damage to creatures larger than them. Attacks are sword strikes, fired arrows, or a monster’s savage bites. If your Attack value is greater than your opponent’s Initiative, you deal 1 Wound. If your Attack value is less than their Initiative, it is deflected and no harm is done. Ties go to the attacker unless the defender has a shield. In either event, reveal your opponent’s Initiative card. Successful melee attacks cause both combatants to be engaged.

372.title: Riposte
372.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Swords actions › Riposte
372.body: Ripostes are counterattacks that make it clear you’re not to be fucked with. Play your card facedown. When you’re next targeted by an Attack, Roughhouse, or similar action, you must reveal the card. If your Riposte value is greater than the attacker’s action value, you deal 1 Wound to your attacker. If it is less than the value, your counterstrike misses. Ties go to the Riposter unless the attacker is wielding a shield. A Riposte action is resolved after the initial attack. Once your Riposte card is resolved, discard the card.

373.title: Pentacles actions
373.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Pentacles actions

374.title: Avoid
374.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Pentacles actions › Avoid
374.body: Avoid to get past a danger, threat, or guard that’s trying to stop your movement. If your Avoid value is greater than your opponent’s Initiative, you get past the threat and can move to an adjacent zone. If you are engaged and want to disengage safely, use the Avoid action. - If your Avoid value is equal to or greater than your opponent’s Initiative, you disengage and can move to an adjacent zone . - If your Avoid value is less than your opponent’s Initiative, your opponent may deal 1 Wound to you. Once this is resolved, you can move to an adjacent zone . - If engaged with multiple opponents, compare your Avoid card towards each opponent’s Initiative. Each opponent you fail to Avoid may deal 1 Wound to you. You might successfully Avoid some while being harmed by others.

375.title: Dash
375.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Pentacles actions › Dash
375.body: Dash to leave your current zone and move two zones away .

376.title: Dodge
376.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Pentacles actions › Dodge
376.body: Dodge to evade your foes’ attacks against you. Play your card facedown. When you’re next targeted by an Attack, Roughhouse, or similar action, add your card’s value to your Initiative. If your new Initiative is greater than the attacker’s action value, the attack misses. Otherwise, the action is resolved as normal. Once your Dodge card is resolved, discard the card.

377.title: Roughhouse
377.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Pentacles actions › Roughhouse
377.body: Roughhouse to attempt some maneuver against your opponent: charge them with your shield, tackle them, rip their helm from their head, place your thumbs in their eyeballs. If your Roughhouse value is greater than your opponent’s Initiative, you choose to either Disarm, Displace, Root, or Trip them (see Effects). They must use the Recover action to get rid of this effect.

378.title: Cups actions
378.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Cups actions
378.body: Fastball specials Aid Another allows adventurers to set up one-two punches and special maneuvers. Sometimes, very large and very powerful monsters will have Initiatives that are above 14, which makes them difficult to hit with normal attacks. In these cases, adventurers will have to use Aid Another to coordinate their Attacks for team-based assaults.

379.title: Aid Another
379.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Cups actions › Aid Another
379.body: Aid Another allows you to work with a companion towards a single objective. Describe what you want to do and how you want to do it. Play your card facedown and set another adventurer’s action as the trigger . When that adventurer performs the appropriate action, reveal your card and add this action’s value to theirs.

380.title: Command
380.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Cups actions › Command
380.body: Order an animal companion (or similar) to perform one of their known commands (see Beast Master). - If the command has no specific target, this card can be any value. For example, fetching an item in its zone. - If the command targets a combatant, compare your action’s value against your opponent’s Initiative. For example, siccing your animal on a foe. Animal companions don’t take actions outside of you Commanding them.

381.title: Pull Item from Pack
381.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Cups actions › Pull Item from Pack
381.body: Pull an item from your backpack and swap it with an item you're holding.

382.title: Use Item
382.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Cups actions › Use Item
382.body: Use an item that you’re holding. - If you’re using it on yourself, this card can be of any value. For example, chugging a potion. - If you’re using it against a combatant, compare your action’s value against your opponent’s Initiative. For example, throwing a bomb. - Throwing a bomb is similar to attacking, and is treated as an Attack in almost every respect, except it is tied to the attribute of Cups.

383.title: Wands actions
383.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Wands actions

384.title: Banter
384.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Wands actions › Banter
384.body: Morale Morale is a way to track how confident and self-assured the GM’s characters are in stressful situations. Adventurers don't need to track a Morale rating—it is only for the GM’s characters. During Challenges, the Banter action is used to affect an enemy’s Disposition (Social Encounters & Disposition). Your Banter value must exceed an enemy’s Morale to successfully change their Disposition. Unlike Initiative, Morale isn’t determined by cards, but by the situation at hand as determined by the GM. When Banter is used, the GM makes an assessment of the enemy’s current confidence to determine their Morale. As the battle progresses, the GM should reassess their characters’ Morale score. Situation Morale --- :---: Perfectly confident: Overwhelming forces, superior positioning, secret escape route 20 Neutral: Neither in an advantageous or disadvantageous position 18 Wary: Bloodied, wasted resources, no obvious profit in fighting 10 Panicking: Forces annihilated, backed into a corner, grievously injured 8 Banter to taunt, intimidate, or frighten your opponent to try and make them run away or surrender. If your Banter value is greater than your opponent’s Morale score (see sidebar), the GM shifts their Disposition by one step in intensity or to an adjacent emotion based on what was said. For example, you might try to intimidate the cannibal pirates into fleeing the battle (moving them to an adjacent Disposition, from anger to fear). Or, you might taunt the heretical knight in an attempt to force them to face your challenge (moving them from distaste to loathing). The GM may apply favor or disfavor to your Banter based on your opponent's likes and dislikes.

385.title: Speak Incantation
385.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Wands actions › Speak Incantation
385.body: Speak Incantation to intone the magic words to cast a spell. You must have training in the talent for the spell you’re casting and hold its component in one hand. If your Speak Incantation value is greater than your opponent’s Initiative , the spell takes effect. If your Speak Incantation value is less than their Initiative, they resist the spell and nothing happens. Ties go to the caster unless the defender has a shield.

386.title: Recover
386.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Wands actions › Recover
386.body: Recover is a catch-all action that encompasses everything from retrieving your dropped weapon to standing up from prone, pulling clinging vines from your legs, or wiping mud out of your eyes. Use this action to remove one Effect you’re currently suffering from. Some Effects are derived from situations that are hard to escape—chains, curses, petrification, etc. The GM will specifically state which Effects you can Recover from and which you cannot.

387.title: Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit)
387.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit)
387.body: Out of cards? If either the players or the GM must draw cards but there are not enough remaining, shuffle the discard pile and continue drawing. This happens more frequently for the GM because they draw bigger hands of cards and the major arcana deck is smaller, but is a relatively rare event either way. With three or four players, the Fool is drawn every few rounds. Miscellaneous actions can be performed using any card, regardless of suit or value.

388.title: Bid Lore
388.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit) › Bid Lore
388.body: Bid lore to try and recall some esoteric detail. As usual, the GM can accept your lore bid and answer it fully, reject the lore bid and establish that you do not know the answer to your question, or ask you to rephrase the bid. Whether or not the GM accepts or rejects the lore bid, you must still spend a card and perform this action to bid lore.

389.title: Guard
389.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit) › Guard
389.body: If you have a shield, you may replace your Initiative with any card from your hand as a miscellaneous action. Your old Initiative is discarded.

390.title: Move
390.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit) › Move
390.body: Move from your zone to an adjacent zone.

391.title: Pull Item from Belt
391.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit) › Pull Item from Belt
391.body: Pull an item from your belt and swap it with an item you're holding.

392.title: Reload Crossbow
392.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit) › Reload Crossbow
392.body: You must reload crossbows after each shot. Use a miscellaneous action to fit another bolt into your crossbow and crank the cranequin.

393.title: Test Fate
393.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit) › Test Fate
393.body: If you’re attempting a feat that seems more complex than a Trivial Action and has an element of chance or danger —like leaping a chasm, holding a door closed, hiding, participating in a ritual, etc.—the GM can call for a test of fate mid-Challenge . Play any card to attempt a test of fate. However, the card played is not counted as part of the test. To resolve the test of fate, draw a new card from the top of the minor arcana deck. The test of fate proceeds per the rules see Tests of Fate: You may spend Resolve for favor. You may push fate. You may bid your motifs.

394.title: Trivial Action
394.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit) › Trivial Action
394.body: This is a catch-all option for anything not covered by the other actions. Opening a door, throwing a lever, picking up an item from the ground, dropping prone—anything that takes only a moment and isn’t contested can be done by playing a card of any value and any suit.

395.title: Vigilance
395.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Challenge Actions › Miscellaneous actions (Any Suit) › Vigilance
395.body: Vigilance is watching for a particular circumstance before you act, waiting for your moment to strike. When you use Vigilance, you declare that you will use an action in response to a specific trigger. Vigilance is a special exception to the category of miscellaneous actions. Instead of using a card of any suit or value, Vigilance uses the same suit as the action you are attempting. Play your card facedown and set another character’s action as the trigger . Describe what you’re doing and how you're doing it. For example, you might wait until your companion gets through the door before you lower the crossbar (a Trivial Action), wait until the sorceress becomes visible before you throw a dagger at her (Attack), or trip the first foe that tries to get past you (Roughhouse). When the trigger occurs, flip this card over to take your designated action.

396.title: GMing the Challenge
396.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge
396.body: GMs follow slightly different rules during Challenges than the players. The basic concepts are the same: the GM acts on their turn based on their Initiative, they play cards from their hand to take actions, they use the same actions (generally) as the players do, etc. However, it’s not practical to draw four cards per opponent and keep track of different hands. The major differences for the GM are explained below.

397.title: 0. Set the scene
397.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge › 0. Set the scene
397.body: Empty rooms and deserted forest corridors make for dull combats. Create cool spaces by filling them full of potential energy: curtains to hide behind, casks of wine to be toppled, runaway carts to dodge, chandeliers to swing from, puddles of oil to be lit aflame. Chapter 10: The Worm Turns has some advice for this.

398.title: 1. Draw Challenge cards
398.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge › 1. Draw Challenge cards
398.body: Mulligans Sometimes, the GM can draw all greater dooms and have no legal cards to play for your Initiative or actions. As a GM, you can elect to mulligan a hand that’s mostly greater dooms . When you mulligan, discard all drawn cards and draw again. Mob rule: Many enemies vs. the adventurers In general, the players are going to take more actions than the GM. By contrast, the GM brings their characters to bear en masse . If you are taking an action for a group, the entire group takes the same action: Moves to a new zone, makes an Attack, etc. Each member of the group can use this action differently: for example, if a pack of five unwolves attacks the guild, each unwolf can Attack a different adventurer. When a group gangs up on a single adventurer, they gain the following advantages: - If 2+ enemies are fighting the same adventurer, they gain favor on their actions. - If 4+ enemies are fighting the same adventurer, they gain favor on their actions and their Attacks deal Piercing damage. Piercing damage cannot be absorbed by armor (Piercing and Critical damage). - If 8+ enemies are fighting the same adventurer, they gain favor on their actions and their Attacks deal Critical damage. Critical damage causes you to mark Injured (Piercing and Critical damage). During step 1, draw 3 Challenge cards from the major arcana deck , and add: - +1 card for each type of enemy - +1 card if the enemies outnumber the adventurers - +1 card if there are twice as many enemies as adventurers - +1 card for each enemy that’s physically larger than a human - +2 cards if there is an elite enemy - +3 cards if there is a dungeon lord (Elite enemies and dungeon lords are defined in Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens, see Dungeon Lord.) Each of these additional cards is cumulative . Check to see which are applicable at the start of each round. Therefore, if the number of enemies decreases, you will draw fewer major arcana cards. For example, if there are twelve imps facing four adventurers, the GM draws 6 cards from the major arcana deck. That includes: 3 cards to start, +1 for the one type of enemy (imps), +1 for having more enemies than adventurers, +1 for having twice as many enemies than adventurers. If, over the course of the Challenge, the adventurers reduce the number of imps to seven, the GM will draw 5 cards at the beginning of the next round: 3 + 1 for having one enemy type (imps) and +1 for having more enemies than adventurers.

399.title: 2. Play Initiative for each significant enemy
399.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge › 2. Play Initiative for each significant enemy
399.body: Play one Initiative card facedown from your hand for each enemy or enemy group. Groups of the same enemy share an Initiative card. For example, a group of six goblins should all act on the same Initiative turn, performing the chosen action against different adventurers. Every enemy that has an Initiative card can have one facedown Challenge Action (Facedown cards). Make it clear which card represents the Initiative for which enemy. For example, you might say “The card on my left, near my beer, is for the goblins. The card on my right is their orc leader, Throm.”

400.title: 3. Enemy actions
400.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge › 3. Enemy actions
400.body: When the Initiative count reaches the number of an enemy’s Initiative, flip it face up and take a turn for that character. Play a Challenge card from your hand to take an action. The number of the major arcana is the card’s value (e.g., Temperance \[XIV] has a value of 14). Because the major arcana spans the values 1–21, they are categorized into two types of doom : lesser dooms and greater dooms . These speak to the sorts of dangers they involve for the adventurers. Major arcana from I-XIV are lesser dooms . Major arcana from XV-XXI are greater dooms . Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens has examples of lesser and greater dooms for each creature.

401.title: Lesser dooms
401.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge › 3. Enemy actions › Lesser dooms
401.body: Lesser doom cards have values of 1–14. These are analogous to the minor arcana (which are also rated from 1–14). Play any lesser doom card to make any Challenge Action (Attack, Dash, Dodge, etc.). Only add the enemy’s attributes to the action’s value on their turn, as normal. You also play a lesser doom card to use an enemy’s lesser doom abilities . These are special powers or tactics unique to that creature.

402.title: Greater dooms
402.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge › 3. Enemy actions › Greater dooms
402.body: Greater doom cards have values of 15–21. Play a greater doom to activate an enemy’s greater doom abilities . These represent a creature’s most potent powers. - If the greater doom only affects the environment or yourself, the greater doom occurs as soon as you play the card. - If the greater doom targets an adventurer, your greater doom is played at the same time as a lesser doom card used as an Attack action. If the Attack is successful, the greater doom effect occurs. - The greater doom card is played regardless of whether the Attack hits or not. For example, a dragon has a greater doom called “Breath of Fire.” To use it on an adventurer, use a lesser doom card (like the Hanged Man \[XII]) to make an Attack action. At the same time, play any greater doom card (like the Star \[XVII]) to activate Breath of Fire. If the Attack is successful, the adventurer is roasted by the dragon’s fiery breath and takes that effect. You cannot typically play a greater doom card to make Challenge Actions like Attack, Dash, Dodge, etc. You can play greater doom cards to use any miscellaneous action except for Vigilance. You can discard a greater doom to gain favor on another Challenge Action. Lastly, some opponents have the ability to use greater doom cards for Challenge Actions. This represents a creature’s overwhelming, extra-human capabilities. For example, a giant may be able to use a greater doom like the Tower \[XVI] as an Attack with a value of 16.

403.title: 4. Minor actions
403.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge › 4. Minor actions
403.body: Cards from the major arcana do not have suits. You can make minor actions with any major arcana card . As usual, use lesser doom cards to use Challenge Actions and greater doom cards to activate greater doom abilities , etc. Each enemy or enemy group can make one minor action on another character’s turn. If one of your characters just had their turn, other characters you control can take a minor action.

404.title: 5. End the round
404.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › GMing the Challenge › 5. End the round
404.body: When every player and each GM character has had a turn (and all minor actions on that turn have been resolved), the round is over. Make a quick assessment of the current state of the Challenge. If it seems clear that the guild is victorious, have the enemies surrender. If the guild is in a bad position, ask them if they want to retreat. If the Challenge continues, facedown actions are left facedown for each enemy and adventurer. Any remaining Challenge cards in your hand are discarded. If the Fool was drawn in this round (regardless of whether or not it was played), shuffle both the minor and the major arcana decks before dealing new cards. As the new round begins, restate where every character is and what’s happening to keep the table on the same page.

405.title: Retreating
405.body: Avoiding the sunk cost fallacy is a virtue . If the adventurers choose to cut their losses and retreat, use this procedure. Begin by determining whether or not the guild can actually run away. - If the monster is particularly fast or has a magical form of locomotion, the monster can probably just automatically hunt the guild down. - For example, a guild scurrying over open fields has no hope of outpacing a flying dragon. - If the monster is slow or awkward or is tied to its lair, it probably won’t pursue the guild in the first place. - For example, a fire elemental bound to a magical hearth has no ability to pursue the guild. The guild merely needs to leave the zone to end this Challenge. - If the enemy’s mobility is about equivalent to the guild’s, or if the guild has the opportunity to shake off pursuit by utilizing difficult terrain, they can attempt to flee using a group test . To successfully escape, the guild needs to make a group test of Pentacles (Tests of Fate). If this attempt takes place during a Challenge, each adventurer needs to play a card as a miscellaneous action . Then, following the rules for group tests, the player with the highest Pentacles and the player with the lowest Pentacles each test fate. If any adventurers do something clever, like pushing over a bookcase as they run past, they give favor to one of these tests. - If the guild gets 2 hits , they get away cleanly. - If the guild only gets 1 hit , the GM introduces a complication. For example, the pursuing creature catches up and grapples the character in the last place of the marching order, or it triggers a trap that makes the obvious escape route dangerous. - If the guild gets 0 or fewer hits , the guild is cornered by the enemy with no clear path of escape.

406.title: Wounds
406.body: Splatbook Note The book is ambiguous about whether only mastered talents can be Wounded. Josh has said on the HMtW Discord that the errata he would add here is a sentence saying: "Only mastered talents can be wounded." When a foe or hazard harms an adventurer, they suffer a Wound. When you take a Wound, choose one of the following options: - Notch a piece of armor - Wound a talent (up to two, max) - Mark the Staggered condition - Mark the Injured condition - Mark the Death’s Door condition You can choose the above options in any order you choose, marking any condition, Wounding any talent, or Notching any worn armor. However, as you take Wounds and mark conditions, fewer of these options are available to you. For example, if you have already Wounded two talents, you cannot Wound any more and must choose another option instead. Similarly, if you are already Injured you must mark Death’s Door the next time you take a Wound. Note that Wounds cannot mark the Stressed Condition. See Conditions for more information on conditions. “Let’s talk of graves, of worms, and epitaphs, Make dust our paper, and with rainy eyes Write sorrow on the bosom of the earth.” – William Shakespeare, Richard II

407.title: Notching armor
407.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Wounds › Notching armor
407.body: Wounds can be absorbed by armor and shields. When you would suffer a Wound, you may instead Notch any armor, helm, or shield you’re wearing. Once a piece of armor has 0 Notches, it is Destroyed. Destroyed items can only be repaired during the City Phase and provide no benefit until they are repaired. The different types of armor you can wear are detailed in the Omphalic Market see Armor.

408.title: Piercing and Critical damage
408.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Wounds › Piercing and Critical damage
408.body: There are two types of attacks that have special rules: Piercing damage and Critical damage. Creatures in Appendix C: Dungeon Denizens occasionally have abilities that deal one or both types of damage.

409.title: Critical
409.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Wounds › Piercing and Critical damage › Critical
409.body: When struck by Critical damage, mark Injured. If already Injured, mark Death’s Door. If you are already at Death’s Door and take Critical damage, you die. Critical damage towards enemies reduces their Health to 0. They are at Death’s Door.

410.title: Piercing
410.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Wounds › Piercing and Critical damage › Piercing
410.body: We fragile things Almost all weapons and enemies deal 1 Wound. A knife can kill you just as dead as a battle axe. Assuming that everybody in the combat is a competent fighter struggling hard against each other, every real weapon in the battle will deal equally-deadly damage. If not everyone is a competent fighter, why are you bothering with a Challenge? Just have the adventurers put down the non-combatant. The GM should use their discretion to frame the impact of different weapon types. For example, some enemies (like skeletons) might be completely immune to sharp weapons like daggers; the adventurers would need something like a mace to bash the skeletons to dislocate their bones. Piercing damage cannot be absorbed by armor, shield or helm. A successful Piercing attack always causes a Wound. Piercing damage toward enemies bypass their Defense and directly reduce their Health (see below).

411.title: Health and Defense: Tracking enemy damage
411.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Wounds › Health and Defense: Tracking enemy damage
411.body: Weapon properties Each type of weapon has a special property that changes the way you use it in combat. See Weapons for a list of special weapon properties. Taking the murder out of murder-hobo If someone is taken down by an Attack, the person striking the finishing blow can elect to spare their life, disabling, knocking out, or subduing their enemy, per the GM’s discretion. As the GM tracks the status of several combatants, they track Wounds in a simplified way. Each enemy has a Health and Defense (HD) rating. Health represents a creature’s ability to absorb damage. For example, a giant can shrug off many small stings from puny humans. A skeleton has no vitals and must be bashed apart before it stops moving. Defense represents a creature’s ability to deflect damage. For example, the plate armor of a death knight or the overlapping scales of a dragon. A creature with 3 Health and 5 Defense would be rendered like so: HD: 3/5 As a GM’s character is Wounded, the GM reduces either its Health or Defense points. - Reduce the enemy’s Defense first. - When there’s no Defense left, reduce the enemy’s Health. - Piercing attacks bypass Defense and always reduce Health. - When an enemy reaches 0 Health, they are at Death’s Door. - Some creatures bypass Death’s Door and are simply destroyed. For example, neither a clockwork statue nor a zombie are living and would simply fall apart.

412.title: Death’s Door
412.breadcrumb: Chapter 7: The Challenge Phase › Death’s Door
412.body: Death is strange in the Underworld. In the depths, powerful magics shackle the souls of the dead to their corpses. If left unattended, these souls become terrifying undead. If healed, however, even fallen heroes may rise and live again. (Trying to understand what magics operate in the Underworld that allow a dead body to be healed is one of the chief reasons that adventurers explore that hateful realm.) When your adventurer takes another Wound after taking the Injured condition, check the Death’s Door condition. While at Death’s Door, you are unconscious and in a quasi-state of death.
